toll.note: No low or high is given: the figures are single-battle claims from late Han-era records, some of them doubted by the scholars cited.

events.says: Seven main Chinese states fought almost continuously after the Zhou kings lost control, ending in 221 BC when Qin completed the conquest of the rest and its ruler took the title First Emperor. Qin's campaigns of 230-221 BC took Han, Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan and Qi.
events.open: Start dates differ (481, 475 or 403 BC). Soldiers were paid by the number of enemy killed and the Han dynasty had reason to paint the earlier age as bloodier, so the large figures are doubted; Sawyer and Lewis argue they may be less inaccurate than thought because states could mobilise a high share of adult males. Excavation at Changping confirms a large battle, but not a burial of that size. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: Wars of Alexander the Great

toll.text: No source read gives a total. Wikipedia's infobox says 'more than 1 million' without breaking it down; its text gives 30,000 people of Tyre sold into slavery after the siege and says Curtius reports the whole population of Massaga slaughtered. Plutarch is cited there for three-quarters of Alexander's army lost on the Gedrosian march. World History Encyclopedia says the people of Tyre 'were slaughtered' and, citing Arrian, that Alexander lost 1,000 men at the Hydaspes.
toll.note: No low or high is given because the infobox figure is not supported by a count in the text read.

events.says: Campaigns of Alexander III of Macedon from 336 to 323 BC in which he led Greek and Macedonian armies across the Persian Empire into Egypt, Central Asia and the Indus valley, and ended the Achaemenid dynasty.
events.open: The ancient authors (Arrian, Diodorus, Curtius, Plutarch) wrote long after the events and give figures for single battles and sieges, not for the whole war. Death of civilians, enslavement and later disease and famine are not separated in any total. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: First Punic War

toll.text: About 100,000 men were lost in the storm that wrecked the Roman fleet returning from Africa in 255 BC, most of them non-Roman Latin allies (Wikipedia, citing Tipps, Miles and Erdkamp); World History Encyclopedia says 'as many as 100,000' drowned. It also gives 12,000 Romans and 800 Carthaginians killed near Tunis that year. The number of adult male Roman citizens fell 17 percent over the war (Bagnall, in Wikipedia). Later claims of 20,000-30,000 Carthaginian dead at Panormus are thought improbable (Goldsworthy).
toll.note: Low is the storm of 255 BC alone, at least; neither source totals the war's dead and Carthaginian, mercenary and civilian deaths are not counted.

events.says: Twenty-three years of war between Rome and Carthage for control of Sicily, fought on land and sea around Sicily and North Africa. It ended with a Roman naval victory at the Aegates Islands in 241 BC, Carthage leaving Sicily and paying an indemnity.
events.open: Polybius is the main source and is largely trusted, but his losses are given for fleets and citizens, not for all the dead. Whether the storm figure counts crews only or also troops is not settled in the sources read. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: Kalinga War

toll.text: Ashoka's own account, as given in Wikipedia: 150,000 deported, 100,000 killed and many more dead of other causes; Wikipedia also lists Hemchandra Raychaudhuri's 250,000 killed. World History Encyclopedia gives 100,000 killed and 150,000 deported without a source and 'thousands of others' dead of disease and famine.
toll.note: Low is the number killed in Ashoka's account; high is Raychaudhuri's 250,000. The 150,000 deported are not counted as dead.

events.says: A war in which the Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga, on the east coast of India in present-day Odisha, around 261 BC. The scale of the killing is said to have led him towards Buddhism.
events.open: The numbers come from Ashoka's own record and a modern historian's reading of it; the battle site and exact date (261 or about 265 BC) are not firmly fixed, and the deaths from disease and famine were not counted. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: Second Punic War

toll.text: Roman dead at two battles: about 50,000 killed at Cannae in 216 BC against 5,700 Carthaginian (World History Encyclopedia) and about 15,000 killed at Lake Trasimene in 217 BC with 10,000 taken (both sources). Wikipedia says at least 67,500 Romans were killed or captured at Cannae and more than 120,000 Roman troops were killed or captured in under three years, and that a Roman army of 25,000 was destroyed by Boii Gauls at Silva Litana.
toll.note: Low is the Roman dead of Cannae and Trasimene only, at least; neither source totals the war, and Carthaginian, allied, Spanish and civilian deaths are not counted.

events.says: War between Rome and Carthage from 218 to 201 BC, begun by Hannibal's march from Spain over the Alps into Italy, and fought also in Spain, Sicily and North Africa. It ended with Scipio's victory at Zama and Carthage losing its overseas empire.
events.open: Polybius and Livy differ on battle figures, and 'killed or captured' sums combine two different outcomes. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: Third Punic War

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox says 'up to 750,000 killed, including civilians' and 50,000 survivors enslaved; modern estimates of Carthage's population run from 90,000 to 800,000. World History Encyclopedia puts the population at the start of the siege at 200,000 and says all inhabitants were enslaved and the city destroyed, with no count of the dead.
toll.note: No low or high is given: the infobox ceiling is not matched by any count in the sources read and the population estimates differ eightfold.

events.says: The last war between Rome and Carthage: a three-year Roman siege ending in 146 BC with the city taken after days of street fighting, burnt, and its people killed or sold.
events.open: Appian, the main narrative, wrote some three centuries later, relying largely on Polybius, and historians have found problems with it; the size of Carthage's population is itself disputed. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: Social War (91-87 BC)

toll.text: World History Encyclopedia says over 100,000 were dead by the end of 89 BC, without naming a source; Wikipedia's infobox gives 50,000 killed on each side, about 100,000 in all.
toll.note: Low is the figure both sources give; neither gives an upper end, so it is a floor.

events.says: A war between Rome and most of its Italian allies, begun in 91 BC at Asculum, fought across central and southern Italy. Rome ended it by granting citizenship (Lex Julia, Lex Plautia Papiria), though fighting lasted to 87 BC.
events.open: Neither source says where the 100,000 comes from, and ancient accounts give few figures. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: Mithridatic Wars

toll.text: The massacre of Romans and Italians in Asia in 88 BC (the Asiatic Vespers): some 80,000 (Wikipedia, citing Hind 1994) against 150,000 (Plutarch, Sulla 24.4, 'in a single day'). Plutarch also has Sulla say Archelaus fled Chaeronea 'with a few survivors out of one hundred and twenty thousand men' (Sulla 22.4). No source read totals the three wars.
toll.note: Low and high are the two figures for the Asiatic Vespers only; deaths in the battles, sieges and sacks over 25 years are not counted.

events.says: Three wars between Rome and King Mithridates VI of Pontus and his allies, fought in Asia Minor and Greece from 88 to 63 BC. They ended with Pontus and Syria Roman provinces and Judea a client state.
events.open: The two figures for the Vespers differ and may not mean the same thing. Battle figures for Chaeronea and Orchomenus come from Sulla's own side and are not verified. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: Third Servile War (Spartacus)

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 41,000 rebels killed (30,000 by Gellius, 6,000 and 5,000 crucified) and about 40,000 for the other column. Ancient figures it cites: Plutarch 12,300 rebels in one fight, Livy 35,000 in one fight and some 60,000 in the last, Appian about 6,000 crucified on the Appian Way. World History Encyclopedia gives about 6,000 killed in Bruttium, 5,000 by Pompey and over 6,000 crucified.
toll.note: Low is Wikipedia's infobox total for rebel dead; no source gives an upper end.

events.says: A revolt of enslaved gladiators and others led by Spartacus from Capua in 73 BC, which grew past 70,000 people and beat several Roman armies before Crassus crushed it in 71 BC.
events.open: Appian, Plutarch and Livy differ on who was killed where, and the infobox does not say which side its second figure counts. Appian is unsure whether up to 4,000 Roman legionaries were executed by decimation after a defeat. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: Gallic Wars

toll.text: Plutarch (Caesar 15.4): 'one million in hand to hand fighting' and as many more prisoners, from three million fought (Wikipedia gives the same figure for Plutarch and Appian). Caesar claims 430,000 Germani killed after the Rhine crossing and 40,000 slain at Avaricum. Wikipedia notes that Henige considers all contemporary numbers not credible, and that historians put the Helvetii at 20,000-50,000 against the 368,000 in Caesar's census.
toll.note: No low or high is given: every figure is Caesar's or a later writer's and the one scholar cited rejects them all.

events.says: Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul from 58 to 50 BC, fought against the Helvetii, Belgic and other Gallic peoples and Germanic groups, and ending with the surrender of Vercingetorix at Alesia in 52 BC and the pacification that followed.
events.open: The only detailed account is Caesar's own, written for a Roman audience; Plutarch's totals are round numbers. Some scholars describe the campaigns as genocide, a judgement not made by the sources read here. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: Liberators' civil war

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives a total of 40,000 dead for the war, cited to a World History Encyclopedia article that was not read; it gives army strengths of 53,000-108,000 (Triumvirs) and 60,000-105,000 (Liberators) after Goldsworthy. The EBSCO overview read gives no casualty figures.
toll.note: No low or high is given: only one unverified total exists.

events.says: A war from 43 to 42 BC between the Second Triumvirate (Antony, Octavian, Lepidus) and Caesar's assassins Brutus and Cassius, decided in two battles at Philippi in Macedonia in October 42 BC, after which both Liberators killed themselves.
events.open: Ancient sources give few casualty numbers and the 40,000 total has not been traced to one. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: Antony's Parthian campaign (Atropatene)

toll.text: Plutarch (Antony 50): on review 'twenty thousand of the infantry and four thousand of the cavalry had perished', more than half of them from disease rather than at enemy hands. Wikipedia's infobox gives about 32,000 men lost on the Roman side, citing the Encyclopaedia Iranica (not read), while its text says a survey suggested 24,000. Parthian losses are given as unknown but minimal.
toll.note: Low is Plutarch's 24,000; high is the infobox figure of about 32,000, probably including camp followers.

events.says: Mark Antony's invasion in 36 BC of Media Atropatene (north-west Iran, Azerbaijan), where he besieged Phraaspa, lost his siege train, and retreated through Armenia in winter, losing a large part of his army.
events.open: The 32,000 has not been traced to an ancient author, and the sources read do not say whether it counts non-combatants. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: Roman conquest of Britain

toll.text: Tacitus (Annals 14.33) says close upon 70,000 Roman citizens and allies fell at Camulodunum, Verulamium and London in Boudica's revolt, and (14.37) little less than 80,000 Britons and about 400 Romans in the final battle; Cassius Dio (62.1) says 80,000 Romans and allies perished. The Loeb editor calls the first 'probably valueless' and the two 'equally incredible'. Wikipedia's infobox lists 30,000-40,000 killed in the Boudican revolt (Gillespie 2018) and, in a second unlabeled entry, 100,000-250,000 (Crane 2016; Copeland 2014).
toll.note: Low is the modern figure for Boudica's revolt alone; high is the largest modern infobox entry. The ancient 70,000 and 80,000 sit inside this range and are not accepted by the editor cited.

events.says: The Roman invasion under Claudius in AD 43 and the advance north over the next four decades, through campaigns against the Catuvellauni, Silures, Ordovices and Brigantes, the revolt of Boudica in AD 60-61, and Agricola's campaigns to Mons Graupius in AD 83 or 84.
events.open: The two ancient accounts (Tacitus and Dio) differ on causes and numbers, and the modern figures disagree about what the second infobox entry counts. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

sources.title: Roman History, Book 62 (Cassius Dio, Loeb translation)

events.name: Jewish-Roman wars

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 350,000-1,400,000 for the three wars together. Josephus (War 6.420-421): about 1,100,000 perished in the siege of Jerusalem in AD 70 and 97,000 were taken captive. Cassius Dio (68.32): 220,000 perished in Cyrene and 240,000 in Cyprus in the revolt of AD 115-117 (Wikipedia's infobox reads 200,000 for Cyrenaica); Dio (69.14): 580,000 slain in raids and battles in Judaea under Hadrian, with those lost to famine, disease and fire 'past finding out'.
toll.note: Low and high are Wikipedia's infobox range for all three wars; the single ancient figures sit inside it and several are doubted.

events.says: Three Jewish revolts against Roman rule: the First Jewish-Roman War of AD 66 to 73 or 74, ending with the destruction of Jerusalem; the diaspora revolt of AD 115-117 (the Kitos War) in Cyrenaica, Egypt, Cyprus and Mesopotamia; and the Bar Kokhba revolt of AD 132-135 in Judaea.
events.open: Josephus wrote under Flavian patronage and Dio a century after the Bar Kokhba revolt; Wikipedia says the Kitos War figures are the least certain and the Cyrenaica figure likely exaggerated. Applebaum estimated two-thirds of Judaea's Jews died in the last revolt, while Cotton and Raviv with Ben David defend Dio's figures as based on Roman records. The Kitos War has its own Wikipedia article but is counted here, not as a separate entry. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

sources.title: Wars of the Jews, 6.420-421 (Josephus, Whiston translation)
Roman History, Book 68 (Cassius Dio, Loeb translation)
Roman History, Book 69 (Cassius Dio, Loeb translation)

events.name: Yellow Turban Rebellion

toll.text: Figures from the Hou Hanshu as reported by Wikipedia: 30,000 rebels killed with Zhang Liang plus about 50,000 drowned fleeing across a river (late 184); more than 7,000 killed at Cangting, about 10,000 at Wancheng and over 10,000 in Sun Xia's pursuit; over 300,000 rebels and more than a million family members surrendered to Cao Cao in 192. Wikipedia cites Michaud (1958) for rebel deaths in the hundreds of thousands but notes that no statistical evidence confirms the scale. The EBSCO overview gives no figures.
toll.note: Low is the two figures for the defeat of Zhang Liang in 184, at least; no source totals the rebellion.

events.says: A religious and peasant uprising against the Eastern Han from 184, led by Zhang Jue and his brothers, which spread across north China and was put down by Han armies by the end of 184 though bands survived to 205. It left the Han court dependent on regional warlords.
events.open: The record is the Hou Hanshu, compiled long after, and its numbers are not checked by a count. Survivors who surrendered are not deaths. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

events.name: Roman invasion of Caledonia (208-211)

toll.text: Cassius Dio (77.13.2) says 'a full fifty thousand died' during Septimius Severus' campaign in Caledonia, from ambush, the terrain and Romans killed by their own men to avoid capture (Wikipedia's infobox: 50,000 Roman dead, mostly from disease and exhaustion). Caledonian losses are unknown.
toll.note: No low or high is given: there is a single ancient figure and no second source to set against it.

events.says: A campaign led by the emperor Septimius Severus and his son Caracalla into northern Britain from AD 208. Severus died at York in February 211, Caracalla ended the war, and Roman forces withdrew to Hadrian's Wall.
events.open: The 50,000 comes from one writer, Dio, a generation later, and what it counts is not clear from the sources read. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any surviving register.

sources.title: Roman History, Book 77 (Cassius Dio, Loeb translation)

events.name: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy

toll.text: The Anonymus Valesianus, a fourth-century Latin chronicle, gives 20,000 of Licinius' foot soldiers killed at Cibalae (316) and 25,000 soldiers killed at Chrysopolis (18 September 324). The later historian Zosimus gives 34,000 dead on Licinius' side at Adrianople (3 July 324) and 100,000 at Chrysopolis; modern historians treat both as exaggerated and consider the Anonymus Valesianus figure for Chrysopolis the more plausible (Wikipedia, citing Grant and Nicasie 2023). No ancient source gives a total for the whole series of wars.
toll.note: Low is the two Anonymus Valesianus battle figures added together (20,000 + 25,000), one side's soldiers only; it leaves out the other battles (Milvian Bridge 312, Tzirallum 313, Mardia 317, Adrianople) and all civilian deaths. There is no upper bound.

events.says: A series of wars between rival Roman emperors after the Tetrarchy broke down in 306. Constantine I defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge in 312 and, with Licinius, Maximinus Daza in 313; he then defeated Licinius at Cibalae, Mardia, Adrianople and Chrysopolis, and ruled the empire alone from 324. Licinius was executed in 325.
events.open: Ancient battle figures are round numbers from chroniclers and are disputed: Zosimus's 34,000 and 100,000 are considered exaggerated, and the Wikipedia infobox's 'approx. 50,000+ at Adrianople and Chrysopolis combined' carries no source. No ancient source counts the dead of the war as a whole. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Excerpta Valesiana, first part (Anonymus Valesianus), sections 16 and 27

events.name: Goguryeo-Sui War

toll.text: The Zizhi Tongjian and the Korean Samguk Sagi say that of the 305,000 Sui troops who crossed the Liao River in 612, only 2,700 returned, a loss of about 302,300 (Wikipedia infobox). The World History Encyclopedia gives it as 'according to legend' that of a 300,000-strong Sui army only 2,700 returned, and Necrometrics lists the same 300,000 and 2,700 from the chronicler James Trager. No source gives Goguryeo's losses.
toll.note: Both ends are the same traditional figure for the Sui army's losses in the 612 campaign alone. It counts soldiers who did not come back, not a count of the dead, and it leaves out the other three invasions.

events.says: Four invasions of the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo by the Chinese Sui dynasty, in 598, 612, 613 and 614. Goguryeo held out, the large 612 army was defeated at the Salsu River, and the failed campaigns fed the revolts that brought down the Sui in 618.
events.open: Wikipedia notes that Tang historians may have exaggerated the numbers: the Book of Sui's 1,133,800 nominal combat troops in 612 compare with a modern estimate of 670,000 (Graff 2001). The 305,000 and 2,700 are traditional. The campaigns overlap the Sui-Tang transition entry from 613, so the two tolls are not additive. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Selected Death Tolls for Wars, Massacres and Atrocities Before the 20th Century (Twentieth Century Atlas, Historical Body Count)

events.name: Byzantine-Sasanian War of 602-628

toll.text: No source gives a count of the dead for the whole war. Wikipedia's infobox lists 200,000+ dead on each side without an attributable source. For single events it reports a total death count of 20,000 near Emesa in 613 (both sides), 57,000 or 66,500 people killed at Jerusalem in 614 by ancient sources with 35,000 more deported, and an alleged 70,000 Thracian peasants captured and killed in 623. The World History Encyclopedia articles on Khosrow II and Heraclius give no casualty totals.
toll.note: No range is set because every figure above is a single-event claim by an ancient writer or an unsourced infobox entry.

events.says: A war between the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) and Sasanian Persian empires that began in 602 after the murder of Emperor Maurice. Persian armies took Syria, Jerusalem (614) and Egypt (by 618); the Byzantine counter-offensive under Heraclius from 622, the defeat of the Persian army at Nineveh in 627 and the fall of Khosrow II led to a peace in 628 that restored the earlier borders.
events.open: The start is given as 602 or 603 depending on the source, and the Jerusalem figures are ancient claims (57,000 or 66,500) that no source checks. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

events.name: Transition from Sui to Tang

toll.text: No source gives a count of the dead. Wikipedia's infobox says 'at least 1 million deaths' with no source, and its text says about 300,000 men were lost in the first Goguryeo campaign of 612. The Necrometrics list quotes a census of 46 million in 606 and 12 million in 627 but marks the entry with a question mark and states no loss.
toll.note: No agreed figure. A fall in registered population is not a count of deaths.

events.says: Rebellions and civil war across China from about 613, after the failed Sui campaigns against Goguryeo. Emperor Yang was assassinated, Li Yuan founded the Tang dynasty, and by 628 his son Li Shimin had defeated the rival regimes and united most of China under the Tang.
events.open: The death toll is unquantified. The 300,000 lost in 612 belongs to the Goguryeo-Sui War entry and is not part of any total here. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Selected Death Tolls for Wars, Massacres and Atrocities Before the 20th Century (Twentieth Century Atlas, Historical Body Count)

events.name: Reconquista

toll.text: No source reached gives a total for the Reconquista. The World History Encyclopedia article gives no casualty figures. The Wikipedia article gives population movements only: about three million Muslims emigrated or were driven out of Spain between 1492 and 1610, and some 200,000 Jews were expelled in 1492. The Necrometrics list has one battle figure, 400,000 Moors killed at Rio Salado in 1341 (Contamine, War in the Middle Ages, citing Hillgarth).
toll.note: No agreed figure. The Rio Salado number is a single battle claim and the expulsions are not deaths.

events.says: The campaigns of the Christian kingdoms of the Iberian peninsula against the Muslim-ruled territories of al-Andalus, traditionally dated from the battle of Covadonga (c. 718 or 722) to the fall of Granada on 2 January 1492.
events.open: A long series of campaigns, not one war, so no total exists and the start date is traditional (718 or 722). The final war, 1482-1492, has its own Granada War entry and is not additive here. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Selected Death Tolls for Wars, Massacres and Atrocities Before the 20th Century (Twentieth Century Atlas, Historical Body Count)

events.name: Fatimid invasion of Egypt (914-915)

toll.text: Wikipedia, citing Yaacov Lev (Arabica 35, 1988), reports 7,000 Fatimid troops killed and 7,000 taken prisoner in the first round, about 10,000 of the Fatimid general Habasa's men killed in the second, 10,000 to 20,000 Egyptian conscripts dead, and an estimate by Imad al-Din of Egyptians killed 'as high as 50,000'. Its infobox gives 50,000 killed on the Abbasid-Egyptian side and over 24,000 killed or taken prisoner on the Fatimid side.
toll.note: High is the upper estimate for the Egyptian side. There is no low bound because the figures are given per side and per round, not as a total.

events.says: An attempt by the Fatimid caliphate of Ifriqiya, led by the heir al-Qa'im and the general Habasa, to take Egypt from the Abbasids between January 914 and May 915. The Fatimids took Alexandria and the Fayyum but were beaten at Giza on 8 January 915 by Abbasid reinforcements under Mu'nis and withdrew to Ifriqiya.
events.open: The casualty numbers are medieval chronicle estimates passed on by one modern study and are not reconciled between sides. The Ismaili heritage page used gives no figures. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: The Fatimid invasion of Egypt in 914 (article on the Fatimid expedition under Hubasa and al-Qaim)
sources.publisher: Heritage Society, First Ismaili Electronic Library and Database (F.I.E.L.D.)

events.name: Third conflict in the Goryeo-Khitan War
events.wiki: Third conflict in the Goryeo–Khitan War

toll.text: Wikipedia gives over 90,000 Khitan (Liao) dead and Goryeo losses unknown, citing Seth 2006. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture puts the invading Khitan army at 100,000 of whom only several thousand returned, and records that the Chinese Xu Zizhi Tongjian Changbian gives about 200,000 Khitan killed.
toll.note: Both ends count Khitan losses only. The 200,000 is a Chinese chronicle figure that is larger than the 100,000 army size given in the Korean entry, so the two cannot both be exact.

events.says: The third Khitan (Liao) invasion of the Korean kingdom of Goryeo, which crossed the Yalu in December 1018. The army, under Xiao Baiya, was defeated by Goryeo forces under Gang Gam-chan at the battle of Gwiju (Kuju) in 1019 and withdrew; Goryeo resumed tribute in 1020 and the Khitan recognised its king in 1022.
events.open: Army sizes differ (100,000 Khitan against 208,000 Goryeo in the Korean entry) and the Goryeo dead are unknown. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Third conflict in the Goryeo–Khitan War (Wikipedia)
구주대첩 (Battle of Kuju), Encyclopedia of Korean Culture

events.name: Song-Dai Viet war

toll.text: The Song Shi (History of Song), chapter 446, says the invaders took Qin and Lian prefectures and that after a 42-day siege of Yongzhou they killed more than 50,000 residents. Wikipedia lists 100,000 killed in Guangxi (the 14th-century Viet sử lược), as many as 58,000 at Yongzhou (Pease 2021), 200,000 Song deaths (the 12th-century Xu Zizhi Tongjian Changbian) and 150,000 (the 13th-century Yuhai), and a modern estimate of at least 250,000 to 400,000 troops and civilians (Chapuis 1995, Kiernan 2019).
toll.note: Low is the Yongzhou killing alone in the Song Shi, a floor for one city. High is the top of the modern estimate, which counts both sides, the Viet invasion of Guangxi and the Song counter-invasion, soldiers and civilians. Kiernan (2019) says Song forces lost 50 to 60 percent before retreating, half of them to disease.

events.says: A war between the Ly dynasty of Dai Viet and Song China. Viet forces raided Guangxi and took Yongzhou in 1075-76; a Song army counter-invaded; both sides withdrew and captured territory and prisoners were exchanged in 1082. Wikipedia gives the result as indecisive.
events.open: Every figure is a medieval chronicle claim or a modern estimate built on them, and they differ by a factor of eight. Deaths from disease in the Song army are mixed with battle deaths. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Song Shi (History of Song), chapter 446, biography of Su Jian
sources.publisher: Song Shi (compiled by Tuotuo and others), text on Chinese Wikisource

events.name: The Crusades

toll.text: Writers have put total deaths at 1 million (Hittell 1874; Wertham 1966), 2 million (Mackay 1841, Europeans), 3 million (Garrison 1922; Matthew White 2012), 5 million (Elson 1921) and 9 million (Robertson 1902), as compiled by the historian Andrew Holt. Necrometrics uses a median of 3 million and notes that no scholar has published a toll under 1 million or over 9 million.
toll.note: Both ends are older or popular estimates for all the Crusades together; none is a count. Holt writes that modern historians tend not to make or trust such totals.

events.says: A series of religious wars launched from Latin Christendom, chiefly against Muslim-ruled lands in the Near East, from the First Crusade in 1095 to the fall of Acre to the Mamluks in 1291.
events.open: No total is agreed and the spread from 1 to 9 million is itself the finding. Necrometrics also lists single events: up to 8,000 Jews killed in the Rhineland in 1096 (Davies) and, from Gibbon, 70,000 Muslims at Jerusalem in 1099. Whether a series of separate expeditions is one war is a choice; the Third Crusade has its own entry and is not additive here. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Death Estimates for the Crusades (Andrew Holt, 30 January 2019)
Selected Death Tolls for Wars, Massacres and Atrocities Before the 20th Century (Twentieth Century Atlas, Historical Body Count)

events.name: Fang La rebellion

toll.text: The Necrometrics list gives 2 million for the Fang La rebellion of 1120-22, citing Samuel Lieu (Manichaeism in Central Asia and China, p. 135), who cites a Chinese source, the Qingxi kou gui. Wikipedia gives the same 2 million for the total casualties of massacres by the rebels and the Song army, with no citation.
toll.note: A single claim, so low and high are the same figure. It counts massacres by both sides, not combat deaths alone.

events.says: A rebellion in south-eastern China against the Song dynasty led by Fang La, which began in 1120. A Song army under Wang Yuan was sent in 1121; Fang La was captured, taken to Kaifeng and executed.
events.open: No second figure was found and the original Chinese source is not given in Wikipedia. Whether the number is a count or a round estimate is not stated. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Selected Death Tolls for Wars, Massacres and Atrocities Before the 20th Century (Twentieth Century Atlas, Historical Body Count)

events.name: Third Crusade

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 50,000+ Frankish losses as a Muslim estimate (Gibb 1973) and says crusader casualties were greater than Muslim ones. The Necrometrics list, from Trager, has the crusader army shrinking from 100,000 to 5,000 through famine, plague and desertion, and from Gibbon, 3,000 Muslim prisoners executed by Richard. The World History Encyclopedia gives 2,500 prisoners ordered executed (main text) or over 2,000 (timeline) and no siege losses.
toll.note: Low is the Muslim estimate of Frankish losses, so at least 50,000; the army-shrinkage figure counts deserters and survivors, not only dead. There is no upper bound.

events.says: A crusade led by Richard I of England and Philip II of France, with Frederick Barbarossa until he drowned in 1190, to recover Jerusalem after Saladin's conquests of 1187. Acre fell in July 1191 after a siege begun in August 1189; Jerusalem was not retaken and the Treaty of Jaffa of 2 September 1192 let unarmed Christian pilgrims visit it.
events.open: The Frankish figure is a Muslim-side estimate. The execution numbers at Acre differ between sources. This war is part of the Crusades entry and its dead are not additive to that total. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Selected Death Tolls for Wars, Massacres and Atrocities Before the 20th Century (Twentieth Century Atlas, Historical Body Count)

events.name: Mongol conquests

toll.text: Necrometrics lists: 11.5 million (Humphrey Clarke), 20 million for Genghis Khan (Godbey 1974), 29.9 million (R. J. Rummel, 13th to 15th centuries), about 30 million (its own median), 37.75 million fewer people across Eurasia, rounded to 40 million (Matthew White, from McEvedy 1978), and over 60 million in China alone dying or never replaced (Alan McFarlane). Chinese census figures are read as a fall from about 100 million to 70 million (Morgan), from 102 million (1125) to 55 million (1250) (Komarova and Korotayev), or 60 million to 10 million (Man).
toll.note: Low is Clarke's 11.5 million; high is McFarlane's figure for China alone. Most are falls in population, which include famine, disease and people never born, not counts of killed.

events.says: The expansion of the Mongol Empire from the unification of the Mongol tribes in 1206 across Asia and into Eastern Europe, including the conquest of Khwarazm, northern China, Rus' cities (1237-40) and Baghdad (1258), through to the end of Mongol rule in China in 1368.
events.open: The totals depend on population censuses and chronicle claims: Jack Weatherford calls the high numbers 'preposterous' (cited by Necrometrics), and the plague that spread in the same period overlaps the decline. The invasions of Japan and Vietnam have their own entries. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Selected Death Tolls for Wars, Massacres and Atrocities Before the 20th Century (Twentieth Century Atlas, Historical Body Count)

events.name: Mongol invasions of Vietnam

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 90,000 Yuan killed or drowned in 1287-88 (Lo 2012), 10,000 Tran army dead in two battles in January 1258 (the chronicler Le Tac), and 50,000 captured in 1285 (Man 2012). Tran Trong Kim's Viet Nam su luoc (1920) says that in the retreat after Bach Dang in 1288 five or six parts in ten of the Yuan army were lost, and that over 400 warships were taken.
toll.note: Low is the 1288 figure alone; high adds the 1258 Viet dead. The 50,000 captured in 1285 are not counted as dead.

events.says: Three Yuan (Mongol) invasions of Dai Viet in 1258, 1285 and 1287-88, with campaigns against Champa in 1282-84. The Yuan forces withdrew each time, and Dai Viet and Champa accepted tributary status.
events.open: Few counts of the Viet dead exist beyond 1258. Tran Trong Kim gives a share of the army lost, not a number. This war is part of the Mongol conquests; its dead are not additive to that total. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Viet Nam su luoc, book I, part III, chapter VIII: the Mongol invaders, 1284-1288 (Tran Trong Kim, 1920)
sources.publisher: Tran Trong Kim, text on Vietnamese Wikisource

events.name: Mongol invasions of Japan

toll.text: Wikipedia, citing Turnbull (2010), gives 13,500 of the 30,000-strong 1274 force not returning and over 120,000 casualties among about 140,000 men in 1281, including 7,592 of 26,989 Koreans; Chinese and Mongol sources indicate a casualty rate of 60 to 90 percent. The World History Encyclopedia says half to two-thirds of the 1281 force was killed. Gibbon, via Necrometrics, gives 100,000 lost. Conlan argues the 140,000 was exaggerated about tenfold, to about 14,000, and Rossabi proposes 70,000.
toll.note: Low is the 1274 figure alone; high is 1274 plus the 1281 'over 120,000'. Both count invaders who did not return, not only dead. Japanese losses are mostly not given (a third of the defenders at Hakata died in 1274, per Delgado).

events.says: Two attempts by the Yuan dynasty under Kublai Khan, with Korean and Chinese contingents, to invade Japan: in November 1274 at Hakata Bay and in the summer of 1281, when a typhoon in August destroyed much of the fleet. Both failed.
events.open: The size of the 1281 force is disputed by an order of magnitude, so the loss is too. If Conlan's estimate is right the total would fall below the 20,000 that qualifies a war for this list. This war is part of the Mongol conquests and its dead are not additive to that total. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Selected Death Tolls for Wars, Massacres and Atrocities Before the 20th Century (Twentieth Century Atlas, Historical Body Count)

events.name: Hundred Years' War

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives about 185,250 French and English soldiers killed in combat and about 556,000 total military deaths. Necrometrics lists the same battlefield figure (Sorokin) and, from historians' population falls in France (Pregill, Baumgartner, Heller), attributes between 0 and 3.3 million deaths to the war, with a headline of 3 million, while noting that the Black Death falls in the same years.
toll.note: Low is soldiers killed in combat; high is all military deaths including disease. Population-based figures up to about 3 million count civilians and are mixed with the plague, so they are not used as a bound.

events.says: A series of wars between the kingdoms of England and France over the French throne and English lands in France, 1337 to 1453. England won at Crecy, Poitiers and Agincourt; France won at Patay, Formigny and Castillon, the last battle, after which England held only Calais in France.
events.open: No source separates civilian war deaths from plague, famine and disease. The World History Encyclopedia gives no casualty figures. Nobles killed in battle are named in the chronicles; no total of ordinary soldiers is. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Selected Death Tolls for Wars, Massacres and Atrocities Before the 20th Century (Twentieth Century Atlas, Historical Body Count)

events.name: Bahmani-Vijayanagara War of 1362-1367

toll.text: Wikipedia, citing Sarma and Allan (1964), gives 400,000 to half a million civilians killed in the massacre at Vijayanagar in 1366-67, including ten thousand Brahmins. The Necrometrics list quotes Robert Sewell (A Forgotten Empire) and Sarina Singh, citing the chronicler Firishta, for 500,000 Hindus killed, mostly by massacre, in the 1366 campaign. At Mudgal, Firishta gives 70,000 killed in the Vijayanagar camp and Vijayanagar sources 90,000, besides the 8,000-man garrison.
toll.note: Both ends count civilians killed by the Bahmani army in the 1366-67 campaign. The Mudgal and Kauthal battle deaths (70,000 to 90,000 at Mudgal) are separate and not included.

events.says: A war between the Bahmani Sultanate under Muhammad Shah I and the Vijayanagara empire under Bukka I . The Bahmanis won at Kauthal on 20 July 1366 and besieged Vijayanagar; Golconda was annexed and Warangal became a Bahmani vassal.
events.open: These are chronicle figures with no census behind them. Wikipedia dates the siege of Vijayanagar to both 1366 and 1367, and gives army sizes at Mudgal from 100,000 to 900,000 infantry. This entry covers the 1362-1367 war only; later Bahmani-Vijayanagara wars to 1443 are not included. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Selected Death Tolls for Wars, Massacres and Atrocities Before the 20th Century (Twentieth Century Atlas, Historical Body Count)

events.name: Luchuan-Pingmian campaigns

toll.text: Jon Fernquest (SOAS Bulletin of Burma Research 4.2, 2006), from the Ming Shilu, writes that the Ming attack on Si Renfa's stronghold on Mulong mountain in the second campaign (1441-42) ended in a Tai defeat with fifty thousand dead, and that fighting on the Irrawaddy in 1449 left casualties and captives 'in the hundreds'. Wikipedia's infobox gives 55,000+ for the Shan side and Ming losses unknown.
toll.note: Low is the Mulong mountain figure alone, so at least 50,000. Ming and Burmese dead are not given, and the 30,000 dead of the earlier Ming-Mong Mao battle of 1388 is not counted.

events.says: Ming punitive expeditions from Yunnan between 1436 and 1449 against Si Renfa, ruler of the Shan (Tai) state of Mong Mao, with troops from Ava and Hsenwi. The Ming broke the state's armies and dispersed its manpower, but its rulers evaded capture for years.
events.open: Figures come from the Ming Shilu, the Ming court's record, and are not independently checked. The number of Ming soldiers lost to disease and supply failure is not given. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Crucible of War: Burma and the Ming in the Tai Frontier Zone (1382-1454), Jon Fernquest
sources.publisher: SOAS Bulletin of Burma Research (via Online Burma/Myanmar Library)

events.name: Wars of the Roses

toll.text: Necrometrics lists 105,000 (Clodfelter, which is also the Wikipedia infobox figure, 'killed in combat') and 100,000 (Thomas Craig, a 16th-century writer, via Charles Carlton). For Towton alone, the heralds counted 28,000 dead in 1461 and Gregory's Chronicle gives 35,000.
toll.note: The only whole-war totals found, both for deaths in fighting. The Towton figures are one battle and are disputed.

events.says: A series of civil wars in England between the houses of Lancaster and York, from the first battle of St Albans on 22 May 1455 to the Yorkist defeat at Stoke Field in June 1487. Edward IV won the crown at Towton in 1461 and Henry Tudor at Bosworth in 1485.
events.open: Terence Wise (1983) argues Tudor historians exaggerated the toll. Dr Simon Payling of the History of Parliament notes that only about 20 lords and MPs are known to have died at Towton, which is hard to reconcile with 28,000 dead. Leading figures killed are named in the sources; no register of the ordinary dead is known. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

sources.title: Selected Death Tolls for Wars, Massacres and Atrocities Before the 20th Century (Twentieth Century Atlas, Historical Body Count)
Was the battle of Towton bloody? (History of Parliament blog, 29 March 2020)

events.name: Granada War

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 100,000 dead or enslaved on the Granadan side, including civilians, citing Henry Kamen (Spain, 1469-1714, 3rd ed. 2005, pp. 37-38), and Castilian and Aragonese losses unknown. It reports that after the fall of Malaga in 1487 Ferdinand punished almost all the inhabitants with slavery, without a number.
toll.note: High counts dead and enslaved together, so the number of dead alone is smaller. There is no low bound.

events.says: The final war of the Reconquista, in which Castile and Aragon under Isabella I and Ferdinand II conquered the Emirate of Granada, ending when Muhammad XI surrendered Granada on 2 January 1492.
events.open: Kamen's book was not read for this entry; the figure is taken as Wikipedia reports it. The World History Encyclopedia confirms the 1492 end but gives no casualty figures. The war is the last phase of the Reconquista entry and not additive to it. No register of this war's dead by name is known to the Atlas, so the records list is left empty.

events.name: New People's Army rebellion

toll.text: Official figures reported by AFP in 2019 put deaths in the insurgency at up to 40,000. A 2013 study by Holden in the Journal of Geography and Geology, cited by Wikipedia, counts more than 43,000 insurgency-related deaths from 1969 to 2008.
toll.note: Both figures count all sides together, combatants and civilians. The first is described by AFP as rarely revised; the second stops at 2008, so deaths since then are not in it.

events.says: A Maoist insurgency begun in March 1969 by the Communist Party of the Philippines and its armed wing, the New People's Army, against the Philippine government. It was still listed as ongoing in 2025, with active rebels reported to have fallen to just over 1,000 by 2024.
events.open: No agency publishes a full-conflict count: the Wikipedia infobox gives 40,000 and its lead gives 43,000 without reconciling them, and Army and government tallies of rebel, soldier and civilian deaths are counted on different dates. The Plaza Miranda bombing of 1971 (nine killed) is attributed to different parties by different historians.

sources.title: Philippine communist rebels: AFP report on the Maoist insurgency

events.name: Dirty War (Argentina)

toll.text: The state's own Registro Unificado de Victimas del Terrorismo de Estado (RUVTE, 2015) counts 8,631 victims of state terrorism in 1966-1983: 7,018 disappeared and 1,613 killed. The CONADEP commission counted 8,961 disappeared. Human-rights organisations have long put the disappeared at 30,000, and Wikipedia gives 13,000 to 30,000 killed or disappeared.
toll.note: Low is the RUVTE total (it covers 1966 to 1983, so includes victims before 1974); high is the figure used by human-rights groups, which no official count reaches.

events.says: Repression of left-wing guerrillas and wider opposition in Argentina by the state and the Triple A death squad from 1974, and by the military juntas after the March 1976 coup, ending with the return of civilian rule in December 1983. Most victims were abducted, held in secret detention centres and not returned.
events.open: The total is contested. Every official register is far below 30,000, and the registers differ in period and in what they count. Many cases were never reported. The registry's own page covers 28 June 1966 to 10 December 1983. Whether a campaign of state terror counts as a war is a matter of definition; the Dirty War is borderline for a 20,000 threshold since the documented count is under 10,000.

sources.title: El numero de 30.000 desaparecidos esta lejos de las victimas registradas por la CONADEP
Area de Investigacion RUVTE-ILID
sources.publisher: Archivo Nacional de la Memoria, Presidencia de la Nacion (Argentina)

events.name: Ethiopian Civil War

toll.text: Wikipedia gives about 400,000 to 579,000 killed in fighting and repression (Sanchez, Washington Post 1991; Obermeyer, Murray and Gakidou, BMJ 2008) and at least 1.4 million dead in total including about 1 million from famine (Woldemariam and Woldgabreal 2023; De Waal 1991). Human Rights Watch (1991, quoted in a 1999 briefing) says at least half a million civilians were killed through the Derg's actions.
toll.note: Low is the lower end of violent deaths; high is the total including famine. The famine deaths are given as 400,000-590,000 (De Waal) in one place and about 1 to 1.2 million in another within the same compilation.

events.says: A civil war in Ethiopia from 1974, when the Derg military committee deposed the emperor, to 1991, when the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front and Eritrean forces took power. It included the Red Terror of 1976-1978, the Ogaden War of 1977-78, insurgencies in Eritrea, Tigray and Oromia, and the 1983-85 famine.
events.open: The Red Terror toll ranges from 10,000 or 20,000 to 30,000 or far higher in different accounts. The famine's death toll and how much of it the war and government policy caused are disputed. Combat deaths, repression and famine overlap, so totals are not simply additive. The Ogaden War is also listed separately.

sources.title: Ethiopian Dictator Mengistu Haile Mariam (background briefing, 24 November 1999)

events.name: Lebanese Civil War

toll.text: The International Center for Transitional Justice says over 100,000 civilians were killed in 1975-1990 and about 17,000 people disappeared. Wikipedia gives 120,000 to 150,000 killed and nearly one million displaced.
toll.note: Low is ICTJ's civilian-only count; high is the upper end of the total in Wikipedia. There is no official comprehensive list of the dead or the missing.

events.says: A civil war in Lebanon from 1975 to 1990 between Christian, Muslim, Druze and Palestinian militias and the state, with intervention by Syria, Israel and others. It ended with the 1989 Taif Agreement and the disarming of most militias.
events.open: Death counts differ by source and by what they include (civilians only or all). A 1991 general amnesty law largely prevented prosecutions; Law 105 on the Missing and Forcibly Disappeared Persons (2018) and a national commission appointed in 2020 aim to account for the missing.

events.name: Third Indochina War

toll.text: No source gives one total. Wikipedia's infobox lists 105,627 Vietnamese military dead for 1975-1991 (a Vietnamese government document), more than 100,000 Khmer Rouge dead for 1978-1989, 20,000 to 62,000 or more Chinese killed or wounded in the 1979 war, and 40,000 to 100,000 Hmong insurgents killed. The Hoover Institution (2022) says each side lost about 30,000 killed in the 1979 Sino-Vietnamese war, with both giving widely different, unverified numbers.
toll.note: Low is the Vietnamese military figure alone; the components cover different periods and overlap, so they are not summed.

events.says: A series of linked conflicts among communist states after 1975: Vietnam's war with the Khmer Rouge and its occupation of Cambodia from December 1978, China's invasion of northern Vietnam in February 1979 and border fighting to 1991, and insurgency in Laos. It ended with the Paris Peace Accords of October 1991.
events.open: Casualty figures for Vietnam, China and the Khmer Rouge are weakly sourced and contested; the Chinese and Vietnamese governments have given different numbers for 1979. Some of the dead are also counted in the Cambodian-Vietnamese War and Sino-Vietnamese War entries, so this entry may duplicate those if they are listed separately. Civilian deaths are not counted in the sources read.

sources.title: The 1979 Sino-Vietnamese War and its consequences (Miles Maochun Yu, 20 December 2022)

events.name: Indonesian invasion and occupation of East Timor

toll.text: The Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation (CAVR, 2005) put conflict-related deaths in 1974-1999 at a minimum of about 102,800: about 18,600 killings and disappearances and about 84,200 deaths from hunger and illness above the peacetime rate. HRDAG's analysis for the commission says hunger and illness deaths could be as high as 183,000. Amnesty International put deaths from military action, starvation and disease at about 200,000, a third of the population.
toll.note: Low is the commission's minimum, which counts only deaths people could recall in 2004; high is Amnesty's figure. Combatants are not in the 18,600 political killings.

events.says: Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975 after Portugal withdrew and annexed it. Resistance by Falintil continued until a UN-run referendum in 1999 voted for independence, followed by militia violence.
events.open: The commission and HRDAG state that their 102,800 is a minimum with a margin of about 12,000, and the hunger-and-illness share depends on assumptions about a peacetime baseline. How many deaths to attribute to the occupation, as against drought, disease and the civil war of August 1975, is argued. The 1974-1999 period covers a few months before the invasion.

events.name: Angolan Civil War

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 500,000 to 800,000 dead by 2002 and over a million displaced. OnWar.com, which collects estimates, reports Clodfelter (1991) at 340,000 soldiers and civilians killed from all causes, Rummel at 20,000 soldiers and 320,000 civilians in 1975-1987, Brogan at 200,000, and UCDP/PRIO at 100,000 battle deaths in 1975-1991, and notes that no definitive count exists.
toll.note: Low is battle deaths only (to 1991); high is the upper end of total war-related deaths. Famine and disease deaths are in the higher figures only.

events.says: A war in Angola from 1975 to 2002 between the MPLA government (backed by the Soviet Union and Cuba) and UNITA and, early on, the FNLA (backed by South Africa and the United States). It ended after the death of UNITA's leader in February 2002.
events.open: No agreed total exists. The infobox figure of 800,000 is not sourced to a count, and civilian deaths from hunger and mines are hard to separate from killing. Wikipedia lists 14,269 Angolan government dead on record, 2,016 to 5,000 Cubans and 2,365 to 2,500 South Africans. The 1977 purge after the Nito Alves coup attempt is estimated at 2,000 to 90,000 dead, with Amnesty at 30,000.

events.name: Mozambican Civil War

toll.text: A country profile in the James Madison University Journal of Mine Action says about a million Mozambicans died from fighting or famine in 1977-1992. Wikipedia's infobox gives 1,000,000 or more, citing the US State Department. Estimates of war-related deaths of about 600,000 to 1,000,000 are quoted by the World Peace Foundation's Atrocity Endings project, which ties the 600,000 to UNICEF and to famine.
toll.note: Low is the lower war-related estimate; high is the round figure for fighting and famine together. Direct killings are far fewer: up to 100,000 attributed to Renamo (from the US State Department Gersony report) is the most cited number.

events.says: A war from 1977 to 1992 between the Frelimo government and the Renamo rebel movement, supported at different times by Rhodesia and South Africa, and by the Soviet bloc, Zimbabwe, Tanzania and Malawi on the government side. It ended with the Rome General Peace Accords of 4 October 1992.
events.open: Totals mix killings, famine and disease. The Gersony report blamed Renamo for about 94 per cent of abuses in its refugee interviews; the historian Michel Cahen disputes this, holding both sides equally brutal. Wikipedia also cites an estimated 30,000 deaths in Frelimo re-education camps, with no source given. A 1992 amnesty covers 1976-1992 and no commander has been prosecuted.

sources.title: Mozambique (country profile)
sources.publisher: James Madison University, Journal of Mine Action / Conventional Weapons Destruction

events.name: Nicaraguan Revolution and Contra War

toll.text: Wikipedia, citing Lacina and others, gives 10,000 to 50,000 killed in the 1978-79 overthrow of Somoza and 32,000 to 43,000 in the Contra war of 1981-1990, 42,000 to 78,000 in all, of whom 4,000 to 22,000 were civilians. The Peace Research Institute Oslo battle-deaths dataset, as shown by the Polynational War Memorial, gives 10,000 to 35,000 for 1978-79.
toll.note: Low and high add the low and high figures for the two phases; the sources do not give one count for the whole period.

events.says: The Sandinista National Liberation Front overthrew the Somoza dynasty in July 1979, and from 1981 the Contras, armed and funded by the United States and based largely in Honduras, fought the Sandinista government until the 1990 elections.
events.open: The 1978-79 range is wide (Wikipedia 10,000 to 50,000; PRIO 10,000 to 35,000). Totals vary by whether civilians and deaths from displacement are counted. Wikipedia lists 3,800 civilians dead in the Contra phase but a wider civilian range of 4,000 to 22,000 overall.

sources.title: Nicaraguan Gvt vs Sandinistas (1978-1979): battle deaths (PRIO Battle Deaths Dataset)

events.name: Insurgency in Punjab (India)

toll.text: Indian government figures in the Wikipedia infobox sum to 23,104: 3,468 security personnel, 7,946 militants and 11,690 non-combatants. Wikipedia also cites about 25,000 Sikh and Hindu deaths (Martin 2017) and says claims of 100,000 to 250,000 are disputed. Ensaaf and HRDAG's analysis of 1984-1995 found 17,582 victims of lethal violence reported in the Tribune newspaper, about 2,196 disappearances and extrajudicial executions documented by two inquiry bodies, and 2,059 illegal cremations acknowledged by the National Human Rights Commission.
toll.note: Low is the government sum; high is the scholarly estimate. The Ensaaf figures are partial counts from specific datasets and are not added.

events.says: An armed Sikh separatist insurgency and the Indian state's counter-insurgency in Punjab, with the army's Operation Blue Star at the Golden Temple in June 1984 and the anti-Sikh riots after the assassination of the prime minister in October 1984. Violence ended by about 1993 to 1995.
events.open: Totals depend on who counts. Human rights groups report thousands of disappearances and secret cremations by security forces, which official figures do not list. Dates vary: some start the insurgency in 1978 or 1981 and end it in 1993. The riots in Delhi and elsewhere in November 1984 killed 2,733 to more than 3,000 Sikhs and are not in these tallies.

sources.title: Violent Deaths and Enforced Disappearances During the Counterinsurgency in Punjab, India: a preliminary quantitative analysis
sources.publisher: Ensaaf and Human Rights Data Analysis Group

events.name: Soviet-Afghan War

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 562,000 to 2,000,000 Afghan civilians killed, with 1 million and 1.5 million also cited, and puts all deaths at 1 to 3 million (Joes 2010). The US Library of Congress Country Study says war dead are estimated at 750,000 to 1.5 million and calls the estimates open to question. Soviet dead are 14,453 by Soviet figures (9,511 in combat, 2,386 from wounds, 2,556 from disease and accidents) and up to 26,000 in another estimate; the Afghan government lost 58,000 or more and the mujahideen 75,000 to 90,000.
toll.note: Low is the lowest civilian estimate; high is the top of the all-deaths range. About 5 million fled abroad and 2 million were displaced inside Afghanistan.

events.says: A war in Afghanistan from December 1979 to February 1989 between the Soviet army with the Afghan communist government and the mujahideen groups, who were backed by Pakistan, the United States, Saudi Arabia and others. Soviet forces withdrew in February 1989.
events.open: No census or survey before or during the war supports any of the totals, which come from demographic modelling. The estimates differ by a factor of about four. Pakistan's 5,775 dead and the loss of an F-16 (shot down or friendly fire) are also in dispute.

sources.title: Afghanistan: Country Study (Library of Congress), chapter on population and the war
sources.publisher: US Library of Congress Country Studies

events.name: Salvadoran Civil War

toll.text: The United Nations figure is more than 75,000 killed in 1979-1992 plus about 8,000 disappeared. The UN Commission on the Truth received over 22,000 complaints of serious violence between January 1980 and July 1991, over 60 per cent for extrajudicial killings, over 25 per cent for disappearances and over 20 per cent for torture, and attributed most to government forces.
toll.note: Low is the UN's killed figure; high adds the disappeared. The Commission's 22,000 are complaints received, not confirmed deaths.

events.says: A war between El Salvador's military-led government and the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front (FMLN) from 1979 or 1980 to the Chapultepec Peace Accords of January 1992, with United States support for the government.
events.open: The UN Commission attributed about 85 per cent of the complaints to state forces and death squads and about 5 per cent to the FMLN, according to Wikipedia. Wikipedia's infobox lists much lower killed counts (10,360 to 15,000 and 12,274 to 20,000), which are not reconciled with the UN figure. Church legal-aid counts of killings by government forces were 11,895 for 1980 and up to 16,000 for 1981.

sources.title: Truth or Reconciliation Mechanism: Chapultepec Peace Agreement
sources.publisher: Kroc Institute, University of Notre Dame (Peace Accords Matrix)

events.name: Ugandan Bush War

toll.text: The US Library of Congress Country Study says the overall death toll under the second Obote government is estimated at as high as 500,000, and that the army's campaign cost more lives than Idi Amin's eight years. Wikipedia gives 100,000 to 500,000 across Uganda, cites the Red Cross estimate of more than 300,000 civilian deaths by July 1985, and says about 750,000 people were moved from the Luwero Triangle into army camps.
toll.note: Low and high are the ends of the range of estimates; many deaths came from disease and hunger after displacement.

events.says: A guerrilla war from February 1981 to January 1986 in which the National Resistance Army fought the Ugandan government of Milton Obote and, after July 1985, the military junta that overthrew him. The NRA took Kampala on 26 January 1986.
events.open: Reliable body counts do not exist for the 1980s. Wikipedia's infobox dates the war from October 1980 to March 1986; the guerrilla attacks began on 6 February 1981. Both the army and the NRA are accused of killing civilians, and the NRA denies it. The Luwero Triangle deaths are often given separately.

sources.title: The Second Obote Regime, 1981-85 (Uganda: A Country Study)
sources.publisher: US Library of Congress Country Studies

events.name: Iran-Iraq War

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 450,000 to 500,000 dead in all (Pfetsch and Rohloff 2013; Britannica). Kurzman (University of North Carolina) says half a million or more is the usual figure, the Battle Deaths Dataset gives over 600,000, and the Correlates of War Project gives 500,000 Iraqi and 750,000 Iranian dead. Iranian official counts are 155,081 to 183,623 front-line dead and about 16,000 killed in air and missile attacks, and an Iraqi general put Iraqi dead at 250,000.
toll.note: Low is the figure in most reference works; high is the Correlates of War total. Kurzman's census study suggests that the true toll may be well below the scholarly estimates.

events.says: A war between Iran and Iraq from the Iraqi invasion on 22 September 1980 to the ceasefire of 20 August 1988, with trench warfare, missile attacks on cities, attacks on shipping and the use of chemical weapons. It ended with the borders unchanged.
events.open: Totals disagree widely. Iran's 1996 census and Iraq's 1997 census show smaller gaps in male birth cohorts than a toll of 500,000 would produce, according to Kurzman, but the censuses may be inaccurate. Iraq's Anfal campaign against Kurds in 1988 is usually counted separately.

sources.title: Death Tolls of the Iran-Iraq War
sources.publisher: Charles Kurzman, University of North Carolina

events.name: Internal conflict in Peru

toll.text: Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2003) estimated 69,280 people killed or disappeared in 1980-2000, with a 95 per cent range of 61,007 to 77,552; it attributed 54 per cent to Shining Path and 1.5 per cent to the MRTA. Wikipedia reports a 2019 study that estimated about 48,000 killings, lower than the commission's.
toll.note: Low is the 2019 study; high is the top of the commission's range. Disappeared people are included in the commission's count.

events.says: An armed conflict in Peru from 1980, when Shining Path began its insurgency, to 2000, between Shining Path and the MRTA on one side and the Peruvian state and local self-defence committees on the other. About 75 per cent of the victims spoke Quechua as a first language.
events.open: The commission's findings were criticised by parties, the military and the Church; the 2019 study also concluded that the state accounted for a larger share of deaths than Shining Path. The commission's percentages by perpetrator differ in summaries (54 per cent in its conclusions; 45 per cent in another summary).

sources.title: Conclusiones generales del Informe Final de la Comision de la Verdad y Reconciliacion
sources.publisher: Comision de la Verdad y Reconciliacion (Peru), via Nizkor

events.name: Second Sudanese Civil War

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 1 to 2 million dead, mostly civilians, from starvation, drought and disease, and says the Sudan People's Liberation Army put the dead in the south alone at about 2 million; the US Sudan Peace Act of 2002 cited more than 2 million civilians killed. The New World Encyclopedia gives roughly 2 million, with 1.9 million in its infobox.
toll.note: Low and high are the stated range; the figures are estimates, not counts, and the sources do not break deaths down by year or cause.

events.says: A war from 1983 to 2005 between the Sudanese government in Khartoum and the Sudan People's Liberation Army in the south, with factions on both sides. About 4 million people in southern Sudan were displaced at least once. It ended with the Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 9 January 2005 and South Sudan's independence in 2011.
events.open: No census or survey gives a death count. The 2 million figure is attributed to the SPLA and to a US law, and these are political statements; Famine and drought deaths cannot be separated cleanly from killing.

events.name: Sri Lankan civil war

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 80,000 to 100,000 killed in 1983-2009 as the UN estimate of 2009, and at least 100,000 elsewhere. The UN Secretary-General's Panel of Experts (2011) said there could have been as many as 40,000 civilian deaths in the final months of 2009; a later UN review put it at up to 70,000. The International Truth and Justice Project (2021) gave 169,796 Tamil civilian deaths for January to May 2009.
toll.note: Low is the UN's 2009 estimate; high is the round total of at least 100,000. Wikidata records 100,001.

events.says: A war from July 1983 to May 2009 between the Sri Lankan government and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, with an Indian peacekeeping force present in 1987-1990. It ended with the government's military defeat of the Tigers in May 2009.
events.open: The government has rejected the UN panel's estimate and refused an independent international inquiry; the 2021 figure for 2009 alone is far above UN figures. Sri Lankan forces lost 28,708 dead and the Tigers about 27,000 according to reports cited by Wikipedia. Tens of thousands of Tamil civilians are listed as unaccounted for.

sources.title: UN: Sri Lanka mass deaths may be 'war crimes'

events.name: Kurdistan Workers' Party insurgency

toll.text: Al Jazeera (2011) reports more than 40,000 killed since the PKK took up arms in 1984, and 37,000 in the same article's subheading. Wikipedia's lead says an estimated 40,000 died between 1984 and 2012; it also lists Turkish government counts (for example 5,478 civilians killed in 1984-2013) and a PKK count of 22,660 killed.
toll.note: The 40,000 count covers 1984 to about 2011-2012 and all sides together; deaths since 2015 and in Syria and Iraq are in addition.

events.says: An armed conflict between Turkey and the Kurdistan Workers' Party, begun on 15 August 1984, mostly in south-eastern Turkey and later in northern Iraq and Syria. A peace process began in 2024, the PKK declared a ceasefire on 1 March 2025 and announced its dissolution on 12 May 2025.
events.open: Turkish government, PKK and Crisis Group counts differ, and some government totals include people captured or surrendered. Wikipedia dates the conflict from 27 November 1978 (the PKK's founding) to 12 May 2025; Turkey stated its forces would continue operations wherever the PKK remained active.

sources.title: Timeline: PKK attacks in Turkey (19 October 2011)

events.name: 1987-1989 JVP insurrection

toll.text: The Daily FT (Colombo, 2023) says the total killed in the second JVP insurgency is estimated at 60,000 to 100,000 and that the government's own commissions of inquiry recorded over 46,000 disappearances for 1987-89. Wikipedia lists 60,000 to 80,000 killed and more than 20,000 disappeared, and about 6,700 killed on the government side by insurgents.
toll.note: The ends are the Daily FT range; commission figures on disappearances overlap with the killed and are not added.

events.says: An armed uprising by the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna in southern Sri Lanka from 1987 to 1989 against the government and the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord, put down by security forces and pro-government paramilitary groups. Its leaders were killed in late 1989.
events.open: Counts of the dead and the disappeared are contested and were never fully recorded; the commissions dealt with disappearances from 1988 and 1989 to 1991, and none of the cases from 1987-89 has been resolved by the Office on Missing Persons, according to an editorial. Paramilitary involvement of the government is alleged rather than established.

sources.title: Address the ghosts of the 'Bheeshanaya' (21 January 2023)

events.name: Lord's Resistance Army insurgency

toll.text: A 2013 report of the UN Secretary-General said the LRA was responsible for more than 100,000 deaths and that 60,000 to 100,000 children are believed to have been abducted. Wikipedia's infobox gives 100,000 to over 200,000 killed (the 200,000 from the 2006 US Congressional Record) and notes a US government estimate of up to 12,000 that leaves out deaths from disease and malnutrition.
toll.note: Low is the UN figure; high is the Congressional Record figure. They count deaths in fighting and from the conflict's effects across four countries.

events.says: An insurgency begun in northern Uganda in 1987 by the Lord's Resistance Army against the Ugandan government, which spread to South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Central African Republic after 2005, with mass abduction of children. By 2025 its activity was low-level.
events.open: Estimates vary by source and by whether disease and hunger among displaced people are counted. Abduction figures range from about 20,000 (2004) and 25,000 children (UN, mid-2000s) to 60,000 to 100,000 (UN, 2013). About 2.5 million people were displaced.

sources.title: Kony's LRA has killed more than 100,000: UN (20 May 2013)

events.name: First Nagorno-Karabakh War

toll.text: Azerbaijani authorities published a list in 2014 of at least 11,557 soldiers killed in 1991-1994 (including those missing), and an earlier Azerbaijani president gave about 21,000 dead overall. The Armenian side reported about 7,000 soldiers and over 1,260 civilians dead. Wikipedia lists 5,856 to 6,000 Armenian dead and 25,000 to 30,000 in Western and Russian estimates, and 16,000 Azerbaijani and 4,000 Armenian civilians dead in one estimate.
toll.note: Low is the sum of the official Azerbaijani military count, the Armenian military count and the Armenian civilian count (11,557 + 7,000 + 1,260), which leaves out Azerbaijani civilians; high is the top of the Western and Russian estimates. The low end is just under 20,000.

events.says: A war from February 1988 to a ceasefire on 12 May 1994 between Armenian forces of Nagorno-Karabakh, backed by Armenia, and Azerbaijan over the region, which ended with Armenian control of Karabakh and surrounding districts and about a million people displaced on both sides.
events.open: No consolidated figure exists. Official Azerbaijani statements of 12,000 to 15,000 (2011) and 21,000 differ from the 2014 list. Armenian figures for civilian dead and missing differ between state commissions. Khojaly (February 1992) is given as 485 to 613 dead.

sources.title: Azerbaijan Says It Lost 11,557 Soldiers In Karabakh War (13 January 2014)

events.name: First Liberian Civil War

toll.text: Wikipedia gives about 200,000 killed in 1989-1997 (citing BlackPast), roughly one in 17 Liberians. The International Center for Transitional Justice says more than 200,000 died and a million were displaced in 1989-2003, and other sources cite about 250,000 deaths in the two civil wars together.
toll.note: Low is the figure for the first war; high is the figure for both wars, 1989-1997 and 1999-2003, so it is a ceiling for the first war.

events.says: A war that began on 24 December 1989 when the National Patriotic Front of Liberia invaded to overthrow the government of Samuel Doe, and ended with elections in July 1997 won by the NPFL leader, Charles Taylor. Nigeria-led ECOMOG forces and a UN observer mission were deployed.
events.open: The sources do not separate the two wars: the ICTJ figure covers 1989-2003. The 200,000 figure for the first war alone is not tied to a count in the compilation that gives it. Thousands of civilians were massacred on both sides, including about 600 killed at a church in Monrovia on 29 July 1990.

events.name: Insurgency in Jammu and Kashmir

toll.text: India's Ministry of Home Affairs, in an RTI reply reported by Kashmir Life in 2017, counted 40,961 people killed from 1990 to 31 March 2017: nearly 22,000 militants, 5,055 security forces and 13,491 civilians. Wikipedia gives about 70,000 deaths for the Jammu Kashmir Coalition of Civil Society, mostly civilians, and about 80,000 for the Hurriyat Conference, and Human Rights Watch at least 20,000 civilians by 2006.
toll.note: Low is the government count to March 2017; high is the Hurriyat figure. Deaths since 2017 and the conflict's later toll are not in the government figure.

events.says: An armed insurgency in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir from 1989, in which militant groups fought Indian security forces, with Pakistan accused by India of supporting them. Annual deaths fell from hundreds in the 2000s to 92 in 2025 according to a table on Wikipedia.
events.open: Government, human-rights groups and separatists give totals that differ in scope and method. Over 8,000 people are said by activists to have disappeared in custody, which the Indian government does not acknowledge, and a 2011 state inquiry found 2,730 bodies in unmarked graves in four districts. Wikipedia dates the start to 13 July 1989, with protests in 1988 also marking it.

sources.title: Over 40,000 deaths in 27 years of conflict in J&K; confirms MHA

events.name: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire
events.wiki: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 200,000 Aztecs dead including civilians (citing Clodfelter) and about 1,800 Spaniards dead; the History Skills teaching article says historians estimate over 100,000 Aztecs died during the 1521 siege of Tenochtitlan, with tens of thousands more dying in the aftermath. Wikipedia separately reports a claim that the 1520 smallpox wave alone killed 5 to 8 million people.
toll.note: Low is the siege deaths alone; high is all Aztec dead including civilians in the infobox figure. Neither includes the smallpox epidemic, which is counted separately and is far larger by that claim.

events.says: A campaign by Castilian forces under Hernan Cortes and indigenous allies, chiefly the Tlaxcalans, against the Aztec Triple Alliance from 1519 to 1521. It ended with the fall of Tenochtitlan on 13 August 1521 and the creation of New Spain.
events.open: The totals depend on whether siege deaths, starvation and the 1520 smallpox epidemic are counted together; the epidemic figure is cited to a source not identified in the Wikipedia text read. Wikipedia lists tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan and other allied dead without a number. No per-person list of the dead was found in this research.

sources.title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire (Wikipedia)
How the mighty Tenochtitlan, capital city of the Aztecs, fell to Spanish conquistadors

events.name: German Peasants' War

toll.text: Lyndal Roper's Summer of Fire and Blood says the lords put the revolt down by slaying somewhere between 70,000 and 100,000 peasants in just over two months; the Gale Renaissance encyclopedias say about 100,000 combatants and civilians were killed and as many as 100,000 lives lost; Wikipedia's infobox says more than 100,000 killed while its text says up to 100,000 of about 300,000 rebels.
toll.note: Low and high are the two ends of Roper's range; most encyclopedias round to 100,000. Wikipedia's infobox reads as a floor of 100,000, which its own text contradicts.

events.says: A revolt of peasants, townspeople and some local nobles across the German-speaking lands of central Europe in 1524 and 1525, put down by the Swabian League and princely armies. Defeats at Frankenhausen and Königshofen ended it.
events.open: Dates differ between sources (late 1525 or mid-1526). The 100,000 figure is a round number repeated in encyclopedias; the Wikipedia article gives no scholarly basis for the infobox's 'more than 100,000'. No per-person list of the dead was found in this research.

sources.title: Peasants' War, in The Renaissance and Renaissance: An Encyclopedia for Students
Summer of Fire and Blood: The German Peasants' War (publisher description of Lyndal Roper's book)
sources.publisher: Basic Books, via Los Angeles Public Library OverDrive

events.name: French Wars of Religion

toll.text: Wikipedia, citing Knecht (2002), says between 2 and 4 million people died from violence, famine or disease directly caused by the conflict. James B. Wood's The King's Army (Cambridge, 1996) cites a 1581 pamphlet that put the toll at well over one million for 1560 to 1580 alone, and notes the precise accuracy of its figures is uncertain.
toll.note: Low is the 1581 pamphlet's figure for 1560-80 only, as reported by Wood; high is Knecht's upper estimate for the whole war including famine and disease. The Wikipedia text gives 5,000 to 30,000 for the 1572 St Bartholomew's Day massacre alone.

events.says: A series of civil and religious wars in France between Catholics and Protestants (Huguenots) from 1562 to 1598, with foreign powers drawn in. It ended with the Edict of Nantes.
events.open: Totals mix battle deaths with famine and disease and depend on who counts. Wood's pamphlet figure is contemporary and its accuracy is uncertain; Knecht's range is reported through Wikipedia, not read at source. No per-person list of the dead was found in this research.

sources.title: Introduction, The King's Army: Warfare, Soldiers and Society during the Wars of Religion in France, 1562-76 (James B. Wood)

events.name: Japanese invasions of Korea (Imjin War)

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 1,000,000 or more Joseon civilian and military deaths (citing Szczepanski 2017), 30,000 or more Ming deaths and 100,000 or more Japanese killed, captured or missing. War History Network gives about 260,000 Korean military dead and civilian estimates up to 1 million. A Korea JoongAng Daily column by Harold Piper reports Samuel Hawley's estimate that at least 2 million Koreans perished from war and famine.
toll.note: Low is the Korean civilian and military total in the infobox; high is Hawley's at least 2 million Koreans dead of war and famine. Japanese and Chinese dead are in the text only and are not in the range.

events.says: Two Japanese invasions of Joseon Korea ordered by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, in 1592 and 1597, fought across the peninsula against Korean forces and a Ming Chinese army. They ended with the Japanese withdrawal after Hideyoshi's death in 1598.
events.open: Civilian and famine deaths are estimates, not counts; the figures come from a Wikipedia infobox citing one source, an unsourced military-history summary, and a newspaper column summarising Hawley's book, so none is a demographic study. No per-person list of the dead was found in this research.

sources.title: The worst calamity in Korean history (Harold Piper, on Samuel Hawley's The Imjin War), 25 June 2006

events.name: Shimabara Rebellion

toll.text: Wikipedia gives rebel dead of 30,000 to 37,000 (citing Gunn 2017) and a rebel force of 27,000 to 37,000 (citing Morton 2005), with an estimated 37,000 rebels and sympathisers killed after Hara Castle fell.
