Government-side dead are given in its infobox as 10,000 (Sansom 1963) to 70,000 (Clodfelter 2008). World History Encyclopedia says only that tens of thousands of peasants died and that very few survived the final slaughter.
toll.note: Range is the rebel dead only. The government-side figures differ by a factor of seven and are not in the range.

events.says: A rising in 1637 and 1638 of peasants and masterless samurai, many of them Christians, against the Tokugawa shogunate on the Shimabara peninsula and the Amakusa islands. It ended when shogunate forces stormed Hara Castle and killed those inside.
events.open: Rebel numbers come from Wikipedia and are not independently sourced in its text; the article carries an accuracy-dispute banner. The government-side dead differ between 10,000 and 70,000. Historyofwar.org says all inside the castle, women and children included, were killed, with no number.

sources.title: Siege of Hara, 1637-1638 (Japan) (T. D. P. Dugdale-Pointon, 29 April 2002)

events.name: Wars of the Three Kingdoms

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox, citing Carlton (Going to the Wars, 1994), gives 50,700 English and Welsh and 27,895 Scottish killed in combat, 78,595 together, plus about 127,000 non-combat English and Welsh deaths including 40,000 civilians. World History Encyclopedia (Mark Cartwright, 2022) says perhaps 100,000 soldiers died and around 100,000 civilians, some 200,000 deaths in all.
toll.note: Low is the combat dead of England, Wales and Scotland only; high is the World History Encyclopedia total of soldiers and civilians. Irish deaths of the same years are far larger and are counted in the separate entry for the Irish Confederate Wars.

events.says: A linked series of wars from 1639 to 1653 in England, Scotland and Ireland between the crown, parliamentary, Covenanter and Irish Confederate forces. They ended with the Commonwealth of England ruling all three kingdoms.
events.open: The sources do not agree on what is counted: Carlton's combat figures, a non-combat figure, and a round 200,000 that its author does not source. The World History Encyclopedia article does not say whether its total includes Ireland. No per-person list of the dead was found in this research.

sources.title: Consequences of the English Civil Wars (Mark Cartwright, 9 February 2022)

events.name: Irish Confederate Wars

toll.text: Wikipedia gives an estimated 200,000 deaths from fighting plus famine and disease, 25,000 or more battlefield casualties, and William Petty's survey figure of at least 400,000 and perhaps 620,000 dead, citing Kenyon and Ohlmeyer (eds), The Civil Wars (1998). That source is said to treat about 200,000 as the lowest suggested figure and about two thirds of deaths as civilian. History Ireland reports Petty's total as about 618,000, which is not read at source here.
toll.note: Low is the lowest modern figure for war-caused deaths; high is Petty's upper figure from the 1650s, based on an estimated population of about 1.5 million. Both include war, famine and plague.

events.says: A decade of war in Ireland from the October 1641 rising to 1653, between Irish Catholic Confederates, English Royalists and Parliamentarians and Scottish forces. It ended with the Parliamentarian conquest and the annexation of Ireland to the Commonwealth.
events.open: Petty's figures rest on patchy information and estimated births and deaths; an RTÉ article by Clíona Ó Gallchoir (UCC) describes his data that way. The number of Protestants killed in 1641 is itself disputed: Petty's 37,000 is described in the cited source as far too high, perhaps by a factor of ten. No per-person list of the dead was found in this research.

sources.title: William Petty, Oliver Cromwell and Ireland's statistics (Clíona Ó Gallchoir, 25 September 2020)

events.name: Nine Years' War (Ireland)

toll.text: Wikipedia cites Carlton (This Seat of Mars, 2011) for 18,500 military deaths and gives, without a source, 100,000 or more soldiers and Irish civilians dead, mostly of famine, and a total of 120,000 or more; it also reports unnamed Irish sources claiming up to 60,000 dead in the 1602-03 Ulster famine. John McGurk (History Ireland, 1995) counts about 2,640 killed and 1,160 wounded on the English side and over 6,000 killed and wounded on the Irish and Spanish side, excluding non-combatants.
toll.note: Low is the military total; high is the unsourced total including famine. McGurk's battle count is lower than the low figure and he warns that official dispatches exaggerate both sides.

events.says: A war in Ireland from 1593 to 1603 between Gaelic Irish lords led by Hugh O'Neill and Hugh O'Donnell, helped by Spain, and the English crown. It ended in an English victory at the Treaty of Mellifont and led to the Flight of the Earls.
events.open: Whether the war reached 20,000 deaths depends on counting famine and disease: the combat counts read are well below it. Civilian and famine deaths are not quantified by McGurk and the large totals are unsourced in Wikipedia. No per-person list of the dead was found in this research.

sources.title: The Dead, Sick and Wounded of the Nine Years War (1594-1603) (John McGurk), History Ireland, vol. 3 no. 4, Winter 1995

events.name: Transition from Ming to Qing

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 25,000,000 deaths overall including civilians, without a citation. Its text says historians put deaths in Zhang Xianzhong's rebellion at up to one million. The Yangzhou massacre of 1645 is credited by a contemporary account with 800,000 dead, a figure the Sinica Podcast, reporting James Carter, says Antonia Finnane thinks may be ten times too high.
toll.note: No agreed figure: the 25 million has no named source, and the specific massacre figures are disputed.

events.says: The period of civil war, rebellion and Manchu conquest in China from the Later Jin attacks of 1618 to the fall of the Tungning kingdom in 1683. The Ming dynasty collapsed and the Qing dynasty took the whole of China.
events.open: The 25 million figure rests on no source read here; a nationwide count of the dead has not been located in any source fetched. Massacre figures come from contemporary diaries and are disputed. No per-person list of the dead was found in this research.

sources.title: This Week in China's History: The Xiangtan Massacre (James Carter), 1 March 2024

events.name: Cretan War (1645-1669)

toll.text: Wikipedia, citing Paoletti (A Military History of Italy, 2008) and Venetian reports, gives 118,754 Ottoman and 30,985 Venetian dead, 149,739 together, at Candia only, and says the total would possibly be twice as high with the Dalmatian front and naval losses. War History Online (Julia Dzhak, 2016) says over 70,000 Ottoman soldiers and about 38,000 siege workers died in the last 28 months of the siege, and the defenders lost over 29,000.
toll.note: Low is the last-phase siege deaths from War History Online (108,000 Ottoman and 29,000 defenders); high is the Venetian-report total for Candia. Both are for Candia only.

events.says: A war from 1645 to 1669 between the Ottoman Empire and the Republic of Venice with allies, fought over Venetian Crete and in Dalmatia and the Aegean. It ended with the surrender of Candia and Ottoman rule of Crete.
events.open: Figures come from Venetian reports and are not independent counts; one Wikipedia reference is not shown in the text read. Wikipedia also gives the Cretan population falling from about 260,000 to about 80,000 by 1677 (citing Miller 1921), mixing deaths, flight and enslavement. No per-person list of the dead was found in this research.

sources.title: Candia - 21 Years Under Siege Before Finally Surrendering (Julia Dzhak), 18 June 2016

events.name: The Deluge (Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth)

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 3,000,000 to 4,000,000 dead, citing a reference not shown in the text read, and its body says about one third of the population was lost. A Polish Ministry of Education page on zpe.gov.pl gives the population of the Commonwealth as 3.85 million in the mid-17th century, 2.85 million in 1660 and 3.25 million in 1700, a fall of about 26 percent (1,000,000), and says famine and epidemics killed more people than the fighting.
toll.note: Low is the fall in the zpe.gov.pl population table, which counts all causes and any departures; high is the top of the infobox range. The two sets of population figures are not on the same base and are not reconciled.

events.says: A series of invasions and wars on the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth from 1655 to 1660, chiefly by Sweden and also Russia, Brandenburg, Transylvania and Cossack forces. It ended with the Treaty of Oliva in 1660.
events.open: The Wikipedia article is flagged as needing more citations and uses wide date ranges; the 3 to 4 million figure is not sourced in the text read and sits uneasily with the population table. Famine and plague make a war-only count impossible from these sources. No per-person list of the dead was found in this research.

sources.title: Kres potopu szwedzkiego - bilans strat (population table and losses)

events.name: Eighty Years' War

toll.text: No source read gives a total for the war. Wikipedia says about 50,000 people were killed in the Netherlands by executions, burnings and massacres during the Duke of Alba's governorship (1567 to 1573), without naming who made the estimate. Wikipedia's infobox lists troop numbers but no casualties.
toll.note: No agreed figure was found; the Alba estimate covers one period and one cause of death.

events.says: The revolt of the Netherlands against Habsburg Spain, from the late 1560s to the Peace of Munster in 1648. It ended with Spain recognising the Dutch Republic and keeping the Southern Netherlands.
events.open: Historians differ on the start date and the war's framing. A 2025 Leiden doctoral thesis by I. Casteels, which analyses over four thousand chronicle descriptions of executions, calls the Revolt a period with a particularly high number of executions, but the page read gives no count. A total of deaths over the whole war, including sieges, sacks and famine, was not found.

sources.title: Looking for justice: execution spectators and the Revolt in the Low Countries, ca. 1520-1585 (I. Casteels), doctoral thesis, 2025

events.name: Second Anglo-Dutch War

toll.text: Jack Levy (War in the Modern Great Power System, 1983), as reported on Wikipedia, counts 37,000 soldiers killed in action, English and Dutch together. EBSCO's account gives battle figures only: at Lowestoft (June 1665) about 5,000 Dutch and 700 English dead and 17 Dutch ships lost; at the Four Days' Battle (June 1666) 15 to 20 English ships lost and 'thousands of Englishmen', with Dutch losses about half the English; no war-wide total.
toll.note: Low and high are the same single published count of military deaths in action; no second war-wide figure was found, and the battle figures read do not by themselves add up to it.

events.says: A naval war between England and the Dutch Republic, fought at sea and in raids on coasts, with France and Denmark joining the Dutch side. It ended with the Treaty of Breda on 31 July 1667, by which England kept New York and the Dutch kept Suriname and Pulo Run.
events.open: The only war-wide figure found is one scholar's count; the battle-level figures in encyclopedia accounts are far smaller, and no list of the dead by name survives for the war as a whole. Whether the war crosses 20,000 deaths rests on that single count. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any list that survives for the whole war; the individual records that exist are scattered through muster rolls, pay books and parish and town registers.

events.name: Franco-Dutch War

toll.text: Jack Levy (1983), as reported on Wikipedia's list of wars by death toll, gives 340,000 military deaths. Wikipedia's article, citing Clodfelter (1992), gives 120,000 killed or wounded on one side and 100,000 on the other, which counts survivors as well as the dead. Encyclopedia.com says France kept around 250,000 soldiers in the field.
toll.note: Low and high are Levy's single count of military deaths. Clodfelter's 220,000 killed-or-wounded cannot be added to or compared with it directly, but it points to a smaller number of deaths.

events.says: A war in which France under Louis XIV attacked the Dutch Republic in 1672 and then fought a coalition including Spain, the Holy Roman Empire and Brandenburg. The Treaties of Nijmegen (1678-79) left the Dutch Republic intact and gave France Franche-Comté and towns in the Spanish Netherlands.
events.open: The two war-wide figures read count different things (deaths against killed-or-wounded) and do not agree. Civilian deaths from the sieges and the occupation of Dutch provinces are not included in either. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any list that survives for the whole war; the individual records that exist are scattered through muster rolls, pay books and parish and town registers.

events.name: Deccan wars (Mughal-Maratha)

toll.text: No war-wide figure was found in a scholarly source. Wikipedia's list of wars by death toll gives 4.6 to 5 million, citing Matthew White's popular compilation Atrocitology (2011); the Deccan wars article itself and the Gale and Oxford entries on Aurangzeb give no death count. Wikipedia reports that the Mughal army 'lost about a fifth' of its strength (Gascoigne, The Great Moghuls, 1971).
toll.note: No usable range: the 4.6 to 5 million figure comes from a single popular compilation and is not a demographic estimate, so it is left out of low and high.

events.says: A twenty-six-year war in which the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb conquered Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687) and then fought the Marathas across the Deccan until his death in 1707. Encyclopedia entries describe a devastated economy and trade with the north shut from 1702 to 1704; the Mughal empire split into regional states afterwards.
events.open: Deaths from fighting, famine and plague in the Deccan in these years are not separated in any source read, and no census exists to measure them. The dead were not recorded by name.

events.name: Great Turkish War (War of the Holy League)

toll.text: Wikipedia, citing Levy (1983) and Clodfelter (2017), gives 384,000 military deaths across all sides. For the Holy Roman Empire alone it reports about 300,000 killed and wounded, of whom roughly 120,000 were killed (Bodart, 1916). No figure for Ottoman, Polish or Venetian deaths is given. EBSCO's and Encyclopedia.com's accounts of the Austro-Turkish wars give no totals.
toll.note: Low and high are the single all-sides count of military deaths; civilian deaths are not counted.

events.says: A war in which the Holy League of the Habsburg monarchy, Poland-Lithuania and Venice, joined by Russia in 1686, drove the Ottoman Empire back after the failed siege of Vienna in 1683. The Treaty of Karlowitz (26 January 1699) gave Austria most of Hungary and Transylvania, Venice the Morea, and Poland Podolia.
events.open: Only one all-sides count was found, and it covers soldiers only. Ottoman losses are the least documented. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any list that survives for the whole war; the individual records that exist are scattered through muster rolls, pay books and parish and town registers.

events.name: Nine Years' War (War of the League of Augsburg)

toll.text: Jack Levy (1983), as reported on Wikipedia, gives 680,000 military deaths, with a note that Britain lost a further 20,000 outside Ireland. Encyclopedia.com gives battle figures only, for example Neerwinden (1693): 9,000 French and 14,000 Allied casualties. The great French famine of 1693-94 is not included; Wikipedia gives 700,000 to 1,300,000 deaths for it.
toll.note: Low and high are one count of military deaths on all sides; war-related famine and civilian deaths are excluded.

events.says: A war between France under Louis XIV and the Grand Alliance of the Dutch Republic, England, the Holy Roman Empire, Spain, Savoy and others, fought in the Spanish Netherlands, the Rhineland, Italy, Catalonia, Ireland and at sea, with a North American counterpart known as King William's War. The Treaty of Ryswick (1697) restored most conquests.
events.open: Only one war-wide count was found, and the famine deaths in France in the same years are a separate and larger figure. The Williamite war in Ireland (1689-91), a related conflict within this war, is covered here and not listed separately. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any list that survives for the whole war; the individual records that exist are scattered through muster rolls, pay books and parish and town registers.

events.name: War of the Spanish Succession

toll.text: Estimates differ widely: Urlanis, 235,000 killed in battle and 700,000 military killed and dead of disease; Clodfelter, about 400,000 dead on both sides; Bodart, 35,000 to 40,000 Austrian dead; Levy and Eckhardt, 1,251,000 military dead (all as listed by Necrometrics). Encyclopedia.com says Allied casualties at Malplaquet (1709) 'run as high as 25,000'.
toll.note: Low is Urlanis's count of deaths in battle alone; high is Levy's and Eckhardt's military total, which includes disease. Civilian deaths are not counted in either.

events.says: A war over the succession to the Spanish throne after Charles II died in 1700, fought by France and Bourbon Spain against the Grand Alliance of England, the Dutch Republic, the Holy Roman Empire, Portugal and Savoy, across Europe, with a North American counterpart known as Queen Anne's War. The Peace of Utrecht (1713) and the treaties of Rastatt and Baden (1714) ended it.
events.open: The estimates run from 235,000 to over a million because they count different things: battle deaths, all military deaths including disease, or all dead. Wikipedia's infobox gives killed, wounded and disease-struck together, which is not a death count.

sources.title: Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: War of the Polish Succession

toll.text: Jack Levy (1983), as reported on Wikipedia and Necrometrics, gives 88,000 military deaths. Sorokin gives 98,600 killed and wounded together (France 50,400, Austria 32,000). EBSCO notes the heaviest losses fell at Parma (June 1734) and Guastalla (September 1734) but gives no numbers.
toll.note: Low and high are the single count of military deaths; the killed-and-wounded figure counts survivors too and is not added.

events.says: A war over who should be king of Poland after Augustus II died in 1733, in which France, Spain and Sardinia backed Stanisław Leszczyński against Austria, Russia and Saxony, with fighting in Poland, the Rhineland and northern Italy. The Third Treaty of Vienna (1738) recognised Augustus III in Poland, gave Lorraine to Stanisław for his lifetime and then to France, and redistributed Italian territory.
events.open: Only one scholarly death count was found. Civilian deaths, notably from the siege of Gdańsk, are not counted. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any list that survives for the whole war; the individual records that exist are scattered through muster rolls, pay books and parish and town registers.

sources.title: Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: Russo-Turkish War (1735-1739)

toll.text: Levy gives 38,000 military deaths for the Russo-Austro-Turkish war of 1736-39 (Necrometrics); Sorokin gives 38,360 killed and wounded (Austria 22,400, Russia 15,960). Wikipedia, citing Kernosovsky (1938), gives 100,000 to 150,000 Russian dead, mainly from hunger, heat and disease, of which about 8,000 died in battle in one year; it gives Austria 20,000 killed and wounded and the Ottomans 44,427 casualties in battle, with total Ottoman losses unknown.
toll.note: Low is Levy's count of military deaths for both wars together; high is the Russian dead alone including disease, so the two are not like for like.

events.says: A war in which Russia, joined by Austria from 1737, fought the Ottoman Empire over the Black Sea steppe, Crimea and the Danubian principalities. Russia took Azov and Austria lost Belgrade; the Treaty of Nis-Belgrade (1739) ended it.
events.open: The high figure rests on one Russian military historian and counts deaths from disease in the army. Ottoman dead and civilian deaths are not known. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any list that survives for the whole war; the individual records that exist are scattered through muster rolls, pay books and parish and town registers.

sources.title: Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: War of the Austrian Succession

toll.text: EBSCO: 'by one conservative estimate, 100,000 men lost their lives on the battlefields', with scores of thousands more in sieges and occupations. Levy and Eckhardt: 359,000 military dead; Urlanis: 450,000 military killed and dead of disease; Browning: 100,000 soldiers plus 400,000 civilians (Necrometrics). Clodfelter: 28,100 Habsburg killed in action (Necrometrics).
toll.note: Low is the conservative battlefield-only estimate; high is Browning's total of soldiers and civilians. Wikipedia's 750,000 (Clodfelter) counts dead and wounded together.

events.says: A war of dynastic claims after Charles VI died in 1740 and Prussia invaded Silesia, fought by Austria, Britain, the Dutch Republic and Sardinia against France, Prussia, Spain and Bavaria, in central Europe, the Low Countries, Italy, the colonies and at sea, with the Jacobite rising of 1745-46 inside it. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) ended it with few territorial changes.
events.open: Civilian deaths are the main source of disagreement, and the commonly repeated 750,000 is a figure for killed and wounded together rather than deaths. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any list that survives for the whole war; the individual records that exist are scattered through muster rolls, pay books and parish and town registers.

sources.title: Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: Maratha invasions of Bengal

toll.text: Wikipedia, citing Chaudhuri (2006) and Marshall (2006), reports an estimate by the chief of the Dutch East India Company's factory in Bengal that 400,000 civilians died in western Bengal and Bihar in the invasions. Banglapedia gives no death toll for the civilian population; it records the raids, flight of weavers and silk workers, scarce grain and lost trade.
toll.note: Low and high are the single contemporary estimate, for western Bengal and Bihar only.

events.says: Repeated raids into Bengal from 1741 to 1751 by Maratha cavalry (the Bargis) under Raghuji Bhonsle and Bhaskar Pandit, resisted by the nawab Alivardi Khan. Peace in 1751 ceded part of Orissa to the Marathas and committed Bengal to payments of chauth.
events.open: The figure is a contemporary outside estimate, not a count, and covers civilians in two regions. Dates differ: Banglapedia dates the first raid to April 1742, others to 1741. The dead were not recorded by name.

events.name: Qing conquest of Dzungaria (Dzungar genocide)

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 420,000 to 480,000 (70 to 80 percent of the Dzungar population), with other estimates of 600,000 and up to 800,000. Wikidata gives 540,000. Encyclopedia.com puts the pre-war Dzungar population at 600,000 and gives shares: Lattimore 50 percent killed and 20 percent dead of smallpox; Perdue 30 percent killed and 40 percent dead of smallpox; Zlatkin 7 percent survived. Necrometrics lists Eckhardt at 600,000 (300,000 civilian and 300,000 military).
toll.note: Low and high are the ends of the published estimates; all combine killing by the Qing army with smallpox and famine.

events.says: A Qing campaign of 1755 to 1758 under the Qianlong emperor that destroyed the Dzungar Khanate, the last nomad empire of the Mongol steppe, after its leader Amursana rebelled against Qing rule. Dzungaria was afterwards resettled by Manchu, Han, Hui, Uyghur and Sibe people.
events.open: Historians dispute how many died by the sword and how many from smallpox, and whether the term genocide applies; Perdue holds that Qing policy eased after the threat ended. The pre-war population itself is only an estimate (about 600,000 on one Qing reckoning). No list of the dead by name survives.

sources.title: Zunghars (Worldmark and Encyclopedia of World Cultures entries)
Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: Seven Years' War

toll.text: Danley and Speelman (2012), via Wikipedia, list dead by state: France 200,000, Prussia 180,000, Habsburg lands 165,000, Britain with its German allies 160,000, Russia 120,000, Spain over 29,000, Sweden 28,000. Necrometrics lists Urlanis at 550,000 military dead (140,000 in battle), Williams 853,000, Clodfelter 868,000, Levy 992,000, Eckhardt 1,100,000, with a median of 1,300,000. Encyclopedia.com says 'well over a million'.
toll.note: Low is the smallest military total; high is the upper end of Wikipedia's list of wars by death toll (1 to 1.5 million). Civilian dead are partly included in some totals and not in others.

events.says: A global war between Britain, Prussia, Hanover and Portugal on one side and France, Austria, Russia, Spain, Sweden and Saxony on the other, fought in Europe, North America (the French and Indian War), the Caribbean, West Africa, India and the Philippines. The Peace of Paris and the Peace of Hubertusburg (1763) ended it.
events.open: Totals depend on whether disease deaths, civilians and allied armies are counted. Colonial dead, including Native American and enslaved people, are not separated in the sources read.

sources.title: Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: Russo-Circassian War and Caucasian War

toll.text: A journal article of the American University School of International Service puts deaths from military operations, massacres and depopulation at 1.5 to 2 million, citing Karpat's Ottoman Population 1830-1914 and the 1830 population of about 4 million; the same article quotes the Russian consul at Trabzon that about 19,000 of some 240,000 deportees died on arrival there. Wikipedia's article gives 1,615,000 or more civilian dead. Encyclopedia.com's entries give deportation figures instead of deaths: about 1.5 million Circassians settled in Ottoman lands, 'fully half' emigrating, and 'many died of hunger and disease'.
toll.note: Low and high are the single published range of dead; it is close to the deportation figure in encyclopedia entries, so deaths and exiles may be counted together.

events.says: A war of 1763 to 1864 in which the Russian Empire conquered the Circassian peoples of the north-west Caucasus, ending with the 1864 defeat and the expulsion of most Circassians to the Ottoman Empire. The row also covers the wider Caucasian War, including Chechnya and Dagestan.
events.open: The numbers are disputed and rest on 1830 population guesses and Ottoman and Russian correspondence. Whether the removal is genocide is debated; Worldmark notes that contemporary researchers regard it as such, and Russian officials have disputed the account. The Ottoman port records of arrivals and deaths exist but have not been tallied here.

sources.title: The Circassian Genocide: the forgotten tragedy of the first modern genocide
sources.publisher: Journal of International Service, American University

sources.title: Circassians (Worldmark and Encyclopedia of World Cultures entries)

events.name: Sino-Burmese War (Qing invasions of Burma)

toll.text: Wikipedia, citing Harvey (1925), Myint-U and Kohn, adds up Qing dead at 70,000 or more: about 20,000 in the second campaign, over 30,000 in the third (only a few dozen of a 30,000-strong army returned) and over 20,000 in the fourth. Necrometrics lists Clodfelter at 20,000 Chinese killed in action. No Burmese or civilian figure was found.
toll.note: Low is Clodfelter's Chinese deaths in action; high is the sum of Qing losses across campaigns, which is itself a floor. Burmese military and civilian dead are not counted.

events.says: Four Qing invasions of the Konbaung kingdom of Burma between 1765 and 1769, launched from Yunnan after a border dispute over the Shan states, all of which failed. Fighting ended with a truce at Kaungton in December 1769.
events.open: Qing losses include deaths from malaria and other disease, and are inferred from the size of armies that did not return. Dates differ: EBSCO says the war began in 1766. No Burmese casualty figure was found. No list of the dead by name survives.

sources.title: Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: Tây Sơn wars

toll.text: No sourced figure was found. Wikipedia's list of wars by death toll gives 1 to 2 million, citing Dutton (2006) and Tran Khanh, but the Tay Son article itself marks that figure as lacking a citation, and the Library of Congress country study gives no death count. Necrometrics lists only Clodfelter's 10,000 Chinese drowned in the Red River after losing Hanoi in 1789.
toll.note: No usable range: the 1 to 2 million figure could not be traced to a page that states it, so it is left out of low and high.

events.says: A civil war in Vietnam from 1771 in which the Tay Son brothers from Binh Dinh overthrew the Nguyen lords in the south and the Trinh lords in the north, defeated a Qing army in 1789, and were themselves defeated by Nguyen Anh, who took the throne as Gia Long in 1802.
events.open: Deaths from war, famine and natural disaster in these years are not separated in any source read, and the 1 to 2 million figure is unverified. Massacres, including of the Chinese community in the south, are described in the literature but were not tallied here.

sources.title: The Tay Son Rebellion (Vietnam: a country study)
Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: Pugachev's Rebellion

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 20,000 rebels killed and 16,000 captured, and 3,500 government dead. Necrometrics lists Clodfelter at 20,000 rebels killed and Sorokin at 5,000 Russian killed and wounded. Encyclopedia.com says about 3,000 landlords are thought to have died in the revolt.
toll.note: Low is rebel dead alone; high adds the government dead. The landlords killed are part of the civilian dead and are not added separately.

events.says: A rising of Yaik Cossacks, Kalmyks, Tatars, Bashkirs and serfs led by Yemelyan Pugachev, who claimed to be Tsar Peter III, across the Urals and Volga from 1773. Pugachev was handed over by his own Cossacks in September 1774 and executed in Moscow on 10 January 1775.
events.open: Counts of those executed or killed in reprisals after the defeat are not given in the sources read, so the total may be higher. No list of the dead by name survives.

sources.title: Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: American Revolutionary War

toll.text: Totals range with what is counted. Necrometrics lists Eckhardt at 20,000 military dead, Levy 34,000, Burrows 41,100 American dead, Duncan 108,800 (US 70,000, Britain 31,000, German auxiliaries 7,800), and Fenn 130,658 smallpox deaths of which about 6,186 were war-related. Wikipedia gives 25,000 American military dead (6,800 killed in action, 17,000 of disease) and 43,633 British, and its list of wars by death toll 180,000 to 230,000 citing Peckham (1974) and Clodfelter (2017).
toll.note: Low is the smallest military count; high is the upper end of Wikipedia's list, which includes civilians, Native American and allied dead and disease.

events.says: The war in which thirteen British colonies in North America, joined by France from 1778, Spain and the Dutch Republic, won independence from Great Britain. The Treaty of Paris (1783) recognised the United States.
events.open: Totals depend on whether disease deaths, prisoners who died in captivity, civilians, Loyalists, Native Americans and German auxiliaries are counted; most dead of disease are in the American and British totals but not in all.

sources.title: Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: Rebellion of Túpac Amaru II

toll.text: Necrometrics lists Clodfelter at 80,000 lives lost on all sides and from all causes, of which 60,000 died in the siege of La Paz (killed and dead of disease). Wikipedia's article gives 100,000 estimated killed and 10,000 dead of starvation or illness, and its list of wars by death toll gives 100,000 to 150,000, citing Robins (2002).
toll.note: Low is Clodfelter's count for all sides and causes; high is the upper end of the Wikipedia list. Most dead were Aymara and Quechua people.

events.says: A rising of Quechua and Aymara communities in the Viceroyalty of Peru, led first by Túpac Amaru II, a kuraka of Tungasuca, and from 1781 by Túpac Katari around La Paz. Túpac Amaru II was executed in Cusco in May 1781; fighting went on to 1783.
events.open: Totals combine rebels, civilians and royalist troops and the dead of the sieges; the sources read do not separate them.

sources.title: Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: Russo-Turkish War (1787-1792)

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 59,000 to 72,000 Russian dead and 116,000 to 130,000 or up to 200,000 Ottoman dead, and 50,000 Austrian dead in 1788-89 (Groß-Hoffinger, 1847). Low adds Russia's 59,000 and the Ottoman 116,000; high adds 72,000, 200,000 and Austria's 50,000.
toll.note: Both ends are sums of single-state figures from the same article; none is a war-wide count by one author.

events.says: A war begun by the Ottoman Empire in 1787 against Russia, joined by Austria from 1788 to 1791 and Sweden against Russia from 1788 to 1790. Russia took Ochakov and Izmail; the Treaty of Jassy (1792) left Russia the Black Sea coast up to the Dniester.
events.open: The Ottoman figures vary by 84,000 and the Austrian figure includes disease in the army. Civilian dead, including at Ochakov and Izmail, are not counted. Encyclopedia.com's entry gives no casualty figures. The dead of this war were not recorded by name in any list that survives for the whole war; the individual records that exist are scattered through muster rolls, pay books and parish and town registers.

events.name: Australian frontier wars

toll.text: Reynolds (2022), as reported on Wikipedia, gives at least 30,000 Aboriginal people killed and about 2,500 settlers. The University of Newcastle's Colonial Frontier Massacres project estimates more than 10,000 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people killed in at least 414 massacres between 1788 and 1930, and 168 non-Aboriginal people in 13 massacres; its site says 'thousands' were killed and that actual deaths may have been many more.
toll.note: Low is Reynolds's floor for all frontier killings; the Newcastle count covers massacres only, a subset, and is not added.

events.says: A long series of conflicts between British colonists and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples from the first settlement in 1788 across what became every Australian colony, including raids, reprisal killings, massacres and the Native Police, lasting into the 1930s.
events.open: Totals depend on the definition of a massacre or a frontier killing and on records that colonists often did not keep; the mapping project says its count may be a minimum. Whether the conflicts should be called a war is debated, and the end date differs (1930 for the Newcastle project, 1934 in other counts).

sources.title: Colonial Frontier Massacres in Australia, 1788-1930
sources.publisher: Centre for 21st Century Humanities, University of Newcastle

sources.title: Colonial Frontier Massacres in Australia, 1788-1930 (project record)
sources.publisher: Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies

events.name: Haitian Revolution

toll.text: Necrometrics lists Dumas at 160,000 dead in all (French 60,000, whites 50,000, free people of colour 50,000) and Scheina at 350,000 Haitians dead, with only 10,000 of 55,131 French soldiers surviving; Rogozinski, over 145,000 enslaved people dead; Trager, 2,000 whites and 10,000 Black and mixed-race people killed in 1791. Wikipedia gives Haitians 200,000, France 57,000 to 75,000, Britain 100,000 dead or wounded and white colonists 25,000. Encyclopedia.com says Haiti's population fell by at least 125,000 between 1789 and 1804; EBSCO gives about 10,000 Black dead and 2,000 whites in the first uprising.
toll.note: Low is Dumas's total for all groups; high is Scheina's count of Haitian dead alone, to which French and British soldier dead (mostly of yellow fever) would be added.

events.says: A revolution that began with the rising of enslaved people in the northern plain of Saint-Domingue in August 1791, became a war against French, Spanish and British forces under leaders including Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, and ended with the French defeat at Vertières in November 1803 and independence on 1 January 1804.
events.open: Most European dead died of yellow fever, most Haitian dead of violence; sources disagree on both and on whether the massacre of white colonists in 1804 is counted.

sources.title: Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: War in the Vendée

toll.text: Secher counts at least 117,257 dead of 815,029 inhabitants in 773 communes (about 15 percent), by comparing ancien regime estimates with the 1802 census, without allowing for those who fled. Martin gives up to 250,000 insurgents and 200,000 republicans; Chaunu 500,000 insurgent dead, which the reviewer calls 'ridiculous'; Martin and Lardière count 300 to 500 of 2,320 people killed at Les Lucs. Wikipedia gives about 170,000 inhabitants of the Vendée and about 200,000 in all. Necrometrics lists Sorokin 58,000, Clodfelter 80,000 to 100,000 in 1793, Bell 250,000, Rummel 263,000, Trager 300,000 to 600,000.
toll.note: Low is Secher's minimum for the insurgent area; high is Martin's two figures added (insurgents and republicans).

events.says: A counter-revolutionary rising in western France in March 1793 against conscription and the Revolution's religious policy, fought by Catholic and Royal armies of the Vendée against the Republic, and suppressed with columns that burned villages and killed civilians, ending with pacification in 1796.
events.open: Historians disagree on the count and on whether the repression was a genocide, as Secher argues; the review read rejects his method as ignoring those who fled, and some figures are for the Vendée militaire only.

sources.title: Review of Reynald Secher, A French Genocide: The Vendee (H-France Review 4, no. 26, 2004)
Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: White Lotus Rebellion

toll.text: Necrometrics lists about 100,000 rebels killed; Wikipedia gives the same figure for rebel dead and 'unknown' for the Qing side. No count of civilian or government dead was found.
toll.note: Low is rebel dead alone, so it is a floor.

events.says: A rising of followers of the White Lotus millenarian sect against the Qing dynasty in the hills of Hubei, Sichuan and Shaanxi from 1796, put down by 1804 with local militias and a scorched-earth policy against rebel villages.
events.open: The figure counts rebels only; the war's cost in civilian dead, famine and disease is not given in the sources read.

sources.title: Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: Irish Rebellion of 1798

toll.text: Necrometrics lists Foster at 30,000 dead by summer 1798, the BBC at 40,000 dead in the Wexford rebellion, and Smith at 50,000 dead. Wikipedia gives 10,000 to 50,000 combatant and civilian deaths, and 500 to 2,000 government military deaths and about 1,000 loyalist civilians.
toll.note: Low and high are the narrowest published range among the counts read; Wikipedia's lower end is 10,000.

events.says: A rising by the Society of United Irishmen against British rule, strongest in Leinster, Ulster and Connacht, from May to September 1798, with a French landing at Killala in August. The rising was put down and led to the Act of Union of 1800.
events.open: Totals mix combatants and civilians, and most of the dead were rebels and their families killed in the field and in reprisals; the lower and upper ends differ by a factor of five.

sources.title: Necrometrics: death tolls of the wars and atrocities of the eighteenth century

events.name: French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars

toll.text: Estimates of deaths in the whole period run from about 2 million military dead (Delbrück, cited via Dumas) to 5,925,084 dead in 1801 to 1815 including about 1 million French and German civilians (Fröhlich). Urlanis counts 3,105,000 military killed or dead (Russia 450,000, Spain over 300,000, France 1.2 million); Ellis, citing Esdaile, about 3 million European military dead plus 1 million civilians; Clodfelter, as cited in Wikipedia, gives 306,000 French killed (1805-1815) and 396,000 Austrian, 299,000 Russian and 154,000 Prussian killed in action. The Fondation Napoléon puts French dead in 1792-1815 at 600,000 to 1.3 million and Europe-wide losses of the Imperial wars (about 1805-1815) at 1 to 2.5 million men.
toll.note: Low is the lowest whole-war military figure in the sources read (Delbrück); high is Fröhlich's total with civilians. Many of the figures count only soldiers, or only killed in action, or only part of the period, and they cannot be added together.

events.says: A series of wars between France, under the Republic and then the Empire, and shifting coalitions of European powers, from April 1792 to Napoleon's final defeat in 1815. They were fought across most of Europe and ended with the Congress of Vienna settlement.
events.open: The Fondation Napoléon states that an exact total is almost impossible to establish and that civilian losses have barely been studied; the often-quoted 3.1 million French dead (Taine) is described as open to challenge. Clodfelter's separate war-by-war figures in Wikipedia also include 2,400,000 deaths for the Peninsular War, which the same page does not count among the coalition wars. The Peninsular War and the French invasion of Russia (1812) are theatres of this war and have their own entries; their deaths are included in the larger war's totals, so the entries must not be added together.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)
Bullet Point 6: Was Napoleon responsible for the deaths of 'millions of soldiers'?

events.name: Peninsular War

toll.text: Clodfelter (2008) gives 1,000,000 or more military and civilian dead, the figure in Wikipedia's casualty box; Clodfelter's 2017 edition, cited on Wikipedia's page for the wider Napoleonic wars, gives 2,400,000. Other estimates cover parts of it: Urlanis puts Spanish deaths at over 300,000 within his Napoleonic total, and Payne is quoted as saying the war may have cost a quarter of a million Portuguese lives.
toll.note: Low is the 'one million or more' of Clodfelter's earlier edition and high is the later edition; the sources do not separate military from civilian deaths, or deaths in battle from those of famine and disease.

events.says: The war in Spain and Portugal from the French occupation and the Spanish rising of May 1808 to French withdrawal in 1814, fought by Spain, Portugal and Britain against France and her allies. It ended in a coalition victory, the restoration of the Spanish Bourbons and, soon after, revolts in Spanish America.
events.open: The two editions of one source differ by more than a factor of two, and neither is explained. No source read separates civilians from soldiers. The start date is given as 2 May 1808 or, by some, 27 October 1807. Deaths in the war are also counted inside the totals of the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: Russo-Turkish War (1806-1812)

toll.text: Urlanis counts 225,000 soldiers killed and dead; Mackenbach (2020), cited in Wikipedia, also gives 225,000; the OnWar data set gives 170,000 (Russia 70,000, Ottoman Empire 100,000); Eckhardt gives 45,000 military.
toll.note: Low is Eckhardt's military figure; high is Urlanis and Mackenbach. Most figures are soldiers killed and dead of disease; none counts civilians.

events.says: A war between the Russian and Ottoman empires from the Ottoman deposition of the Russian-aligned princes of Moldavia and Wallachia in 1806 until the Treaty of Bucharest in May 1812. Fighting was mainly along the lower Danube and in the Caucasus; Russia annexed eastern Moldavia as Bessarabia.
events.open: The totals do not agree: 70,000 and 100,000 add to 170,000, not the 225,000 listed beside them, and both national figures trace to one web compilation. Some historians call the outcome a Russian victory and others call it indecisive. No per-person roll of the dead was found, so the records listed are archives that hold the armies' and the Principalities' papers, not a death register.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: Musket Wars

toll.text: Te Ara (the Encyclopedia of New Zealand) says there were probably around 20,000 deaths from direct and indirect causes and that the real number is not known. The Oxford Companion to New Zealand Military History, quoted by NZHistory, gives 20,000 to 30,000 dead in battle or of disease, with one estimate as high as 80,000. Wikipedia gives 20,000 to 40,000, with 30,000 enslaved or forced to migrate and about 300 Moriori killed and 1,700 enslaved.
toll.note: Low is Te Ara's and the Oxford Companion's lower figure; high is the single highest estimate the Oxford Companion mentions. All count Maori killed in fighting and those who died of its consequences.

events.says: A series of intertribal wars among Maori in Aotearoa New Zealand, from the first recorded use of muskets in battle in 1807 to the 1840s, in which tribes with early access to muskets raided and displaced others. The wars include the 1835 invasion of the Chatham Islands, where Maori invaders killed and enslaved Moriori.
events.open: Historians dispute the name and the reading: Angela Ballara argues the fighting continued Maori custom but became more destructive with firearms, and James Belich proposed 'Potato Wars'. The period is given as 1806 to 1845 on Wikipedia; its last battles in Southland were in 1836-37 and a final stand-off at Te Ihupuku in 1845. No source read lists the dead by name, so no records are listed here.

sources.title: The musket-wars period
sources.publisher: Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand

events.name: Finnish War

toll.text: Wikipedia's casualty box, citing Hornborg (1955) and Sandstrom (2008), lists 10,000 Russian and 7,000 Swedish killed or wounded, and 53,000 who died of disease and other hardships, without saying which side or sides the 53,000 belong to. A study of the Roback military hospital near Umea (Historical Life Course Studies, 2026) finds that epidemic disease, mainly typhus and dysentery, caused most of the illness and deaths among Swedish soldiers, far outnumbering battle injuries, but gives no total.
toll.note: Low is the one disease figure given; it is not a floor from the sources but the only total, and its scope (one army or both) is not stated. Battle deaths are in the tens of thousands at most and are not separated from the wounded.

events.says: A war between Sweden and Russia, with Denmark-Norway and the United Kingdom also involved on opposite sides, fought mainly in Finland from February 1808 to the Treaty of Fredrikshamn of 17 September 1809. Sweden ceded Finland and Aland to Russia, and Finland became an autonomous grand duchy.
events.open: Whether the 53,000 disease deaths are Swedish, Russian or both is not stated, and the total of killed in action is not separated from the wounded. Whether the war reaches 20,000 deaths depends on that reading. Civilian deaths are not counted in the sources read.

sources.title: Cause-of-Death Statistics in Sweden During the Finnish War 1808-1809: the Wegelius Journal from Roback Hospital

events.name: Mexican War of Independence

toll.text: Scheina (Latin America's Wars) puts the dead at 250,000 to 500,000; Clodfelter at 400,000 to 500,000 violent deaths, Mexican and Spanish; Juan Gonzalez (Harvest of Empire) at 600,000. Wikipedia's casualty box gives 250,000 to 600,000.
toll.note: Low and high are the extremes among the estimates read; all are totals of soldiers and civilians on every side.

events.says: A war between the Viceroyalty of New Spain and insurgents that began with Hidalgo's Cry of Dolores on 16 September 1810 and ended on 27 September 1821 after the Treaty of Cordoba and the joining of the Army of the Three Guarantees. Spain lost the mainland of New Spain; it did not recognise Mexican independence until 1836.
events.open: Historians describe it as a set of local and regional struggles, possibly a revolutionary civil war, not one event. The sources do not give how the estimates were made or separate battle deaths from deaths of disease and famine.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: Venezuelan War of Independence

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 250,000 to 500,000 dead. Necrometrics quotes Harvey (Liberators) that more than a quarter of a million were killed in winning Gran Colombia's independence, Scheina that Venezuela lost about a quarter of its million people, Gonzalez that it lost half of its nearly 1 million, Clodfelter that its population fell by 100,000 (from 300,000) in 15 years, and Eckhardt at 37,000 deaths in the whole New Granada war.
toll.note: Low and high are the range given for Venezuela; the lowest figure in the sources (Eckhardt, 37,000) and the highest (half the population) lie outside it. Population loss includes deaths of famine, disease and flight, not only killing.

events.says: The war between republican governments and the Spanish crown in Venezuela from the junta of 19 April 1810 to the Spanish surrender in 1823, including the First and Second Republics, the 'war to the death' of 1813 and the campaigns of Bolivar. Royalist control of mainland Venezuela ended.
events.open: Population-loss figures mix deaths with emigration; the sources do not separate them. Baselines for the 1810 population differ (about 300,000 to nearly 1 million). The Colombian War of Independence entry covers the neighbouring New Granada theatre; its figure in some sources also includes Venezuela.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: Colombian War of Independence

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 400,000 deaths, about 15 percent of the 1810 population of New Granada and Venezuela together. Necrometrics gives 250,000 for the New Granada (Gran Colombia) wars of independence, quoting Harvey (Liberators) that more than a quarter of a million had been killed; it also quotes Scheina that Ecuador's population fell from 600,000 to 480,000.
toll.note: Low is the necrometrics headline for the whole Gran Colombia war; high is the Wikipedia figure, which also includes Venezuela.

events.says: The wars between Spanish royalists and republican governments in the Viceroyalty of New Granada, from the juntas of 1810 to the royalist defeat at Boyaca (1819), Pichincha (1822) and the end of Spanish power in 1825, and the creation of the Republic of Colombia in 1819.
events.open: The 400,000 figure covers Venezuela as well and so overlaps the Venezuelan War of Independence entry; the two must not be added. Population-loss figures do not separate deaths from flight or from disease. Quito formed a junta before Bogota (1809), and the start date of 20 July 1810 is only the traditional one.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: French invasion of Russia (1812)

toll.text: Wikipedia's casualty box gives 300,000 to 350,000 French and allied dead (about 100,000 in combat, 200,000 from other causes and 50,000 in captivity; sources Clodfelter, Bodart and Lentz) and 210,000 Russian dead (Bogdanovich), together 510,000 to 560,000 soldiers; its text gives about 380,000 French lives lost, dead or missing. Zamoyski (2004), cited there, gives about 1,000,000 military and civilian deaths together.
toll.note: Low is the two military figures in the infobox added together; high is the combined military and civilian figure. Civilian deaths are not separately counted by any source read.

events.says: Napoleon's campaign against the Russian Empire, from 24 June to 24 December 1812. It ended in a Russian victory, with the Grande Armee reduced by battle, disease and other causes.
events.open: The Fondation Napoléon notes that tens of thousands of French deserters may have settled in Russia, so many men listed as missing did not die. Estimates are described as elusive because detailed records are missing, and as sometimes leaving out auxiliary troops. Civilian losses have barely been studied. The campaign is a theatre of the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars and its deaths are included in that war's totals.

sources.title: Bullet Point 6: Was Napoleon responsible for the deaths of 'millions of soldiers'?
Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: War of 1812

toll.text: Wikipedia's casualty box gives up to 15,000 American dead from all causes (Hickey; Stagg), including about 2,200 killed in action and 5,200 of disease, 10,000 British dead from all causes (Clodfelter), and 10,000 allied Indigenous warriors and civilians dead from all causes (Clodfelter). Hickey (cited on necrometrics) counts about 20,000 American dead, of which 2,260 were killed in action and about 17,000 died of disease; Eckhardt gives 4,000 military dead in all.
toll.note: Low is the American and British all-cause figures added; high adds the Indigenous figure. Battle deaths alone are far smaller (about 2,260 American and 2,700 British); most deaths were of disease.

events.says: A war between the United States and the United Kingdom and its colonies in North America, with Indigenous nations allied to the British, from the American declaration of 18 June 1812 to ratification of the Treaty of Ghent on 17 February 1815. It restored the pre-war borders.
events.open: Whether the war reaches 20,000 deaths depends on whether disease deaths and Indigenous deaths are counted: combat deaths on all sides are well under that. The 5,200 American disease figure is flagged on Wikipedia as needing a further citation. No source read gives separate civilian totals. Historians dispute who gained from the war.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: Greek War of Independence

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 15,000 Greek combat dead, 44,000 to 50,000 Ottoman soldiers, 230,000 to 600,000 Greek civilians (Kitromilides) and 15,000 to 25,000 Muslim civilians, a sum of roughly 300,000 to 690,000. Necrometrics lists Urlanis at 60,000, Eckhardt and Correlates of War at 120,000 (105,000 civilians and 15,000 military), and Singer at 15,000 Turks killed; it also reports that on Psara all but 3,000 of 20,000 inhabitants were killed and 7,000 were massacred on Kasos in 1824.
toll.note: Low is Urlanis; high is the sum of the upper figures given on Wikipedia. The estimates count civilians very differently and are not comparable.

events.says: A revolt against Ottoman rule begun with the Wallachian uprising of 21 February 1821 and fought by Greek forces, with British, French and Russian intervention from 1826 against Ottoman and Egyptian forces. It ended with Greek independence confirmed by treaty.
events.open: The Greek civilian toll is given as anything from 230,000 to 600,000 and the earlier compilations give 120,000 or fewer. The Chios massacre of 1822 is put at up to 100,000 killed or enslaved in one popular source. No source read lists the civilian dead by name.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: Java War

toll.text: Carey (1976), cited in Wikipedia, puts Javanese civilian deaths at least 200,000 from violence, disease and starvation, and Dutch military deaths at 15,000 (8,000 European and 7,000 local recruits), with up to 20,000 rebel dead (Blank; Clodfelter). Necrometrics lists Albertini at 200,000 and Clodfelter at 200,000 Javanese, of whom no more than a tenth died in battle, with 8,000 Dutch and 7,000 loyalist native dead. A chapter by Kris Jos van Beurden calls it the deadliest of the Dutch wars in the archipelago, with about 200,000 Javanese dead, mostly of starvation and exhaustion.
toll.note: Low is the Javanese civilian figure; it is stated as 'at least' and does not include about 15,000 Dutch-side and up to 20,000 rebel military dead.

events.says: A war between the Dutch colonial government and Javanese rebels led by Prince Diponegoro, from the first clashes of July 1825 to Diponegoro's capture in March 1830. It ended in a Dutch victory and Diponegoro's exile to Sulawesi.
events.open: How the 200,000 figure was reckoned is not stated. Colonial reports put the population of Mataram, Yogyakarta and Gunung Kidul at just over 400,000 before and under 200,000 after, which mixes death with flight. Wikipedia's casualty box gives 2,000 further Dutch and German elite-corps dead for 1827-1829 and does not say whether they are part of the 15,000.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)
Indonesia, the Netherlands and Diponegoro's kris (chapter by Kris Jos van Beurden)

events.name: Russo-Turkish War (1828-1829)

toll.text: Phillips and Axelrod (Encyclopedia of Wars), cited in Wikipedia, give 42,515 Russian and 80,000 Ottoman dead, 122,515 in all. Necrometrics lists the Correlates of War at 130,000 (Russia 50,000, Ottoman Empire 80,000), Eckhardt at 191,000 (61,000 civilians and 130,000 military) and Urlanis at 205,000 military killed and dead. EBSCO's research starter says Russia lost nearly 140,000 men on both fronts, most of disease, and the Ottoman Empire about 80,000, mainly to disease.
toll.note: Low is the Phillips and Axelrod total; high is the EBSCO total (140,000 plus 80,000). Most deaths are of disease, and the figures count soldiers only except Eckhardt's civilians.

events.says: A war between the Russian and Ottoman empires, declared by Russia on 26 April 1828, fought in the Balkans and the Caucasus, ending with the Treaty of Adrianople in September 1829. Russia gained the east Black Sea coast and the Danube mouth, Serbia gained autonomy and the Ottomans recognised Greek independence.
events.open: Wikipedia dates the treaty both 2 and 14 September 1829. Plague and other disease are said to account for most Russian army losses, but no source read gives a figure for them. Wikipedia also records a migration of about 90,000 Armenians to Russian territory, which is not a death count. No per-person roll was found.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: French conquest of Algeria

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 500,000 to 1,000,000 Algerian deaths in 1830-1862, mostly civilians (Schaller, Jalata, Greenhalgh, Kateb and others); Greenhalgh's conservative estimate is over 480,000 dead on both sides in 1830-1862, mostly civilians of disease. Kiernan (Blood and Soil, cited on necrometrics) gives 825,000 Algerians killed up to 1875. Bennoune puts the population falling from about 3 million in 1830 to 2,462,000 in 1876; Britannica says the best estimates are a fall of nearly one third by the mid-1870s. French military losses: 3,336 killed in battle and 92,329 dead in hospital in 1831-1851, and 7,469 killed in action in 1830-1875.
toll.note: Low is Greenhalgh's figure for both sides in 1830-1862; high is the top of the Wikipedia range. The periods and the groups counted differ between sources and the totals cannot be added.

events.says: The French invasion of the Regency of Algiers in 1830 and the campaigns that followed, against Abd al-Qadir to his surrender in 1847 and then against later risings, until French control of the Saharan south in 1903. Algiers fell in 1830 and the colony was annexed in 1834.
events.open: Whether the conquest was a genocide is disputed: William Gallois (Cambridge World History of Genocide, 2023) writes that Western scholarship has largely contested it while many Algerian accounts treat it as given. The 1830 population base is itself disputed (about 2.5 to 4 million in colonial counts). Most Algerian deaths were of disease and famine, not fighting, and the date range used for the totals varies.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)
The genocidal French conquest of Algeria, 1830-1847 (chapter by William Gallois)

events.name: First Carlist War

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 111,000 to 306,000 dead including civilians, with 5 percent of Spain's 1833 population dead and military deaths about half of that, and elsewhere 'more than 120,000' (Bullon de Mendoza). Necrometrics lists Clodfelter at up to 140,000 (65,000 government and 60,000 Carlist), the Correlates of War at 135,229, Urlanis at 50,000, Eckhardt at 33,000 and Singer at 32,650.
toll.note: Low is Eckhardt's military figure; high is the upper end of Wikipedia's range with civilians. Most estimates cluster at 120,000 to 140,000.

events.says: A civil war in Spain from the death of Ferdinand VII in September 1833, between the Carlists backing his brother Carlos and the Liberals backing the regency for Isabella II, the latter supported by Britain, France and Portugal. It ended in a Liberal victory, with the Convention of Vergara, and is dated to 6 July 1840.
events.open: Wikipedia credits its 111,000 to 306,000 to Salvador (2018), but the abstract of that article gives no figures; it says the war's effects were severe where fighting was heaviest but not grave for Spain as a whole. The Carlist and liberal figures in Wikipedia's casualty box are partly flagged as needing citations. The Carlist Wars of 1846-1849 and 1872-1876 are not included here.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)
Salvador, A. C. (2018), on the First Carlist War's effect on Spain's population and economy
sources.publisher: Cuadernos de Historia Contemporanea (Universidad Complutense de Madrid)

events.name: Cabanagem

toll.text: The Brazilian educational site InfoEscola gives a final toll of 30,000 dead. Wikipedia gives more than 40,000 dead among soldiers, militia, rebels and civilians, and also says 30 to 40 percent of the population of Grao-Para, put at about 100,000, is thought to have died, with a fall from about 100,000 to 60,000 over five years attributed to Renato Cancian. The province's 1833 count was 119,877.
toll.note: Low is the 30,000 toll; high is 40,000, which is stated as 'more than'. The percentage figures measure loss of population, not only deaths.

events.says: A rising in the Brazilian province of Grao-Para from 1835 to 1840, in which the rebels, the cabanos, twice took the capital Belem and held the province for a time before Imperial forces retook it and fought on in the interior. It ended in an Imperial victory.
events.open: The 30,000 figure is repeated but its source is a single 19th-century historian and no census supports it, according to a review of Mark Harris's Rebellion on the Amazon; the 40,000 plus has no source in the Wikipedia text. The population baselines differ (about 100,000 and 119,877). No source read gives the names of the dead.

events.name: First Anglo-Afghan War

toll.text: Wikipedia's casualty box gives 15,000 to 40,000 dead among the British, sepoys and camp followers, and 'unknown' for the Afghans (Dalrymple, 2013). Necrometrics lists the Correlates of War (Singer) at 20,000 British-side killed and Eckhardt at 20,000 military. Historic UK says about 16,000 people left Kabul on 6 January 1842, that over 16,000 lives were lost in a matter of days, and that William Brydon was the only known survivor to reach Jalalabad.
toll.note: Low and high are the extremes in the casualty box; the sources do not say how the range was derived, and Afghan deaths are not counted.

events.says: A war in which the British East India Company's army invaded Afghanistan in 1838 against the Barakzai rulers of Kabul and Kandahar, was besieged in Kabul and was almost completely destroyed on the retreat from Kabul in January 1842; the British left after recovering prisoners, and the war is dated to 12 October 1842.
events.open: The number who left Kabul is given as between 2,000 and 5,000 troops plus civilians, or about 16,000 people in all. Some hostages and prisoners survived and were later recovered, so 'sole survivor' is a figure of speech. No source read counts Afghan deaths.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: Caste War of Yucatan

toll.text: Wikipedia gives an estimated 40,000 to 50,000 dead in the text and, in its casualty box, about 314,000 rebels and 50,000 soldiers dead, 364,000 in all, citing Gabbert (2019). A University of North Carolina exhibit says census data show the population of Yucatan was halved and almost 250,000 people died or fled. Necrometrics lists the Correlates of War at 300,000 for the Yucatan war of 1847-1855. Encyclopedia.com says the peninsula's population fell by at least 30 to 40 percent.
toll.note: Low is the figure in Wikipedia's text; high is its casualty-box total. Population-loss figures mix deaths, flight and migration.

events.says: A revolt by Maya against Yucatecan rule from 1847, in which Maya forces held about three quarters of the peninsula in 1848 before being pushed back, and an independent Maya state, Chan Santa Cruz, lasted in the east until Mexican troops took its capital in 1901.
events.open: The end date is disputed: 1901 (capture of Chan Santa Cruz), 1915 (formal end declared by General Alvarado) and 1933 (last skirmish). The two death figures on Wikipedia differ by a factor of nine and the smaller is uncited. A summary of Reed's 1964 book gives about 147,000 dead in 1847-1855. No source read lists the dead by name.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: Hungarian Revolution of 1848

toll.text: Wikipedia's casualty box gives 45,000 dead from all causes (side unlabelled), 16,600 Austrian killed or wounded, 41,000 Austrian dead of disease, and 903 Russian killed and 13,554 dead of disease. Necrometrics lists Urlanis at 100,000 and Clodfelter at 60,000 for the Hungarian war.
toll.note: Low is the casualty-box figure; high is Urlanis. The figures count soldiers; civilian deaths are not given.

events.says: The war of 1848-1849 between Hungarian revolutionaries and the Habsburg Austrian Empire, joined in 1849 by a Russian army, ending with the Hungarian army's surrender at Vilagos on 13 August 1849. Habsburg rule was restored under martial law.
events.open: The 45,000 on Wikipedia is not labelled as to side, and the Austrian and Russian dead it lists add up to more than 45,000. Other figures in the same box mix killed, wounded and prisoners. Executions after the surrender (including on 6 October 1849) are not counted in any figure read.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: Nian Rebellion

toll.text: Wikipedia gives more than 100,000 killed on the Nian side (Jowett, China's Wars, 2013), the only death figure in its article; Small and Singer (Correlates of War), cited on necrometrics, give 75,000.
toll.note: Low is the Correlates of War figure and the Jowett figure is 'more than'; neither counts the floods and famine of the region or Qing losses.

events.says: A rebellion by the Nian in north China, in the lands between the Huai and Yellow rivers, against the Qing dynasty from the early 1850s, linked to but not fully joined with the Taiping, until the Qing crushed the last forces in 1868.
events.open: Neither source reports Qing army or civilian deaths, and the article describes 'immense loss of life' from Yellow River floods in 1851 and 1855 without counts. No registers of the dead of this rising exist among the sources read.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: Crimean War

toll.text: Clodfelter (2017), cited in Wikipedia, gives 165,363 Allied dead (Ottoman 45,400, French 95,615, British 22,182, Sardinian 2,166), of whom 45,770 died in combat, and, with Figes, 450,015 Russian dead (73,125 in combat); Dumas and Vedel-Petersen give 630,000 and Russian sources (Tashlykov, Kozlovsky) 522,000. Necrometrics lists Singer and Eckhardt at about 264,000, Bodart at 277,173, Urlanis at 309,000, the 1911 Britannica at 508,000 and Mulhall at 609,797; Edgerton says it probably exceeded 1 million.
toll.note: Low is the lowest of the modern compilations (Singer, Eckhardt); high is the top of the range quoted on Wikipedia. Disease killed more men than battle in every army.

events.says: A war between the Russian Empire and an alliance of the Ottoman Empire, France, the United Kingdom and (from 1855) Sardinia, fought mainly in the Crimea and around the Black Sea from October 1853 to the Treaty of Paris of 30 March 1856. Russia lost the Danube delta and southern Bessarabia and could not keep warships in the Black Sea.
events.open: The compilations differ by a factor of four, mostly over Russian deaths from disease. The Wikipedia infobox gives 0.61 to 0.67 million and the older compilations 0.26 to 0.31 million. About 200,000 Crimean Tatars were displaced; this is not counted as death.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: Miao Rebellion (1854-1873)

toll.text: Wikipedia's casualty box gives 5 million, citing a chapter on the end of the Miao rebellions in the Peking Gazette (Brill), and its text elsewhere notes the figures are likely overstated. Farwell (Encyclopedia of Nineteenth-Century Land Warfare), quoted on necrometrics, says casualties including civilians were estimated at one and a half million for the Miao rebellions of 1855-1872; Small and Singer (Correlates of War) give 75,000.
toll.note: Low is the Correlates of War figure; high is the casualty-box figure. The two differ by a factor of about 65.

events.says: A series of risings in Guizhou and neighbouring provinces against the Qing from 1854, by Miao, Buyi (Bouyei), Tujia and Hui people, overlapping with the Taiping Rebellion, which the Qing put down one group at a time after the Taiping were defeated.
events.open: The name is misleading: Robert Jenks estimates that ethnic Miao made up less than half of the participants. Most contemporary records come from Qing officials. No end date is given for the whole, and the war is connected with the Taiping period, so these deaths may be counted in other wars.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: Punti-Hakka Clan Wars

toll.text: Wikipedia says 500,000 perished from fighting (citing a 2003 paper on Taishan County) and up to 1 million in all (Minahan, 2014), with more dying of epidemics than in fighting. Necrometrics gives 500,000 (Jon Kehrer), which it describes as a thinly sourced figure.
toll.note: Low is the fighting-only figure; high is Minahan's 'up to one million'. Epidemic deaths are said to exceed battle deaths but are not counted.

events.says: A series of conflicts between Punti (Cantonese-speaking) and Hakka communities in Guangdong, especially the Pearl River Delta and the Sze Yup counties, from 1855, set off by the Red Turban rising, until about 1867-1868. After the wars Hakka made up about 3 percent of the Sze Yup population and many captives were sold as labourers overseas.
events.open: The sources are weak: a conference paper, a 2014 reference book and a web compilation, none with a method. The end date is given as 1867 or 1868. Hakka losses are said to have been proportionally larger, but no group-level figures are given. No index of the dead was found in the sources read.

sources.title: Nineteenth Century Death Tolls (Statistics of Wars, Oppressions and Atrocities of the Nineteenth Century)

events.name: American Civil War

toll.text: The long-accepted count is about 620,000 soldiers dead. The National Park Service prints Union deaths of 110,100 killed in battle and 224,580 from disease, and Confederate deaths of 94,000 in battle and 164,000 from disease. A census-based study in Civil War History (December 2011) put military deaths at about 750,000, with a range of 650,000 to 850,000. Wikipedia's infobox gives 616,222 to over 1,000,000 dead once civilians and enslaved people are counted.
toll.note: Low is the traditional count of soldiers' deaths; high is the top of the 2011 census-based range for soldiers. Civilian and enslaved deaths are in neither figure.

events.says: War between the United States and eleven Southern states that left it to form the Confederate States of America, fought mainly in the South from 1861 to 1865. It ended with the surrender of the Confederate armies and the abolition of slavery.
events.open: The census-based method cannot split Union from Confederate dead, and it counts all excess male deaths in the decade, not only deaths in service. Disease killed more soldiers than battle. Deaths among civilians and among enslaved people are counted differently by each source.

sources.title: New analysis suggests Civil War took bigger toll than previously estimated (release on Civil War History, Dec 2011, vol. 57 no. 4)

events.name: Indian Rebellion of 1857

toll.text: Conventional histories count about 100,000 Indians killed in reprisals (Dawn, 2007). A British historian quoted there puts the toll at hundreds of thousands. Wikipedia gives about 6,000 British killed including civilians and, from comparing pre-1857 population data with the 1871 census, about 800,000 Indians. A Mumbai-based historian argues for almost 10 million deaths over ten years, which the same report calls an overestimate.
toll.note: Low is the conventional count of Indian dead in reprisals; high is the census-comparison reconstruction. Neither is a count of named deaths; the 10 million claim is outside this range.

events.says: Uprising that began in May 1857 among Indian soldiers of the East India Company's army at Meerut and spread through the Ganges plain, with Delhi, Kanpur and Lucknow as main centres. The Company and British forces had retaken the major cities by 1858.
events.open: No census exists for the period. Population falls in affected areas may reflect flight as well as death, as a historian at the Indian Council of Historical Research argues. Civilian deaths in the fighting and in the reprisals are not separated.

sources.title: Millions died after 1857 war of independence: historian

events.name: Second French intervention in Mexico

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox lists 31,962 killed (including 11,000 executed) for one side and 14,000 dead for the other, about 45,962 together. The encyclopedia entry consulted gives no casualty figures, so these numbers have no second source here.
toll.note: Low is the sum of the two infobox figures; the war has no total from a count of the dead. At least.

events.says: French invasion of Mexico from 1861 with Spanish and British forces at first, then France alone, which set up the Second Mexican Empire under Maximilian. Mexican republican forces under Benito Juarez fought on, French troops withdrew, and the empire fell in 1867.
events.open: Whether the 11,000 executions are included in other sources' totals is not settled here, and deaths from disease and among civilians are not given by the sources read.

sources.title: French Intervention in Mexico (Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture)

events.name: Paraguayan War (War of the Triple Alliance)

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 150,000 to 500,000 dead in all, with Paraguay's losses likely 175,000 to 300,000. A 1999 study in Latin American Research Review, summarised by Encyclopedia.com, puts Paraguay's population at 420,000 to 450,000 in 1864 and 140,000 to 166,000 in 1870, a fall of 60 to 69 percent, higher than earlier estimates. Wikidata records 1,000,000 deaths.
toll.note: Low and high span the published estimates of deaths on all sides. The 1864 to 1870 population fall (roughly 254,000 to 310,000 people by simple subtraction) counts all causes of loss and is not a death count.

events.says: War of Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay against Paraguay, fought from 1864 to 1870 after Paraguayan forces entered Brazilian and Argentine territory. It ended with the death of Paraguay's president Francisco Solano Lopez in 1870 and heavy losses for Paraguay.
events.open: The size of the population fall is disputed, since the 1870 census and the pre-war base are both uncertain. Disease, hunger and flight are not separated from killing. Wikidata's 1,000,000 is far above the demographic estimates.

sources.title: Paraguay, Demography (Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture)

events.name: Franco-Prussian War

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox lists 138,871 French dead and 44,781 German dead, together 183,652, and separately 450,000 French civilians dead. The encyclopedia entry consulted gives no casualty figures, so these numbers have no second source here.
toll.note: Low is soldiers' deaths on both sides from the infobox. The civilian figure is not added because it is a single-source figure that mixes disease with war. At least.

events.says: War between France and a North German-led coalition under Prussia, fought in 1870 and 1871 mainly in northern and eastern France. It ended with the French surrender at Sedan and Paris, the proclamation of the German Empire and the French loss of Alsace and most of Lorraine.
events.open: Civilian deaths, especially from smallpox and from the siege of Paris, are counted very differently from source to source.

events.name: Aceh War

toll.text: Correlates of War data, quoted by the Polynational War Memorial, give 24,200 battle deaths and say the figure may be considerably higher. The same page's text estimates 50,000 to 60,000 Acehnese dead. Wikipedia's infobox gives 37,000 killed on the Dutch side (2,200 European), including cholera, and 60,000 to 70,000 on the Acehnese side.
toll.note: Low is the Correlates of War battle-death count. High adds the two infobox figures (37,000 and 70,000), which include cholera deaths.
