events.says: Colonial war between the Netherlands and the Sultanate of Aceh in northern Sumatra, begun in 1873. The sultanate surrendered in 1904 and guerrilla resistance continued afterwards.
events.open: The dating, the share of deaths caused by cholera and the Acehnese civilian toll are all uncertain; the polynational page's own dating of the war varies.

events.name: Mahdist War

toll.text: World History Encyclopedia gives 3,000 Mahdist dead at Atbara, 11,000 Sudanese killed at Omdurman and at least 4,000 civilians massacred at Khartoum, 18,000 in those three episodes alone. Wikipedia quotes Sir Reginald Wingate that Sudan's population fell by more than half under Mahdist rule, with estimates of 4 to 6 million, which some later academics consider exaggerated.
toll.note: Low is the sum of three episodes only (a floor, not a war total). High is a population loss from war, famine and disease, not a count of the dead in fighting.

events.says: War from 1881 between the Mahdist movement led by Muhammad Ahmad and the Egyptian state, later Britain. The Mahdists took Khartoum in 1885 and held Sudan until an Anglo-Egyptian army won at Omdurman in 1898; fighting ended in 1899.
events.open: No census exists for Sudan in these years. The population-loss estimates are disputed and mix famine and disease with fighting. Totals for the war as a whole were not found in the sources read.

sources.title: Mahdist War: Holy War in Sudan, 1881-99

events.name: Cuban War of Independence

toll.text: A 2015 paper (University of Nottingham author, Clark University conference proceedings) gives more than 150,000 victims of the reconcentration camps alone. Wikipedia's infobox lists 300,000 Cuban civilians dead, 9,413 Spanish killed and 53,313 Spanish dead of disease, and 5,480 killed and 3,437 dead of disease on the Cuban side.
toll.note: Low is the camp deaths named in the paper; high is the infobox figure for Cuban civilians. Combatant deaths are additional.

events.says: Third Cuban war against Spanish rule, begun in February 1895. Spain's reconcentration policy moved the rural population into fortified towns. US entry in 1898 ended the war and Spanish rule.
events.open: Estimates of civilian deaths from reconcentration range widely, and it is disputed how far the policy was intended to destroy a population or was a wartime measure whose results were worse than planned.

sources.title: Interpreting Reconcentration Camps in Cuba (1895-1898): Collateral Damage or Undercover Genocide?
sources.publisher: Clark University Center for Holocaust and Genocide Studies (conference papers)

events.name: War of Canudos

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives almost 25,000 dead on the Canudos side and fewer than 5,000 on the army side. A ReVista (Harvard Review of Latin America) essay says the fourth expedition took the lives of nearly 30,000 people.
toll.note: Low is the Canudos-side figure alone; high is the essay's total for the final expedition.

events.says: Conflict in 1896 and 1897 between the Brazilian republic and the followers of the preacher Antonio Conselheiro at Canudos in Bahia. Three army expeditions failed; the fourth destroyed the town in October 1897.
events.open: Neither source separates the dead of the town, the army and the survivors who were shot, and no list of names is given. How many of the dead were killed in the fighting rather than after surrender is not settled in the sources read.

sources.title: A Tale of the Three Canudos
sources.publisher: ReVista, Harvard Review of Latin America

events.name: Second Boer War

toll.text: South African History Online gives 27,927 Boer deaths in the white concentration camps (4,177 women, 22,074 children under sixteen, 1,676 men) and an official minimum of 14,154 Black African deaths in the separate camps, with one researcher's estimate of at least 20,000. Wikipedia's infobox adds 22,092 British and 6,189 Boer combatants dead.
toll.note: Low sums 28,281 combatants (Wikipedia), 27,927 Boer camp deaths and 14,154 Black camp deaths. High replaces 14,154 with 20,000. Deaths outside the camps are not included.

events.says: War from October 1899 to May 1902 between Britain and the two Boer republics, the South African Republic and the Orange Free State. Britain won; the republics became colonies. Boer civilians were held in camps, and separate camps held Black Africans.
events.open: The camp counts rest on incomplete British records, so the official totals are called too low. The combatant figures come from Wikipedia alone and include deaths from disease.

sources.title: Women and Children in White Concentration Camps during the Anglo-Boer War, 1900-1902
Black Concentration Camps during the Anglo-Boer War 2, 1900-1902

events.name: Thousand Days' War

toll.text: The Banco de la Republica's encyclopedia entry says the most conservative figures put the dead at about 100,000, 2.8 percent of Colombia's population, without naming who produced them. Wikipedia gives 100,000 to 180,000.
toll.note: Low is the conservative traditional figure; high is the top of Wikipedia's range.

events.says: Civil war in Colombia from October 1899 to November 1902, between the Liberal Party and the government. The Liberals lost the decisive battle of Palonegro in May 1900 and the war ended with three peace treaties in 1902. Fighting reached the Isthmus of Panama.
events.open: The 100,000 figure is traditional and its origin is not given in the entry read. Later demographic studies of the war's mortality exist and may give different totals; they were not read.

sources.title: La guerra de los mil dias
sources.publisher: Enciclopedia, Red Cultural del Banco de la Republica

events.name: Philippine-American War

toll.text: Wikipedia says modern historians generally place civilian deaths at 200,000 to 250,000, mostly from famine and disease, with 16,000 to 20,000 Filipino fighters and about 4,200 US dead (1,020 killed, 3,176 of disease). An Encyclopedia.com literary-history entry says more than 4,200 Americans and upwards of 17,500 Filipino soldiers were killed and puts the civilian toll at more than half a million.
toll.note: Low is 200,000 civilians plus about 20,000 combatants; high is 500,000 civilians plus the 17,500 and 4,200 combatants. Some estimates of civilian deaths exceed one million.

events.says: War from February 1899 between the United States and the First Philippine Republic, begun after the Spanish-American War transferred the islands to the United States. Main resistance ended in 1902, though fighting with other groups, especially in the south, went on to 1913.
events.open: Civilian deaths cannot be counted from the records and range from about 200,000 to well over a million. The end date is disputed: the US declared the war over in July 1902.

events.name: Panthay Rebellion

toll.text: No agreed figure was found. Wikipedia says the rebellion caused the deaths of up to a million people in Yunnan; the scholarly review consulted gives no number and describes massacres of Muslims by Han officials and militia.
toll.note: No range given because the up to a million claim has no second source here.

events.says: Rebellion of Hui Muslims and other groups against Qing rule in Yunnan, begun after the 1856 massacre of Muslims in Kunming. The rebels held Dali as the Pingnan Kingdom until Qing forces retook it in 1873.
events.open: A 2006 review of a book on the Panthay rebellion in the American Journal of Islam and Society describes the revolt as a Hui-led, multiethnic resistance, not only a religious one. Population loss estimates for Yunnan vary widely and are not agreed. No name-level source for the dead is listed here.

sources.title: Review of The Chinese Sultanate: Islam, Ethnicity, and the Panthay Rebellion in Southwest China, 1856-1873
sources.publisher: American Journal of Islam and Society

events.name: Federal War

toll.text: No agreed figure was found. Wikipedia's infobox gives 100,000+ dead without attribution; the Encyclopedia of Latin American History entry gives no figure for deaths or population loss.
toll.note: No range given because the 100,000+ figure has no second source here.

events.says: Civil war in Venezuela from February 1859 to April 1863 between the Conservative government and Liberal Federalists. It ended with the Treaty of Coche, and the Liberal Party emerged as the political victor.
events.open: Total deaths are not given by the encyclopedia entry read; contemporary Venezuelan population was only about a million.

sources.title: Federal War (Venezuela, 1859-1863)
sources.publisher: Encyclopedia.com (Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture)

events.name: Donghak (Tonghak) Peasant Revolution

toll.text: No agreed figure. Gwangju News (republishing a 2015 series) gives about 6,000 Joseon government soldiers and tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of rebels killed, and says only 500 of a 20,000-strong rebel force survived the Ugeumchi fighting. It cites no sources for these numbers.
toll.note: No range given because the rebel figure spans an order of magnitude and is unsourced.

events.says: Peasant uprising in Korea in 1894 and 1895 by followers of the Donghak movement against local officials and foreign influence. Joseon and Japanese forces crushed it, notably at Ugeumchi in late 1894.
events.open: Counts of the rebel dead are not agreed. The Wikipedia infobox gives about 200 Japanese soldiers killed. No name-level source for the dead is listed here.

sources.title: The Donghak Peasant Rebellion: A Bloody Chapter in Jeolla History

events.name: Gulf War

toll.text: Iraqi military dead are put at 20,000 to 26,000 by a 2003 Project on Defense Alternatives study; Iraqi civilians killed directly at 3,664 (a reconstruction by Daponte, accepted in the same study); coalition deaths at 292 (147 in action, 145 non-hostile); Kuwaiti dead at 420 military and over 1,000 civilians with 600 missing. Medact puts all Iraqi deaths, including the 1991 uprisings, at 142,500 to 206,000. Wikipedia's infobox total of 175,000 to 300,000+ carries no source.
toll.note: Low is the lowest direct counts added together (about 25,000). High is the Medact total, which includes deaths in the 1991 uprisings and is not limited to the war.

events.says: Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990. A coalition of 42 countries led by the United States fought Iraq from January 1991, and the war ended on 28 February 1991 with Kuwait liberated.
events.open: Iraqi military deaths rest on modelled loss rates, not a count of names, and run from 20,000 to 26,000 up to a Defense Intelligence Agency figure of about 100,000 reported with a margin of 50,000 either way. The uprisings that followed are listed separately. Sources used here give totals, not name rolls.

sources.title: The Wages of War: Iraqi Combatant and Noncombatant Fatalities in the 1991 Persian Gulf War (Appendix 2)

events.name: 1991 Iraqi uprisings

toll.text: The range printed for the uprisings is 25,000 to 180,000 killed, mostly civilians (press reports of 2006 and 2007 and Human Rights Watch, 1992). Human Rights Watch wrote in 1992 that tens of thousands of civilians were killed in the suppression and thousands more died in the flight of refugees, and that it could not verify the numbers. A Greenpeace estimate it cites puts deaths among Kurdish and Shia refugees at about 1,000 a day in April to June 1991. The prosecution in the 2007-08 Baghdad trial of former officials alleged 60,000 to 100,000 killed.
toll.note: Low and high are the published range, not a count. Human Rights Watch gives no total. Deaths among refugees and in the Gulf War itself are not separated.

events.says: Shia and Kurdish uprisings against the Iraqi government from 1 March to early April 1991, after the Gulf War. Government forces retook the cities and announced on 5 April that the uprisings were crushed; the Kurdistan Region became a de facto autonomous region under no-fly zones.
events.open: Totals differ by a factor of seven. A figure of about 5,000 is also attributed to Human Rights Watch. Iraq's Human Rights Ministry registered 200 mass graves between 2003 and 2006, one believed to hold as many as 10,000 bodies. The dead were not recorded by name in the sources used.

sources.title: Endless Torment: The 1991 Uprising in Iraq and Its Aftermath

events.name: Sierra Leone Civil War

toll.text: A 2006 Benetech and American Bar Association report says most analyses put killings in the conflict at 50,000 to 75,000. Wikipedia gives 50,000 to 70,000, from two academic studies of 2005 and 2006. JusticeInfo says tens of thousands died, with some 5,000 dead after the rebel seizure of parts of Freetown in January 1999. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission took 7,706 statements.
toll.note: Both ends are published estimates, not counts. The Benetech report goes on to estimate killings by statistical methods from several datasets.

events.says: A civil war in Sierra Leone from 23 March 1991, begun by the Revolutionary United Front, with the army, the Civil Defence Forces, ECOMOG, Guinea and, from 2000, the United Kingdom against the rebels, their allies and Liberian forces. President Kabbah declared it over on 18 January 2002.
events.open: The totals are estimates; the Truth and Reconciliation Commission recorded statements and a documented subset of victims, not every death. The Special Court tried ten people for crimes after 30 November 1996.

sources.title: Truth and Myth in Sierra Leone: Using Scientific Evidence to Investigate Violations in 1991-2000
sources.publisher: Benetech Human Rights Data Analysis Group

sources.title: Transitional justice in Sierra Leone in brief

events.name: Somali Civil War

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 350,000 to 1,000,000+ killed for 1991 to 2022, with no source named in the article. Listed apart from it are 200,000 to 300,000 deaths in the 1992 famine and 50,000 to 200,000 in the 1987-89 killings of Isaaq civilians. A US Centers for Disease Control survey counted 12,255 deaths in Baidoa town between 9 August and 14 November 1992, about 37% of its estimated population of 37,000, and found that 94 of 1,004 people surveyed in Afgoi (9%) died between April and December 1992.
toll.note: The range includes famine and disease deaths and is not limited to combat. The CDC figures are local surveys and cannot be generalised to all Somalia.

events.says: Armed conflict in Somalia since the central government collapsed, involving clan militias, UN-authorised forces in 1992 to 1995, Ethiopia in 2006 to 2009, African Union missions and, since 2006, the Islamic Courts and al-Shabaab. It is listed as ongoing.
events.open: The start is dated 1978, 1981, 1988 or 1991. Famine deaths and violent deaths are not separated in the totals, and the war-wide range names no study. Somaliland declared independence in 1991 and is a separate party.

sources.title: Mortality among displaced and resident populations in Baidoa and Afgoi, Somalia, 1992
sources.publisher: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (MMWR)

events.name: Afghan Civil War (1992-1996)

toll.text: The Uppsala Conflict Data Program count reported by Wikipedia is 26,759 killed. The Afghanistan Justice Project is cited there for 25,000 killed through June 1994. Wikipedia's text also says at least 60,000 civilians were killed in the fighting for Kabul, without naming a source. Human Rights Watch wrote that tens of thousands of civilians were killed or injured in Kabul in 1992-93.
toll.note: Low is the UCDP count. There is no agreed ceiling; the other figures are for Kabul or for part of the period.

events.says: Fighting among the mujahideen factions of the Islamic State of Afghanistan, Hezb-e Islami and, from late 1994, the Taliban, from 28 April 1992 to 27 September 1996, when the Taliban took Kabul. Kabul's population fell from about 2,000,000 to 500,000.
events.open: The counts come from event data and advocacy reports, not a register of the dead. The Afghanistan Justice Project report covers 1978 to 2001 and gives no Kabul total in its summary.

sources.title: Blood-Stained Hands: Past Atrocities in Kabul and Afghanistan's Legacy of Impunity
Casting Shadows: War Crimes and Crimes against Humanity, 1978-2001

events.name: Tajikistani Civil War

toll.text: RFE/RL says the war killed more than 150,000 people; Wikipedia's lead gives 20,000 to 150,000 and its infobox 50,000 to 100,000 (one academic source cited there gives 40,000 to 100,000). Earlier RFE/RL reporting said tens of thousands. About 1.2 million people were displaced.
toll.note: Low and high are the extremes of the published estimates, from a 2017 and a 2021 RFE/RL piece. Neither is a count.

events.says: A civil war in Tajikistan from May 1992 between the government, backed by Russia and Uzbekistan, and the United Tajik Opposition, ended by the General Agreement signed in Moscow on 27 June 1997.
events.open: Estimates differ by a factor of seven and no register of the dead is cited. An estimate of 20,000 to 60,000 killed in the first year alone is also quoted.

sources.title: The Peace Deal That Ended Tajikistan's Bloody Civil War

events.name: Algerian Civil War

toll.text: The International Center for Transitional Justice says the 1990s conflict led to about 150,000 deaths and at least 7,000 disappeared. Britannica says some 100,000 civilians had died by the time the 2005 Charter was proposed, and an Al Jazeera opinion piece says as many as 200,000. Wikipedia's infobox gives about 150,000 and its text 44,000 (a 2008 study) and 40,000 to 50,000 (a 2010 estimate).
toll.note: Low is the lowest study cited by Wikipedia; high is the highest figure reported by Al Jazeera. The Algerian authorities have not published a detailed count.

events.says: A conflict from January 1992 to February 2002 between the Algerian state and Islamist armed groups (the Islamic Salvation Front's armed wing, the Armed Islamic Group and later the Salafist Group for Preaching and Combat). It ended with an amnesty under the 2005 Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation.
events.open: Who carried out the 1997-98 village massacres is disputed. The Charter pardons armed rebels and clears the security forces and sets up no truth-seeking body (ICTJ). The sources used here give totals, not name rolls.

sources.title: Algeria: Civil war, the Islamists versus the army
There must be truth and justice for Algeria's disappeared

events.name: Burundian Civil War

toll.text: The Tufts University Atrocity Endings project gives 150,000 to 300,000 as the most often cited range for 1993 to 2005, saying most deaths came from displacement and forced relocation rather than combat. Wikipedia's infobox gives about 300,000 (BBC, 2008). The killings after the October 1993 coup are put at 50,000 to 100,000 within a year (International Commission of Inquiry), and at about 116,000 for October to December 1993 (a 2002 study by the UN Population Fund and the Burundian government, as cited by Tufts).
toll.note: Low and high are the Tufts range. The 1993 figures overlap the war-wide range and are not additional.

events.says: A war from October 1993, after the coup of that month, between the Tutsi-led army and Hutu rebel groups (CNDD-FDD, Palipehutu-FNL). The Arusha Agreement of 2000 and later ceasefires ended it; the FNL signed in 2006.
events.open: The end date is given as 15 May 2005 in the infobox and as August 2005 in the text. The sources disagree on how many deaths were from violence and how many from displacement, hunger and disease. Earlier killings in 1972 are not in this count.

events.name: First Chechen War

toll.text: Civilian deaths are given as 30,000 to 40,000 (the Russian state statistics office) and 50,000 (Memorial), both quoted in a 2005 Jamestown report, and 30,000 to 100,000 in a scholarly estimate cited by Wikipedia. Russian military dead are 5,500 (official) to 14,000 (independent); Chechen fighters 2,800 (the Chechen commander's figure) to 10,000 or more. Estimates for Grozny's first five weeks run from 27,000 to 35,000 dead.
toll.note: Low and high count civilians only. Soldiers and fighters on both sides are separate and would raise both ends.

events.says: Russian federal forces fought Chechen separatists from 11 December 1994 to 31 August 1996, with the storming of Grozny at its start. It ended with the Khasavyurt Accord, which withdrew federal forces by the end of 1996 and put off the decision on Chechnya's status to 2001.
events.open: Russia never counted civilian losses, according to Memorial. Figures for Grozny come from officials and monitors who disagree on the share who were ethnic Russians.

sources.title: Dzhabrailov: 160,000 People Killed in Two Chechen Wars

events.name: Second Chechen War

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 50,000 to 80,000 military and civilian dead, and its lead over 60,000. Memorial and Human Rights Watch estimate about 25,000 civilians killed since 1999, up to 10,500 in the Grozny fighting of winter 1999-2000; Amnesty International puts civilian dead at 30,000 (25,000 killed and 5,000 missing). In 2002 Memorial said civilian deaths were more than 10,000 and clearly under 20,000. Russian forces lost 6,000 to 14,000; Chechen fighters 3,500 to 14,000 or more.
toll.note: Low and high are the combined range printed in the infobox. Each side counts its own dead and the civilian counts differ.

events.says: A war from August 1999 in which Russian federal forces retook Chechnya from separatist and Islamist forces. The main phase ran to April 2000, an insurgency followed, and the counter-terrorism operation was officially ended in April 2009.
events.open: Memorial noted that it could monitor only about a quarter of Chechen territory. An early claim of 80,000 dead was called unreliable by Human Rights Watch. Totals for both wars together run from 75,000 to 160,000 depending on who counts.

sources.title: Chechnya: how many civilians have died (RFE/RL)
Dzhabrailov: 160,000 People Killed in Two Chechen Wars

events.name: Afghan Civil War (1996-2001)

toll.text: The Uppsala Conflict Data Program count reported by Wikipedia is 35,775 killed, for clashes between the Taliban and the opposing United Front. The Afghanistan Justice Project is cited there for about 3,000 prisoners killed in May 1997, about 4,000 civilians killed at Mazar-i-Sharif in September 1998, and 1,500 to 3,000 killed in 1998 at Qalai-Zaini. The Project's report says crimes from 1978 to 2001 included massacres, disappearances and executions of at least tens of thousands of Afghans.
toll.note: Low is the UCDP count. The massacre figures are part of it, not additional, and no ceiling is given.

events.says: A war from 27 September 1996, when the Taliban took Kabul, to 7 October 2001, between the Taliban and the Northern Alliance. The Taliban held about 85% of the country, and the conflict was followed by the US-led invasion.
events.open: The massacre counts are estimates and the sources do not say how they relate to the UCDP total. Thousands of Hazara civilians are said to have starved during the siege of Hazarajat, with no figure given.

sources.title: Casting Shadows: War Crimes and Crimes against Humanity, 1978-2001

events.name: Eritrean-Ethiopian War

toll.text: A Congressional Research Service report of July 2000 estimates the death toll at 50,000 to 100,000 and says close to a million people were displaced. The International Crisis Group range of 70,000 to 100,000 is printed in Wikipedia's infobox, and about 70,000 is called the figure in most international reports. Regional analysts quoted there go up to 300,000. Eritrea said it lost 19,000 soldiers; Ethiopian officials have given figures of 34,000 to 60,000 for Ethiopian losses.
toll.note: Low and high are the Congressional Research Service range for both sides together. Claims up to 300,000 rest on analysts' estimates.

events.says: A border war between Eritrea and Ethiopia from May 1998 to June 2000, fought along the frontier, including Operation Sunset in February 1999. The Algiers Agreement of 12 December 2000 ended it, and a boundary commission awarded Badme to Eritrea in April 2002.
events.open: No joint count exists and each government's figures serve its own side. Operation Sunset is put at about 30,000 dead on both sides by independent observers. There is no consensus on who won.

events.name: Ituri conflict

toll.text: Human Rights Watch (2003) cites the UN estimate of 50,000 civilians dead in Ituri since 1999, and itself counts at least 5,000 civilians killed by direct violence between July 2002 and March 2003; more than 500,000 people fled. A figure of 60,000 or more killed since 1998-99 is reported by the BBC (2006) and IWPR. Wikipedia's infobox gives about 63,770.
toll.note: Low is the UN figure cited by HRW for 1999 to 2003; high is the infobox total to 2006-07.

events.says: A conflict in Ituri province in north-eastern Congo, set off by a local Hema-Lendu land dispute that Ugandan involvement and the wider Congo war made far deadlier. Militias including the UPC and the FNI fought, and Uganda occupied the district from 1998 to 2003.
events.open: Many of these deaths also fall inside the Congo wars total listed separately, so the two should not be added. The sources give estimates, not name lists. Nyakunde alone saw at least 1,200 civilians killed.

sources.title: Ituri: Covered in Blood. Ethnically Targeted Violence in Northeastern DR Congo

events.name: War in Afghanistan (2001-2021)

toll.text: The Costs of War project (Brown University) is cited for 176,206 direct war deaths: Afghan security forces 66,000 to 92,000, civilians 46,319, opposition fighters 52,893 to 80,000+ (some 2,000 al-Qaeda), and US and NATO troops 3,579. The Uppsala Conflict Data Program figure given is 212,191+. Both exclude indirect deaths from hunger, disease and lost health care.
toll.note: Low is the Costs of War total and high the UCDP count. Neither includes indirect deaths, which the project says are not counted in these figures.

events.says: A war that began on 7 October 2001 when a US-led coalition attacked the Taliban government after the September 2001 attacks. It continued as an insurgency until the Taliban retook Kabul and the last US forces left on 30 August 2021.
events.open: Counts of insurgent dead are the least certain. Pakistan's related insurgency is counted separately. The Costs of War page gives its figures in a chart without a table.

sources.title: The human cost of the post-9/11 wars: direct war deaths in major war zones
sources.publisher: Brown University Costs of War Project

sources.title: Human cost of the post-9/11 wars
sources.publisher: Brown University Costs of War Project

events.name: Iraqi conflict (Iraq War and aftermath)

toll.text: The Costs of War project is cited for 275,000 to 306,000 killed in Iraq from March 2003 to August 2021. Iraq Body Count documents 200,065 to 226,628 violent civilian deaths since the 2003 invasion and about 300,000 violent deaths including combatants. Neither counts indirect deaths.
toll.note: Both ends are the Costs of War range, which runs to 2021 and so slightly beyond the 2003-2017 period of the main hostilities. Iraq Body Count's civilian count is a documented minimum.

events.says: The conflict that began with the American-led invasion of Iraq on 20 March 2003 and continued as an insurgency, sectarian war and the war against the Islamic State. High-intensity hostilities are dated to 9 December 2017, with low-intensity fighting after.
events.open: Documented counts are minimums. The two sources cover different periods and populations. Deaths from the 1991 uprisings and the Gulf War are listed separately.

sources.title: The human cost of the post-9/11 wars: direct war deaths in major war zones
sources.publisher: Brown University Costs of War Project

events.name: Mexican drug war

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 350,000 to 400,000 total deaths for 2006 to 2021, and 41,034 dead in conflicts between identified parties for 2006 to 2020. Excelsior, citing INEGI, reports 208,223 intentional homicides from 2019 to 2024. A Mexican Interior Ministry official reported 80,888 people disappeared or not located from December 2006 to December 2020.
toll.note: Low counts only deaths in clashes between identified parties. High counts all homicides in the period, which is not the same as war deaths.

events.says: A conflict that began on 11 December 2006 when the Mexican government sent the armed forces against drug cartels, among them the Sinaloa Cartel, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and the Gulf Cartel. It is listed as ongoing.
events.open: Whether all homicides count as war deaths is contested, and the disappeared are counted separately. The sources give national homicide statistics, not a list of the dead of this conflict.

sources.title: Mexico lives a long decade of homicidal violence (INEGI figures)
In Mexico there are 80,888 disappeared or unlocated persons since 2006

events.name: Boko Haram insurgency

toll.text: A UNDP report of June 2021 estimates about 350,000 deaths in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states from 2009 to 2020, of which 314,000 were indirect (hunger, disease, lost health care) and about 35,000 direct. About 324,000 of the dead were children under five.
toll.note: Low is the direct deaths; high is direct and indirect deaths together to the end of 2020.

events.says: An insurgency begun in 2009 in north-eastern Nigeria by Boko Haram, later split into factions including the Islamic State West Africa Province, spreading to Niger, Chad and Cameroon and met by Nigerian and regional forces. It is listed as ongoing.
events.open: The UNDP total is a statistical estimate, not a count. It covers three Nigerian states only. Violence in the Lake Chad area also falls within the Sahel war total listed separately.

sources.title: Northeast Nigeria conflict killed more than 300,000 children: UN
Boko Haram: 350,000 dead in Nigeria, UN

events.name: War in the Sahel

toll.text: Wikipedia's infobox gives 68,933+ killed, 46,859+ of them since 2023, with the source tagged only as GCRP. ACLED recorded 11,276 civilians killed in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger from 2012 to mid-2022, and more than 8,000 people reported killed in Burkina Faso in 2023 alone. The Council on Foreign Relations says the Liptako-Gourma border region accounts for over half of global terrorism-related deaths.
toll.note: Low is the infobox total. There is no ceiling; ACLED's 2012-2022 figure counts civilians only.

events.says: A war that began on 16 January 2012 with a Tuareg rebellion and Islamist takeover of northern Mali, spreading to Burkina Faso and Niger, with French intervention from 2013, French withdrawal by 2025 and Russian forces since. It is listed as ongoing.
events.open: Counts by event data differ from totals compiled elsewhere. The Burkina Faso insurgency is included here and not listed separately. Wagner Group operations in Mali, including at Moura in March 2022 (more than 300 civilians according to press reports), are disputed by Mali.

events.name: South Sudanese Civil War

toll.text: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine estimated 382,900 excess deaths in South Sudan from December 2013 to April 2018: 1,177,600 deaths from any cause against 794,600 expected without the war. About half of the excess deaths were reported as violent injuries. Before the study, estimates were in the tens of thousands.
toll.note: Low is about half of the excess deaths (the violent share as reported); high is all excess deaths, violent and not. The study period ends in April 2018.

events.says: A civil war from December 2013 between forces loyal to the president and those of the former vice-president, which spread along ethnic lines and was followed by peace agreements in 2015, 2018 and 2020.
events.open: The estimate is a statistical model that was not peer reviewed at release; the authors note the confidence intervals may be too narrow and child deaths may be under-reported. Deaths after April 2018 are not covered. Refugees outside South Sudan are excluded.

sources.title: War in South Sudan estimated to have led to almost 400,000 excess deaths
sources.publisher: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine

sources.title: Nearly 400,000 'excess deaths' caused by South Sudan war

events.name: Russo-Ukrainian war

toll.text: Russian military dead are put at 518,224 to 633,384 by BBC News Russian and Mediazona (to 30 October 2026; 285,023 confirmed by name), about 500,000 by the UK and NATO, and 400,000 to 450,000 by CSIS. Ukrainian military dead are 106,285 (UALosses, with 105,786 missing), 125,000 to 150,000 (CSIS) and 200,000 (BBC News). The UN human rights office has confirmed 17,257 civilians killed to 31 August 2026 and says the real number is higher. Le Monde gave 500,000 total deaths by February 2026. The Council on Foreign Relations says the war has caused more than one million casualties.
toll.note: Low is the Le Monde all-sides total, and the Russian military figures alone reach it. No ceiling exists; the sides' figures are not additive without overlap.

events.says: War between Russia and Ukraine that began with Russia's seizure of Crimea and support for separatists in the Donbas in 2014 and became a full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022. Fighting continues. The UN counted 14,200 to 14,400 killed in the Donbas from April 2014 to the end of 2021.
events.open: Both governments withhold or discount their own losses. Civilian totals confirmed by the UN omit areas it cannot reach, and a Ukrainian prosecutor suggested in 2023 that as many as 100,000 civilians may have been killed.

sources.title: Ukraine civilian deaths in 2025 highest since 2022, UN says

events.name: Yemeni civil war (2014-present)

toll.text: A UNDP report projected 377,000 deaths by the end of 2021, 60% from indirect causes such as hunger and preventable disease and 40% (about 150,000) from direct causes such as ground fighting and air strikes. About 70% of the dead were children under five. The Yemen Data Project counts 25,054 coalition air raids between 25 March 2015 and April 2022.
toll.note: Low is the direct share; high is the total to end 2021. Deaths from 2022 onward are not in either.

events.says: A war that began in 2014 when Houthi forces took the capital, followed in March 2015 by a Saudi-led coalition campaign in support of the government. The Council on Foreign Relations reports Houthi forces advancing toward Aden in early November 2026.
events.open: The UNDP figures are a projection to the end of 2021, not a count. The direct total of about 150,000 is the 40% share, as reported in news coverage of the UNDP report. Deaths after 2021 are not estimated in these sources.

sources.title: Yemen war deaths will reach 377,000 by end of the year: UN

events.name: Tigray War

toll.text: The Uppsala Conflict Data Program and a University of London study each put deaths at about 100,000 or more (102,000). Ghent University first estimated 162,000 to 378,000 and in an update gave an average of 518,000 civilian deaths to 31 December 2022, with a range of 311,000 to 808,000, about 10% from killings, 30% from collapse of health care and 60% from famine. The African Union's envoy said as many as 600,000 may have died in northern Ethiopia. ACLED recorded 9,861 reported fatalities in Tigray, Afar and Amhara from November 2020 to January 2023.
toll.note: Low is the UCDP and University of London figure; high is the upper bound of the Ghent update, which counts civilians, indirect deaths included.

events.says: A war between the Ethiopian federal government, Amhara forces and Eritrea, and the Tigray People's Liberation Front, from 3 November 2020. A cessation of hostilities was agreed on 2 November 2022, and the TPLF agreed to disarm. About 2,750,000 people were displaced.
events.open: The total is unknown and the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission's chief said it may never be known. The figures cover different areas and periods, direct and indirect deaths, and ACLED's count is of reported events only. Fighting resumed in 2026.

sources.title: Death toll in the Tigray war: Ghent University estimates and ACLED

events.name: Gaza war

toll.text: Wikipedia, citing the Gaza Health Ministry, gives at least 77,632 deaths in the war to 9 October 2026: 75,586+ Palestinians and 2,046+ Israelis; 1,195 people were killed in the 7 October 2023 attack, and around 8,000 were reported missing under rubble. A peer-reviewed capture-recapture study in The Lancet estimated 64,260 deaths from traumatic injury in Gaza to 30 June 2024, about 41% above the ministry's 37,877 then. A later analysis puts violent deaths at 78,318 (70,614 to 87,504) to the end of 2024, and a Max Planck Institute study at 100,000 to 126,000 by November 2025.
toll.note: Low is the combined ministry total for both sides; high is the upper bound of the Max Planck estimate of violent deaths in Gaza. Indirect deaths from hunger and lost health care, and deaths in the West Bank (1,216) and Lebanon, are not included.

events.says: A war that began on 7 October 2023 with a Hamas-led attack on Israel and Israel's military campaign in Gaza. A ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025, but strikes continued, and by 20 October 2026 at least 1,400 Palestinians and 5 Israeli soldiers had been killed since it began.
events.open: The ministry's data are disputed: the US president said in October 2023 that he had no confidence in them, the UN humanitarian office uses them as clearly sourced, and The Lancet concluded they were accurate in December 2023. Studies disagree on how many deaths are missing from the ministry total and on the combatant share, which they do not estimate.

sources.title: Gaza war toll likely significantly undercounts deaths, says study
Gaza war toll likely significantly undercounts deaths, says study

events.name: Sudanese civil war (2023-present)

toll.text: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine estimated over 61,000 deaths in Khartoum State alone in the first 14 months, 26,000 of them from violence. Berkeley public health researchers combined ACLED's 18,916 direct deaths with 43,507 indirect deaths for more than 62,000 to November 2024. PRIO and Uppsala researchers say ACLED recorded about 19,000 direct deaths in 2025, other teams put the toll above 70,000, and their own model puts it close to 80,000 for 2025, possibly up to 100,000. Wikipedia's infobox gives a highly uncertain 150,000 to 400,000.
toll.note: Low is the minimum total to November 2024; the 2025 estimates come on top of it. No ceiling can be set from the sources.

events.says: A war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces that began on 15 April 2023 in Khartoum and spread to Darfur and Kordofan. The Rapid Support Forces took El Fasher on 26 October 2025. More than 14 million people have been displaced.
events.open: The Sudanese health ministry's own tally was 5,565 in 2024, far below independent estimates. Figures for El Fasher range from 60,000 to 70,000 to satellite-based estimates as high as 150,000, none with a named method. Famine deaths are not counted.

sources.title: Sudan's death toll in 2025 could be as high as 100,000: how we did the count

Sudan's civil war has left at least 62,000 dead by our estimate
sources.publisher: UC Berkeley School of Public Health

events.name: Russo-Japanese War

toll.text: Tabulations of published estimates give 129,400 combatant dead (Japan 86,100, Russia 43,300) from Dumas's statistics, with an alternate set of 80,378 for Japan and 71,453 for Russia; 130,000 (Correlates of War); 139,000 (Urlanis: 99,000 killed, 40,000 of disease); and 178,000 (Gilbert: Japan 58,000, Russia 120,000). An Italian Ministry of Defence volume, citing Urlanis and Seaman (1906), gives 64,938 Japanese dead from an American medical source, or over 58,800 killed by Russian official sources, and about 27,200 Japanese and 11,170 Russian Army deaths from disease.
toll.note: Low is the lowest Japanese figure (80,378) plus the lowest Russian figure (43,300) in the Dumas tables; high is Gilbert's total. All figures count soldiers and sailors, killed in action, died of wounds and died of disease.

events.says: War between the Russian Empire and the Empire of Japan over rival claims in Manchuria and Korea, fought on the Liaodong Peninsula, around Mukden and at sea at Tsushima. It ended with the Treaty of Portsmouth of 5 September 1905, which recognised Japanese interests in Korea and gave Japan the Liaodong lease and the southern half of Sakhalin.
events.open: Sources agree on the order of 130,000 to 170,000 dead but not on the split, because bodies were not counted on either side; the disease share differs most between sources. The tabulations cover combatants only, and none of the sources read gives a count of civilian deaths in Manchuria.

sources.title: Conflitti Militari e Popolazioni Civili, Tomo I (XXXIV Congress, International Commission of Military History), p. 466
Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: Mid-Range Wars and Atrocities of the Twentieth Century

events.name: Maji Maji Rebellion

toll.text: The official German estimate was about 75,000 dead (listed with the 1911 Britannica's 120,000). Later figures run to 150,000, 200,000 (Cambridge History of Africa, with about 400 dead on the German side), and 250,000 to 300,000. The Encyclopedia of Western Colonialism since 1450 puts famine deaths alone at an estimated 250,000 after the Germans destroyed villages and crops.
toll.note: Low is the official German estimate. High is the top of the modern estimates; the larger figures include deaths from famine and disease after the fighting, not only killed in battle.

events.says: Rising of peoples of south-eastern German East Africa against German colonial rule, begun in July 1905 and ended in August 1907. German forces and their African troops put it down with machine guns and a scorched-earth campaign that was followed by a severe famine.
events.open: Whether the toll counts battle deaths only or famine and disease as well, and how many of the famine deaths were the result of German scorched-earth tactics, differ between sources; the larger figures are modern estimates without a recorded count. The dead were not recorded by name.

sources.title: Maji Maji Revolt, in Encyclopedia of Western Colonialism since 1450
Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: Mid-Range Wars and Atrocities of the Twentieth Century

events.name: Mexican Revolution

toll.text: A University of Minnesota Population Center study puts excess deaths at 1.4 million (plausible range 0.8 to 1.7 million) within a total demographic cost of 2.1 million that also counts about 550,000 lost births and about 350,000 emigrants; it cites nearly 1.5 million excess deaths for 1910-1921 from a 1993 demographic study and a population loss of two million for 1910-1921, mostly from the 1918 influenza, from Loyo (1960). A tabulation of 17 published estimates has a median of 1,000,000 and ranges from 500,000 to 2,142,000 (Rummel); battle deaths are put at 200,000 to 250,000. Wikipedia's infobox gives 1.7 to 2.7 million.
toll.note: Low is the most conservative published estimate; high is the upper figure in Wikipedia's infobox. Most estimates are population shortfalls, not counted deaths, and include disease, including the 1918 influenza.

events.says: Civil war and series of coups in Mexico from November 1910, when the Diaz government was challenged, to 1920. It produced the Constitution of 1917 and ended with northern generals holding the presidency.
events.open: Census-based figures measure missing people, not confirmed deaths: scholars attribute different shares to excess mortality, lost births, emigration and census undercount, and no consensus exists on the human cost.

sources.title: Missing millions: the human cost of the Mexican Revolution, 1910-1930
Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: Death Tolls and Casualty Statistics for Wars, Dictatorships and Genocides

events.name: Balkan Wars

toll.text: Tabulated estimates of combatant dead for the two wars together: 129,500 (a US casualty reference), 142,500 (Correlates of War: 82,000 in the First War and 60,500 in the Second), 143,000 (Eckhardt) and 224,000 (Urlanis, all parties: 122,000 killed in action, 82,000 dead of disease and 20,000 dead of wounds).
toll.note: Low and high are the lowest and highest published totals of soldiers killed, dead of wounds and dead of disease on all sides. None counts civilians.

events.says: Two wars. In the First (8 October 1912 to 30 May 1913) Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro defeated the Ottoman Empire and took most of its European provinces; in the Second (16 June to 10 August 1913) Bulgaria fought its former allies, Romania and the Ottoman Empire and lost much of its gains.
events.open: Civilian deaths, ethnic cleansing and the cholera epidemics are not in these totals and have no agreed count; all parties are recorded as committing atrocities against civilians.

sources.title: Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: Mid-Range Wars and Atrocities of the Twentieth Century

events.name: Central Asian revolt of 1916

toll.text: Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported in 2006 that even the lowest estimates put the Kyrgyz death toll above 100,000, and that by some accounts nearly half the Kyrgyz of the northern part of the country died. Wikipedia lists about 270,000 Central Asian dead (Sokol, all five peoples), 40,000 Kyrgyz (a historian's count from population tallies), 100,000 to 270,000 (Kyrgyz sources) and 500,000 (Toynbee, whom Wikipedia reports as calling it speculative). Russian settler losses are given as 2,325 killed and 1,384 missing.
toll.note: Low is the lowest published count, for the Kyrgyz alone; high is the largest estimate, which covers all Central Asian peoples and includes disease, famine and flight. Most figures include deaths on the flight to China.

events.says: Rising against the Tsarist order of 1916 that ended the exemption of Central Asian Muslims from military service, begun in July 1916 in Russian Central Asia. Russian troops and settler militias put it down under martial law, and hundreds of thousands fled over the mountains to China.
events.open: Kazakh and Kyrgyz deaths are not counted separately; what share died by violence, in the mountain passes or of cold and hunger is unsettled, and the percentage of the Kyrgyz population lost (up to 40 per cent in some accounts) is disputed. No death register was kept.

events.name: Russian Civil War

toll.text: An Italian Ministry of Defence volume gives 2 to 5 million dead, mostly civilians from famine and disease, with Red Army losses of almost 940,000 for 1918-1922 (a 1993 Russian military-losses study). Ten complete estimates tabulated by Necrometrics have a median of 8.8 to 9.0 million, from 800,000 (Eckhardt) and 2,825,000 (a military-history companion) through 7 to 10 million (a school history text), 9 million (two historians) and 9,494,000 (Rummel) to 10 million (a 1997 history of the revolution). Wikipedia's infobox gives 7 to 12 million total casualties, mostly civilians.
toll.note: Low is the Italian Ministry of Defence range. High is the upper figure in Wikipedia's infobox, which counts famine and epidemic deaths as well as combat, terror and pogroms. Direct military deaths are far lower, in the order of 825,000 to 1,000,000.

events.says: Multi-sided civil war in the former Russian Empire that followed the Bolshevik seizure of power in October 1917, between the Red Army and the White movement, with Ukrainian, Polish, Czechoslovak and other forces, and foreign intervention. It ended in a Bolshevik victory and the creation of the Soviet Union.
events.open: The toll depends on whether the 1921-22 famine, epidemics, the Red and White terror and the pogroms are counted; sources overlap with the Polish-Soviet war and the First World War, and Eckhardt's First World War figures exclude it. Data for White-held areas are less reliable than Soviet data.

sources.title: Conflitti Militari e Popolazioni Civili, Tomo I (XXXIV Congress, International Commission of Military History), p. 468
Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: Source List and Detailed Death Tolls for the Primary Megadeaths of the Twentieth Century

events.name: Finnish Civil War

toll.text: The US Library of Congress Finland study, as cited by Necrometrics, gives a total of 30,000 with fewer than a quarter killed in battle: 1,649 killed in the Red Terror, 8,380 Reds killed in the White Terror and 12,000 who died in camps; another account cited there gives 31,000. Wikipedia gives around 38,000 (about 5,500 on the White side and 32,000 to 33,000 on the Red side, including about 9,000 Reds executed and about 12,500 prisoners who died in camps). The Aalto University portal built on the National Archives of Finland database holds some 40,000 death records for 1914-1922, most from this war.
toll.note: Both ends count all sides together: battle deaths, executions and deaths in prison camps. The database figure covers 1914-1922 and is not a count of this war alone.

events.says: Civil war in Finland between the Red Guards and the government's White Guards, fought in 1918 with Russian troops on the Red side and German troops and Swedish volunteers on the White side. The Whites won, and thousands of Red prisoners died in camps afterwards.
events.open: The total depends on whether deaths in the prison camps after the war are counted and on how many are attributed to the Spanish influenza; the figure of around 38,000 is higher than the earlier 30,000.

sources.title: War Victims in Finland 1914-1922 (WarVictimSampo project page)
sources.publisher: Aalto University, Semantic Computing Research Group (SeCo)

sources.title: Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: The Lesser Multicides of the Twentieth Century

events.name: Polish-Soviet War

toll.text: The Correlates of War project and Eckhardt give 100,000 (USSR 60,000, Poland 40,000); Wikipedia's text puts those killed at about 100,000. Poland's Institute of National Remembrance gives 54,281 Polish Army deaths for 1 November 1918 to 31 December 1920 (all fronts) and 14,000 to 16,000 Soviet prisoners dead in Polish camps; Wikipedia gives 47,551 Soviet dead and about 20,000 of 51,000 Polish prisoners dead in Soviet and Lithuanian custody.
toll.note: Low is the combatant total as published. High is the sum of the Polish Army deaths (54,281), Soviet dead (47,551) and prisoner deaths on both sides (about 15,000 and 20,000), rounded; the Polish figure covers other fronts as well.

events.says: War between the Second Polish Republic, with Ukrainian allies, and Soviet Russia, fought from February 1919 to the armistice of October 1920 and the Treaty of Riga of March 1921. It decided Poland's eastern border.
events.open: Totals are inconsistent between Polish and Soviet sources, and the Polish prisoner deaths are not confirmed by the Institute's own page, which says some 5,000 repatriable Poles are unaccounted for. Some estimates for the Russian Civil War cover the same dead.

sources.title: Polish prisoners of war in Soviet captivity
Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: Mid-Range Wars and Atrocities of the Twentieth Century

events.name: Turkish War of Independence

toll.text: Necrometrics lists, for the Greco-Turkish War of 1919-22, 52,000 battle deaths (Urlanis; Greek killed in action 26,000 and Turkish about the same), 70,000 (Eckhardt, military and civilian), 400,000 (headline) with 264,000 Greeks killed by Turks and 15,000 Turks killed by Greeks (Rummel), and 353,000 Pontian Greeks killed (AIHGS); Churchill wrote that a quarter of a million died. Wikipedia's infobox lists about 41,000 Turkish and about 24,000 opposing combatant dead beside 264,000 Greek civilians, 60,000 to 250,000 Armenian civilians and over 15,000 Turkish civilians.
toll.note: Low is the published battle-death figure for the Greco-Turkish War only; high is the sum of the combatant deaths and the civilian figures in Wikipedia's infobox, rounded. The high end includes civilians counted under other entries.

events.says: Struggle of the Turkish national movement, from May 1919 to the Treaty of Lausanne of July 1923, against the occupying Allied powers and Greek, Armenian and French forces. It ended the Ottoman sultanate and led to the Republic of Turkey.
events.open: Civilian deaths in this war overlap with the Greek and Armenian genocide entries, and the 1920 Turkish campaign against Armenia is counted here, not separately; the Armenian civilian figure runs from 60,000 to 98,000 or from 198,000 to 250,000. The figures for Smyrna in 1922 range from 2,000 to over 100,000.

sources.title: Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: Secondary Wars and Atrocities of the Twentieth Century

events.name: Rif War

toll.text: A tabulation of estimates gives 40,000 (Eckhardt: 11,000 civilians and 29,000 military), about 67,500 (a US casualty reference: French 10,000, Spanish 50,000 and Rif rebels 30,000 killed and wounded, all causes), and 36,000 (OnWar: Berbers 5,000, French 16,000, Spanish 15,000). Wikipedia gives 40,000 to 80,000 killed, combatants and civilians. Spain reported 13,192 dead at Annual and in the rout of July 1921 to its Cortes, and French deaths from battle and disease totalled 8,628.
toll.note: Low is the lowest tabulated total; high is the largest tabulated total. Figures count combatants of all sides, and some include civilians and deaths from disease.

events.says: Anti-colonial war fought between 1921 and 1926 by the Berber tribes of the Rif mountains of northern Morocco, led by Abd el-Krim, against Spain and from 1924 also France. It began with the Spanish disaster at Annual and ended with the Rif forces' defeat by Franco-Spanish forces.
events.open: The Rifian death toll is the least certain figure: no source counts it directly, and the effects of aerial bombing and chemical weapons on civilians are described but not counted. Several tabulated figures cover only part of the war or mix killed with wounded.

sources.title: The Many Repercussions of the Rif Rebellion
sources.publisher: The New York Review of Books

sources.title: Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: The Lesser Multicides of the Twentieth Century

events.name: Second Italo-Senussi War (Italian reconquest of Libya)

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 20,000 to 100,000 civilians killed. Del Boca is cited for 40,000 to 70,000 dead in the camps; Mack Smith for 20,000 dead in camps and perhaps 100,000 Bedouins overall; other authors for 100,000 dead in camps, for 40,000 combat deaths in 1923-31 with 100,000 Senussi dead from all causes, and for a fall of 125,000 in the native population. Necrometrics also lists a UN estimate of 250,000 to 300,000 native deaths from all unnatural causes under Italian rule from 1912 to 1942.
toll.note: Low and high are the lowest and highest published figures for deaths in Cyrenaica and the war years 1923-1932; they count civilians in camps and deportations as well as fighters, and the high figure is a fall in population, not a count of deaths.

events.says: Italian campaign to subdue Cyrenaica in eastern Libya against the Senussi resistance led by Omar Mukhtar, ending with his capture and hanging in 1931 and Badoglio's declaration of the end of the campaign in January 1932. About 100,000 people were interned in camps, where many died.
events.open: Whether deaths from the camps, deportation and chemical attacks are counted, and the pre-war population base used, give very different totals. The dead of the camps were not recorded by name in any source found.

sources.title: Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: Mid-Range Wars and Atrocities of the Twentieth Century

events.name: Cristero War

toll.text: An Americas Quarterly article of 2025 quotes a historian's estimate of 90,000 casualties and says the exact toll will never be known. Wikipedia gives about 90,000 (56,882 federal soldiers and about 30,000 Cristeros, with civilians not counted) and an estimated 250,000 dead including civilians.
toll.note: Low is the estimate of 90,000, which counts combatants; high is the estimate that includes civilians.

events.says: Armed rising of Catholic Mexicans, mostly in the centre and west of the country, against the anticlerical laws of the government, begun in August 1926. It ended on 21 June 1929 when church and state reached an agreement and the Cristeros laid down their arms.
events.open: The exact toll is unknown; the 250,000 estimate has no breakdown of civilian deaths and later killings of Cristeros and of teachers after the peace are counted differently. A second rising began in the mid-1930s.

sources.title: The Long Shadow of Mexico's War Over Catholicism
sources.publisher: Americas Quarterly (Americas Society/Council of the Americas)

events.name: Chinese Civil War

toll.text: Necrometrics tabulates the two phases separately. For the first (1928-37) it lists battle deaths of 275,000 (Correlates of War) and 406,000 (Rummel), with Rummel's democide subtotal of 3,130,000 and a further 6,500,000 from famine and flood. For the second (1945-49): 1,000,000 battle deaths (Correlates of War), 263,800 Communists killed and about 370,000 Nationalists killed (Ho Ping-ti), and Rummel's 6,194,000 total including 2,645,000 killed by the Nationalists and 2,323,000 by the Communists.
toll.note: Low is the sum of the Correlates of War battle deaths for the two phases (275,000 and 1,000,000); high is the sum of Rummel's totals (3,130,000 and 6,194,000), which include civilians killed by each side but exclude famine. Neither covers the years 1937-45.

events.says: Conflict between the Kuomintang government and the Communist Party of China, in a first phase from 1927 and an all-out war after 1945. It ended in 1949 with the Communist victory on the mainland, the founding of the People's Republic on 1 October 1949 and the Nationalist retreat to Taiwan.
events.open: The two phases are counted separately and the years of the war with Japan are excluded; civilian deaths from terror and famine are the least certain, and no source found counts them directly. Some estimates run into the tens of millions for 1927-1949 as a whole because they include the Japanese war.

sources.title: Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: Death Tolls and Casualty Statistics for Wars, Dictatorships and Genocides
Chinese Revolution of 1949
sources.publisher: Office of the Historian, US Department of State

events.name: Chaco War

toll.text: The Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture gives about 57,000 Bolivian and some 36,000 Paraguayan dead. The US Library of Congress Bolivia study says 65,000 Bolivians were killed. Necrometrics lists 85,000 (Dictionary of Twentieth-Century World History: Bolivia 50,000, Paraguay 35,000), 90,000 (a history of the war), 93,000, 100,000, 130,000 (Correlates of War), 135,000 (Gunther) and 200,000 (Eckhardt: 70,000 civilian and 130,000 military).
toll.note: Low and high are the lowest and highest of the combined figures for both armies, from all causes including disease; the 200,000 figure also counts civilians and is not used for the range.

events.says: War between Bolivia and Paraguay over the Chaco Boreal, from the clash of June 1932 to the cease-fire of 12 June 1935 and the peace settlement of 1938. Paraguay held most of the Chaco and was awarded most of it.
events.open: Deaths from disease and thirst, which were heavy, are mixed with combat deaths in most counts, and the Bolivian figure differs by 15,000 between sources.

sources.title: Chaco War, in Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture
Bolivia - The Chaco War (Country Studies)
sources.publisher: Library of Congress, Federal Research Division

events.name: Second Italo-Ethiopian War

toll.text: Necrometrics tabulates for the conquest of 1935-41: 20,000 battle deaths (Correlates of War: Italy 4,000, Ethiopia 16,000); 275,000 Ethiopian battle deaths (accepted by three sources); and the Ethiopian government's 1945 memorandum, quoted by Del Boca, of 760,300 dead (battle deaths 275,000, refugee hunger 300,000, patriots killed 75,000, concentration camps 35,000, the February 1937 massacre 30,000, executions 24,000, air raids 17,800). It puts unnatural civilian deaths at probably 120,000 to 160,000. Italian battle deaths are given as 4,359 to 15,000.
toll.note: Low is the Correlates of War battle-death count for 1935-36; high is the Ethiopian government's 1945 total for the whole occupation to 1941, which includes famine and deaths in camps.

events.says: Invasion of Ethiopia by Fascist Italy from Eritrea and Somaliland, begun on 3 October 1935 and completed with the capture of Addis Ababa in May 1936, using aircraft and mustard gas. Italy annexed the country; its occupation ended in 1941.
events.open: The Ethiopian memorandum of 1945 is a claim for the war crimes commission and its parts are disputed; Del Boca doubts the 30,000 killed in the Addis Ababa massacre of February 1937 and suggests 3,000, and a 2017 history estimated 19,200. Wikidata lists two values, 20,000 and 275,000, for the number of deaths.

sources.title: Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: Secondary Wars and Atrocities of the Twentieth Century

events.name: Spanish Civil War

toll.text: Necrometrics lists 365,000 (Hugh Thomas: 110,000 Republicans and 90,000 Nationalists killed in combat, 75,000 executed by the Nationalists, 55,000 by the Republicans, 10,000 by bombing, 25,000 of malnutrition); 380,000 (Gabriel Jackson: 200,000 executed by the Nationalists); 268,500 violent deaths, or 433,500 with disease (a 1977 Spanish military study); 650,000 (Correlates of War); and 1,200,000 (Eckhardt). A dictionary of world history gives about 750,000 lives, the same as a 2019 El Pais count of the population shortfall. Wikipedia's table runs up to 2,000,000, and says the 'million dead' figure was inflated for propaganda.
toll.note: Low is the violent-death count of the 1977 military study; high is the 750,000 population-shortfall figure. Figures differ on whether executions, bombing, hunger and disease are counted, and the post-war repression is excluded.

events.says: Civil war in Spain between the Republican government and the Nationalist rebels led by General Franco after the military coup of 17 July 1936, with German and Italian aid for the Nationalists and Soviet aid and international volunteers for the Republic. It ended on 1 April 1939 with a Nationalist victory.
events.open: The toll is disputed on whether to count executions behind the lines, deaths from hunger and disease, the post-war executions (at least 30,000, with estimates from 50,000 to 200,000) and the population shortfall. About 500,000 Republicans fled to France.

sources.title: Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: Secondary Wars and Atrocities of the Twentieth Century

events.name: Winter War

toll.text: Necrometrics lists 74,900 (Correlates of War: USSR 50,000, Finland 24,900), 85,000 (Gilbert), 90,000 (Singer; Eckhardt) and 126,875 Red Army killed and missing (a 1990s Russian study). Wikipedia gives, for Finland, 25,904 dead or missing (revised in 2005 by Finnish historians, after 19,576 announced in 1940), and for the Soviet Union 126,875 to 167,976 dead or missing, against the official Soviet figure of 48,475 dead (1940) and other Russian estimates of 53,522 and 63,990.
toll.note: Low is the Correlates of War total; high is the highest Soviet figure (167,976 dead or missing) plus the Finnish 25,904. Both count soldiers dead or missing.

events.says: Soviet invasion of Finland, begun on 30 November 1939 after Finland refused territorial demands, and ended by the Moscow Peace Treaty of 13 March 1940, by which Finland ceded territory on the Karelian Isthmus and elsewhere. Finland kept its independence.
events.open: The Soviet toll differs fivefold between the 1940 official figure and later Russian estimates, and the Soviet figures count dead and missing together. Finnish prisoners of war died in Soviet custody (10 to 20 per cent of 800 to 1,100). The war precedes and is separate from the Continuation War; both are inside the wider Second World War.

sources.title: Twentieth Century Atlas - Death Tolls: Mid-Range Wars and Atrocities of the Twentieth Century

events.name: Continuation War

toll.text: Finnish historians count 63,204 Finnish dead or missing. A 2019 presentation of the files of the Finnish National Archives' database of Finnish war dead of 1939-1945 reports 50,780 killed, 17,416 dead of wounds, 7,790 left on the field, 5,202 missing and 682 dead as prisoners, a total of 81,870, plus 10,456 dead of other causes; it covers all of Finland's wars of those years. Wikipedia gives Soviet dead or missing as about 250,000 (a 1997 Russian military-losses study) or at least 305,000 (a 2016 Finnish-language history), and German losses on the Finnish front as 16,400 killed.
toll.note: Low is the Finnish figure plus the 1997 Soviet figure; high is the Finnish figure plus the 2016 Soviet figure plus German killed. Both count soldiers dead or missing and are my sums of figures given separately.

events.says: War between Finland, with German support, and the Soviet Union from the Finnish attack of 25 June 1941 to the armistice of 19 September 1944. Finland regained the territory lost in the Winter War, then lost it again in the Moscow Armistice.
events.open: Whether Soviet civilian deaths in the siege of Leningrad (632,253 to 1,042,000) belong to this war is debated and lacks a consensus. The war is part of the Second World War and overlaps its Finnish and German toll. At least 18,318 Soviet prisoners died in Finnish camps; it is not clear whether the Soviet totals include them.

sources.title: Sodissa 1939-1945 menehtyneiden tiedosto (presentation, 29 November 2019)
sources.publisher: Sotavainajien muiston vaalimisyhdistys (hosted by Aalto University SeCo)

events.name: Indonesian National Revolution

toll.text: Dutch records give 5,281 military dead in Dutch service for 1945-49 (2,777 killed in action, 2,504 in accidents, illness or suicide). The Indonesian toll is unknown. Loe de Jong's 1988 footnote of about 100,000 republican fighters has no traceable basis. A 2017 KITLV count of Dutch field reports reached 97,421, which its authors treat as a lower bound, not a total. Another tally of Dutch reports counted 46,818 Indonesian fighters killed in the first seven months of 1949 alone. A historian cited in the same study gives 45,000-100,000 killed in combat and 25,000-100,000 civilians.
toll.note: Low is the 2017 count of Indonesian dead in Dutch reports (a lower bound). High is the highest estimate listed on Wikipedia (250,000). Neither includes the Dutch dead.

events.says: Armed and diplomatic struggle between the Republic of Indonesia and the Netherlands from 1945 to 1949, with British and Japanese forces also involved in the early period.
events.open: No complete count of Indonesian dead exists; Indonesian wartime administration was thin and Dutch reports do not always separate fighters from civilians. Deaths of Dutch, Indo-European and other civilians in the Bersiap violence of 1945-46 are put at 3,500 to 30,000. The Dutch toll is given as 4,751 (official 1950-51) and 5,281 (recent database count); Wikipedia lists a modern estimate of 15,000 Dutch dead and 980-1,200 British.

sources.title: 'Ze vielen als gemaaid koren': een beschouwing over de verliescijfers in Indonesie, 1945-1949, Militaire Spectator 1/2022
sources.publisher: Militaire Spectator (Netherlands Institute for Military History)

events.name: Greek Civil War

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 80,000 to 158,000 dead overall. A 2016 Ohio State University history article says well over 100,000, possibly close to 150,000. Necrometrics lists estimates from 50,000 (Our Times), 55,066 (a 1951 Greek army count) and 128,000 to 148,000 (Woodhouse, Urlanis) up to 158,000 (O'Ballance, repeated by others) and 160,000. The Hellenic Army General Staff history (1985) records about 21,000 government forces killed or missing.
toll.note: Both ends count all sides together, soldiers and civilians; estimates below 80,000 also exist. The army figures cover only the national forces.

events.says: Civil war between the Greek government army, supported by Britain and then the United States, and the Communist-led Democratic Army, from the Litochoro attack of March 1946 to the insurgents' defeat at Grammos and Vitsi in 1949.
events.open: The total is uncertain and most sources give no method. About 1 million people became homeless. Both sides removed children (about 28,000 are said to have 'disappeared'); the Communist party calls the removals evacuations for safety, other accounts call them abduction. Executions and imprisonments after the war are counted separately from battle dead. No archive of this war's dead by name was surveyed in this pass.

sources.title: The Greek Civil War, 1946-1949 (Origins: Current Events in Historical Perspective, March 2016)
Death-toll compilation for wars and atrocities of the twentieth century (page for tolls of about 100,000 to 300,000)

events.name: First Indochina War

toll.text: Wikipedia gives 400,000 to 842,707 soldiers killed, plus 125,000 to 400,000 civilians. For French forces it gives 74,220 dead (20,685 of them French); Viet Minh dead or missing are 175,000-300,000 (Western historians) or 191,605 (Vietnamese government). Necrometrics compiles 94,581 French Union dead (Bernard Fall), 392,934 in all (Clodfelter, 1995), 400,000 (Karnow, 1983), 630,000 (Tucker, 1998) and 842,707 (Lomperis, 1996, with 250,000 civilians).
toll.note: Low and high are the lowest and highest totals for military dead cited above; civilian deaths are partly included in some totals and not in others.

events.says: War from 1946 to 1954 between France and its allies (the French Union and the State of Vietnam) and the Viet Minh, fought in Vietnam and also involving Laos and Cambodia.
events.open: Totals depend on whether civilians, the Vietnamese National Army and allied colonial troops are counted. Viet Minh losses are estimated from French intelligence and Vietnamese official figures, which differ widely. About 6,000 civilians are said to have been killed in the French shelling of Haiphong in 1946. No archive of this war's dead by name was surveyed in this pass.

sources.title: The First Vietnam War: Colonial Conflict and Cold War Crisis (Cambridge University Press, 2021)
Death-toll compilation for wars and atrocities of the twentieth century (page for tolls of 300,000 and over)

events.name: Malagasy Uprising

toll.text: Estimates run from about 10,000 killed in fighting to over 100,000. Global Voices reports a French historian putting those killed at no more than 10,000, with 20,000-30,000 more dying of hunger or disease in rebel-held areas; Wikipedia cites the same historian for 30,000-40,000 in total, about 30,000 of them violent. The colonial administration counted 11,342 'known dead' in 1950. The French government's first official estimate was 89,000, and the High Commissioner later said over 100,000, counting people who fled into the forest.
toll.note: Low is the lower figure for those killed in fighting; high is the High Commissioner's later 'over 100,000', which includes deaths from starvation and exhaustion.

events.says: Nationalist revolt against French colonial rule in Madagascar in 1947-48, put down by French forces.
events.open: The gap between about 10,000 and over 100,000 turns on whether deaths from hunger, disease and flight into the forest are counted, and on the 1946-49 population trend, which a French historian argues shows no loss on the scale of the high figures. Another view is that malaria control hid the loss. Many Malagasy hold that even the high figures understate the dead. The French side lost about 550 nationals, of whom 350 were soldiers, per Wikipedia citing Le Monde (1989), and 1,900 Malagasy auxiliaries. No archive of this war's dead by name was surveyed in this pass.

sources.title: In Madagascar, People Remember One of the Deadliest French Colonial Wars in History (translated from French, 9 April 2017)

events.name: Indian annexation of Hyderabad (Operation Polo)

toll.text: A committee appointed by the Indian prime minister (the Sunderlal Committee, reported 1949) estimated that at least 27,000 to 40,000 people lost their lives during and after the police action, mostly Muslim civilians. Other observers, cited by Wikipedia from a 1950 account and a later study, put the dead at 200,000 or more. Wikipedia gives 807 Hyderabad State soldiers and 1,373 Razakars killed, and fewer than 10 Indian soldiers.
toll.note: Low is the committee's lower figure; high is the figure given by observers cited in Wikipedia and is not documented.

events.says: Indian military action against the princely state of Hyderabad in September 1948, called a police action by India, followed by communal violence during and after the operation.
events.open: The committee's figure is described in Wikipedia as a very conservative estimate, and the full report is held at a Delhi library. The 200,000 figure rests on unnamed observers. The 27,000-40,000 figure covers deaths 'during and after' the action, not battle deaths alone. No archive of this war's dead by name was surveyed in this pass.

sources.title: Integration of Hyderabad 1948: India's long-suppressed massacre (17 September 2015, updated 2020)

events.name: Jeju uprising and its suppression

toll.text: South Korea's national truth committee (2003) counted 14,373 civilian victims, 86 percent of them killed by security forces and 14 percent by insurgents, and a total of up to 30,000 dead including combatants. A Cornell University Press study (2014) gives about 30,000, around 10 percent of the island's 1947 population. Other estimates are 60,000 (the island's governor at the time, as reported in a 2010 history), 80,000 (the same history) and 100,000 (a 2017 reference).
toll.note: Low is the committee's count of named civilian victims; high is the highest published estimate, which rests on no stated count.

events.says: Armed uprising on Jeju island in 1948 against the authorities of southern Korea, followed by suppression by security forces; the truth committee dates the violence from March 1947 to September 1954.
events.open: The committee's 14,373 is a count of reported victims, not an estimate of all deaths. Wikipedia's infobox also lists 189 'killed' (unexplained) and 1,091 combatants killed (162 soldiers, 289 police, 640 militia). Wikidata holds several values for deaths, from 4,000 to 100,000. In 2003 the president apologised for the state's role. No archive of this war's dead by name was surveyed in this pass.

sources.title: The Massacres at Mt. Halla: Sixty Years of Truth Seeking in South Korea (Cornell University Press, 2014)
The Lesser Multicides of the Twentieth Century (death-toll compilation, 2010)

events.name: La Violencia

toll.text: A 2019 study of death registers by the Banco de la Republica (Cuadernos de Historia Economica no. 50) estimates 57,737 violent deaths for 1949-58 (39,142 on conservative assumptions) and up to 113,032 for 1949-66. Older figures are far higher: about 200,000 (a commonly repeated figure), about 300,000 for 1945-66, and about 400,000 for 1948-56. Necrometrics lists 180,000 through 1958 (Clodfelter) and 200,000 to 300,000.
toll.note: Low is the register-based central estimate for 1949-58; high is the highest older estimate, which has no stated method.

events.says: Period of partisan civil violence in Colombia from 1948 to 1958, following the assassination of the Liberal leader Jorge Eliecer Gaitan in April 1948.
events.open: Sources disagree on the start (1946, 1948 or 1949), the end (1958 or 1966) and on whether deaths were political. Records were incomplete. The Banco de la Republica authors note that few studies had questioned the origin of the older figures. Wikipedia's infobox lists 200,000 civilians (1947-60) with no source.

events.name: Korean War

toll.text: Estimates of all deaths run from about 1.9 million (military only) to 3.5 million. A compilation of 20th-century reference works lists 2,454,000 (Compton's), 2,854,000 (Britannica), 3,000,000 and 3,062,000 (Rummel), and 3.5 million including 2 to 3 million civilians (Lewy). Wikipedia lists South Korea 137,899 dead, North Korea 294,151-316,579 dead, China 183,108-197,653 dead and 1.6-3 million civilians, and the UN side about 210,000 dead and missing, of whom the United States 36,515.
toll.note: Low and high are the lowest and highest totals for all dead, civilians and soldiers together, in the compilation.

events.says: War that began with the North Korean invasion of South Korea in June 1950, in which the United States led a United Nations force on the South's side and China fought for the North, ending in 1953.
events.open: Civilian deaths dominate the total and are poorly counted; the compilation shows the same war's South Korean civilian dead ranging from 315,000 to more than 760,000, and North Korean civilian dead from 1,000,000 to 1,185,000. Military figures differ on whether the missing are counted as dead. The infobox UN total (about 210,000) does not equal the sum of its listed parts.

events.name: Myanmar conflict (civil wars since 1948)

toll.text: A 2008 BMJ survey study estimated 31,000 violent war deaths in Burma for 1955-2002 (95 percent interval 17,000-51,000), against 37,000 in the Uppsala/PRIO database. Necrometrics lists 32,714 (Clodfelter), 20,000-40,000 (1991 atlas), 127,000 (Rummel, 1948-87, including state killings) and 140,000 (1949-95), and 100,000 Karen civilians and rebels for 1949-2001. Wikipedia's infobox gives 180,000 or more for the whole conflict without a source I could read. Wikipedia, citing ACLED, gives about 11,000 killed from February to December 2021, after the military seized power.
toll.note: Low is the survey estimate for 1955-2002 only. High is Wikipedia's infobox total for 1948 onward; it has no readable source and is higher than any figure above.

events.says: A set of overlapping armed conflicts in Myanmar between the central government and ethnic armed groups and communist insurgents since independence in 1948, followed from 2021 by a nationwide armed resistance to the military's seizure of power.
events.open: No source gives a total for 1948 to date. Survey and database estimates for the 1955-2002 period are far below the infobox figure, and counts differ on whether deaths of civilians at the hands of the state are war deaths. The post-2021 fighting is still being counted. The 1988 uprising killed about 350 (authorities) or over 3,000 (The Economist). No archive of this war's dead by name was surveyed in this pass.
